20463-three-years-on-the-plains-observat:
Three Years on the Plains records observations of Native peoples on the American frontier between 1867 and 1870. The writer spent those years where settlers, soldiers, and tribes met in uneasy contact. His contents page asks plain questions, starting with where the Indians came from.

His letters are blunt about policy. To friendly tribes he would give what they ask. To those who chose war, his answer was war until they were satisfied. The book preserves a frontiersman's views in his own harsh words, useful now as evidence of the attitudes that drove events on the plains.
archidoxorvm-avreoli-ph-theophrasti-para: Archidoxa Avreoli Ph, theophrasti paracelci, 1570, the paracelsian archidoxes. This book preserves that work. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
arxiv-2512-00570:
Loop equations tie the behavior of gauge theories to the averages of closed loops of field lines. Hao Shen, Scott Andrew Smith, and Rongchan Zhu derive Makeenko-Migdal equations for lattice Yang-Mills-Higgs theory in 2025. The structure groups covered include the special orthogonal, unitary, and special unitary families.

Adding a Higgs field to the pure Yang-Mills setting creates several new operations in the equations. These master loop equations organize infinitely many relations into one framework that computations can use. They serve probability and mathematical physics, where lattice gauge theory is a testing ground for rigorous quantum field theory. The Higgs field adds mass-giving structure that pure gauge theory lacks.
arxiv-2512-00670:
Diffusion language models refine their answers through many denoising steps, but the answer often stabilizes early. Sebastian Stich and co-authors propose EDIT in 2025, an early termination method for diffusion model inference. The name stands for early diffusion inference termination.

EDIT stops denoising adaptively once the reasoning is stable enough relative to training-time behavior, judged from the dynamics of training gradients. Stopping early saves computation on every query without retraining the model. As diffusion models enter production, such inference-time savings compound into major cost and energy reductions. Diffusion language models are a newer rival to the autoregressive models most people know. Stability relative to training behavior gives the stopping rule its reference point. For firms that serve such models, the gain is plain cash and watts. Each cut step is time and power saved, on each call, all day, at full scale.
arxiv-2512-00970:
Kiran Adhikari studies secret sharing in quantum systems in a 2025 paper. Quantum information scrambling spreads a localized piece of information across a whole system, hiding it from anyone who can see only part. That spreading is tied to chaos in quantum systems and even to black hole models.

Adhikari uses Haar scrambling, a random mixing process, to build quantum ramp secret sharing. In ramp schemes, partial shares reveal partial information, balancing security against efficiency. Scrambling-based schemes could protect quantum data across many parties. The work links a deep dynamical idea, how information hides, to a concrete cryptographic task.
arxiv-2512-01270:
Yuan-Sen Ting and co-authors built a tool that can measure lines in star light on its own. Star spectra have dips where atoms soak up light. The width of each dip tells how much of an element is present. Doing this by hand for many stars is slow work.

Their tool, called Egent, fits each dip with a set of smooth curves. A large language model then looks at each fit and checks it. The model can shift the fit range, add parts for mixed lines, or flag a bad fit. The loop of fit, check, and fix runs with no human help.
arxiv-2512-01370:
Medha Sawhney and co-authors speed up diffusion solvers for physics equations. These solvers guide each step with the leftover error of the equation. That guide needs slow gradient work at test time. It can also wobble when the error signal is noisy.

The team uses the error in a new way. They treat it as a form of attention in the frequency domain. That lets the solver adapt its steps on the fly. It skips the slow guide loop as well. Faster, steadier solvers help engineers run many what-if tests on flows, heat, and stress.
arxiv-2512-01570:
Stephan Druskat and Lars Grunske present a data set on open research software. Much lab work now makes software as it goes. That software is key to results, yet it is hard to track. Open references to it are scattered.

Their set, OpenDORS, gathers openly referenced research software in one place. Each entry is tied to its public reference. Scholars can study how research software spreads and lasts. Funders and labs can spot which tools merit long-term support. The set turns scattered mentions into a base for policy. Each record keeps its source link, so users can trace a software claim back to the paper or page that cited it first.
arxiv-2512-02070:
Forecasting far ahead is hard: transformer models capture long-range patterns but grow costly and overfit sparse data, while lean linear models miss local twists. Qianyang Li and three co-authors propose DPWMixer in 2025, a dual-path design for long-term time series forecasting that tries to keep both strengths.

The mixer's two paths divide the labor, with wavelet analysis supplying a multi-scale view of the signal's ups and downs. Wavelets are well suited to separating slow trends from quick local wiggles, the very dynamics linear models flatten. The design aims at forecasts that stay accurate over long horizons without the transformer's quadratic price tag.
arxiv-2512-02270:
Testing whether a robotic vehicle is safe means hunting for the rare inputs that make it fail, and full simulations are too heavy to search at scale. Nazmus Shakib Sayom and Luis Garcia propose in 2025 a method that strips a system down to only the parts a safety property cares about.

From that reduction they build lightweight surrogate models that keep the property-relevant behavior and drop unrelated complexity. Falsification then runs through trace analysis checked by temporal logic oracles, which flag violations of the stated property. Scalable falsification could let engineers probe far more scenarios before a robotic vehicle ever meets a road.
arxiv-2512-02470:
Maitri Ganguli and Diptiman Sen study a chain of particles whose links switch back and forth in set patterns. Their model is the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain, a standard test bed for how electrons hop between sites. Two switching rules take turns, and they differ in how strongly particles hop between cells.

The pair applies the two rules in three ways: in a steady rhythm, in an almost rhythm, and at random. Each pattern can push the chain into different states with different edge behavior. Comparing the three cases shows how the timing of a drive, not just its strength, shapes a quantum material. The three drives act like three clocks that can clash with or match each other.
arxiv-2512-02570:
Fred Diamond and Shu Sasaki attach Galois symmetries to a broad class of modular forms. Hilbert modular forms live over a totally real number field and act as higher cousins of classical modular forms. Reducing them modulo a prime gives forms on varieties in prime characteristic.

For any Hecke eigenform, of any weight, the authors prove a matching two dimensional Galois representation exists. Such links between analysis and symmetry are the heart of the Langlands program. Extending them to prime characteristic widens the tools for studying number fields and their hidden structures. All weights at once is the strong form of the claim, and it is the form peer work can build on next.
arxiv-2512-02670:
Connor Evans, Zinaida A. Lykova, and N. J. Young develop theory for holomorphic functions on a two variable domain. The domain is the symmetrized skew bidisc, built from pairs of points in the unit disc. The functions studied stay bounded by one in modulus throughout the domain.

Model theory for such functions links algebra, geometry, and interpolation questions. Results here extend methods long used on the disc and bidisc to this skewed setting. Progress on these domains feeds operator theory and control, where bounded analytic functions describe stable systems and their limits. Odd domains test the tools of the trade, and tools that pass here tend to hold up on plain ones too.
arxiv-2512-02870:
Zhaoqing Wang and co-authors teach video generators to obey a moving camera with rewards checked against geometry. Camera controlled generation has improved fast with video diffusion models. Most methods, though, rely only on supervised fine tuning, leaving reinforcement learning post training largely unexplored.

Their framework applies online reinforcement learning to a pretrained generator. A verifiable geometry reward scores how well the video follows the planned camera path. Precise camera obedience matters for film previsualization, games, and simulation, where the shot must match a director's plan exactly. A score can be checked by hand, frame by frame. That turns a vague hope for good shots into a mark a team can train to hit.
arxiv-2512-03070:
Grouping mixed data is a key task in the big data age. Guillaume Guerard and Sonia Djebali survey the field in this 2025 work. Data now arrive in huge amounts, at high speed, and in many forms, both numbers and labels.

The survey maps the main methods and the hard parts that remain. Mixed sets are tough because numbers and labels do not compare in the same way. A clear map of the field helps new researchers pick sound tools. It also shows firms where current methods may fail on their own mixed data. Newcomers to clustering can use the survey to learn key terms before choosing a method.
arxiv-2512-03170:
Some spacetimes leak energy through their edges. Robert McNees and Céline Zwikel build charges for such cases in this 2025 work. They study four-dimensional spacetimes with a nonzero cosmological constant, like de Sitter and anti-de Sitter space.

Their method includes charges that are not conserved because the boundary leaks. It also includes charges tied to corner terms where boundaries meet. The charges stay finite for any boundary conditions, they show. New charges appear for a wider class of field setups, aiding gravity research. Leaky charges reflect real physics, where fields cross borders rather than staying boxed in.
arxiv-2512-03270:
Thin sheets wrinkle and fold in ways that are hard to model. Yael Cohen, Animesh Pandey, Yafei Zhang, Cy Maor, and Michael Moshe offer a new formulation in this 2025 work. Such sheets range from graphene to biological membranes.

Standard weakly nonlinear theories need small slopes and fail when deflections grow large, even if strain stays small. The authors use a curvature potential formulation for thin elastic sheets. A better theory could predict folding in soft materials and tissues. It may also guide design of flexible devices. Graphene and cell membranes both punish weak theories, since their deflections grow large fast.
arxiv-2512-03670:
Vuong Bui and Matthieu Rosenfeld prove a theorem about avoiding repeated patterns in words built from changing alphabets. A cube is the same block written three times in a row, and cube-free words dodge it forever. Their 2025 paper lets every position draw from its own two-letter alphabet.

Whatever sequence of binary alphabets is chosen, an infinite cube-free word respecting them always exists. Counting arguments show such words are plentiful, growing exponentially with length. Better still, when the alphabet sequence is computable, one of these words is computable too. Its nth letter can be produced in time polynomial in n, turning an existence proof into an algorithm.
arxiv-2512-03770:
How a crowd reaches consensus is a classic puzzle in the study of collective behaviour. Xingyu Guo, Xiaoyang Wang, and Lingxiao Wang give the puzzle a quantum twist in a 2025 preprint on social physics. They build models of opinion dynamics that run on quantum hardware available today, using superposition, measurement collapse, and entanglement as modelling ingredients.

Unlike many quantum proposals, their models can be solved exactly, which makes the results interpretable. The framework lets the authors vary network connectivity in a controlled way and watch how consensus formation responds. They demonstrate the approach with practical quantum circuits. Representative cases were validated on IBM Quantum devices for a simple open chain of agents. The authors see the work as an opening for quantum-enhanced social modelling on near-term machines, aimed at complex systems where classical simulation struggles.
arxiv-2512-04070:
Quark-gluon plasma, the soup of particles filling the infant universe, can also be set spinning in theory, and rotation changes its thermodynamics. V. Braguta and colleagues compute those changes from first principles in a 2025 lattice gauge theory preprint. Using numerical simulations of SU(3) Yang-Mills theory, the pure-gluon version of the strong force, they track free energy and angular momentum across temperatures.

The response to slow rotation is organised as a series in angular velocity. Its leading term is a specific moment of inertia; the next is a specific deformation. Both surprise: just above the phase transition, they come out negative. At higher temperatures the deformation turns positive. The calculations span a broad temperature range and several boundary conditions, giving phenomenologists firm numbers instead of model guesses.
arxiv-2601-06770:
Sofiia Huraka and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers structure-preserving learning and prediction in optimal control of collective motion. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. Wide-spread adoption of unmanned vehicle technologies requires the ability to predict the motion of the combined vehicle operation from observations.

While the general prediction of such motion for an arbitrary control mechanism is difficult. For a particular choice of control, the dynamics reduces to the Lie-Poisson equations [ 33 , 34 ]. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-06970:
José de Brito and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers splitting proximal point algorithms for the sum of Prox-Convex functions. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. -34.14322pt Abstract The work addresses the minimization of a finite sum of prox-convex functions under Lipschitz continuity of each component. The authors propose two variants of the splitting proximal point algorithms proposed in [ 2.

5 ] : one deterministic with a fixed update order. And one stochastic with random sampling, and we extend them from convex to prox-convex functions. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07570:
Mitali Mondal reports predictions from the EPOS4 model for lead-lead collisions at a new energy. The 2026 preprint concerns the quark-gluon plasma, a hot state where nuclear matter comes apart into its basic parts. Heavy-ion experiments at the Large Hadron Collider study this plasma. Run 3 of the collider reached a center-of-mass energy of 5.36 TeV per nucleon pair.

Models like EPOS4 predict what detectors should see before data are analyzed. Global observables summarize each collision as a whole rather than tracking single particles. Comparing predictions with measurements tests how well the model captures plasma behavior. Mondal's paper supplies those reference predictions for the new energy. Heavy-ion physicists use such benchmarks to spot where models and reality part ways.
arxiv-2601-07670:
Javier Rubio proposes a new way to create dark matter just after the universe's inflationary burst. His 2026 preprint describes gravitational production driven by curvature-induced tachyonic instabilities. Tachyonic growth means small ripples grow explosively rather than oscillate. The framework uses a real spectator scalar field, one that watches inflation without driving it. That field couples quadratically to invariants of spacetime curvature.

Most earlier work used non-minimal couplings between fields and gravity. Rubio departs from that route deliberately. A purely gravitational production channel is attractive because it needs few new assumptions. If it works, dark matter could arise from gravity and curvature alone. The paper speaks to cosmologists building dark matter origin stories. It adds a fresh mechanism to compare with freeze-out and other standard ideas.
arxiv-2601-08070:
Shailesh Rana studies a simple sounding test that large language models keep failing. His 2026 arXiv paper looks at negative constraints, such as telling a model not to use a given word. Models break such rules with striking regularity, and the reasons have stayed poorly understood.

Rana presents a broad mechanistic study of why negative instructions fail. The title names the effect a semantic gravity well, where the banned word pulls the model toward itself. For readers who build or test language models, the paper gives a clearer picture of a basic instruction-following flaw. It treats the failure as a mechanism to explain, not just an error rate to report.
arxiv-2601-08770:
Sean Siddens and a team from four sites study a hidden leak in chips that run many tasks at once. Chips may swap the order of read and write steps to gain speed. That swap can be seen by a foe who times the chip with care. Past tests made this leak show up by stressing the chip hard.

The team shows the leak can work with no timer and less stress than once thought. The order swaps leave a trace that a smart test can pick up. That trace can cross from one task to a next task on the same chip. A reader who guards chip work gets a clear risk note. Calm use, not just hard stress, can let order leaks show.
arxiv-2601-09070:
Ayumu Shoshi and six co-authors report rings and gaps in a disk round a young star named CrA IRS 2. The star is of Class I, still young and wrapped in fall in stuff. The ALMA scope saw the disk at fine scale. Such rings in old disks hint at new planets. In a young disk, they may show a more early start to world birth.

The team ties the rings to a flux driven bubble in the disk. Field flux can blow a bubble that sweeps gas to a ring. That path needs no planet to start the ring. A reader in star birth gets an early disk with form. It hints that disk shape work starts young, by more than one road.
arxiv-2601-09170:
Dung Ta Nguyen Duc and five co-authors build a lean tool to spot rice leaf ills on a phone. Rice feeds half the world, so leaf ills can cut food for a vast set of folk. Early spots save a crop. But farm zones oft have weak phones and no net. A tool must be small, fast, and true on a plain phone shot.

Their tool is N-EIoU-YOLOv9. Its core is a new box fit loss that weighs hard cases with care. The loss splits shape facts so a box can fit a long or round spot well. A reader in farm tech gets a phone fit spot tool, built for fields, not labs.
arxiv-2601-09670:
Nasser M. Ahmed reports a new star cluster found beside a known one. His 2026 arXiv paper uses Gaia DR3 data to study the region around the Czernik 38 cluster. An earlier study by the same author examined Czernik 38 in detail.

The new cluster sits 32 arcminutes from Czernik 38's center. Its position is given with tight error bars in both sky coordinates. A companion cluster so close may share an origin with its neighbor. The paper also discusses a complex tide linked to the pair, hinting at how the two clusters pull on each other.
arxiv-2601-09770:
Chen Chen and six co-authors give interface agents eyes that choose where to look. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents GUI-Eyes, a reinforcement learning framework for active visual perception in graphical interfaces. Vision-language models have advanced GUI automation, but most still take one static screenshot.

A passive agent cannot zoom, re-check, or look at the right moment. GUI-Eyes learns when, whether, and how to observe the screen. Active looking should ground clicks and typing in what is actually shown. That promises fewer blind errors in agents that book, buy, and fill forms.
arxiv-2601-10370:
Jian-Wen Peng, Jun-Jie Luo, and Abubakar Adamu solve balance tasks in a Hilbert space. Such tasks ask for a point where no move can gain. They span games, flows, and best fit tasks. The cost rule here is quasi monotone, a weak form of a known rule.

The team give a two step method with a drift term. Step sizes set them in two ways. One is self tuned. One is of Armijo type, checked by a line search. They prove the path still lands on a solve point. They do so with no bound on how fast the cost can shift.
arxiv-2601-10670:
Archita Gupta, Tejbir Lohan, and Pooja Singla study characters of two matrix groups over local rings. The groups are GL2 and GU2, built from two-by-two matrices. The base ring comes from a non-archimedean local field, cut down modulo powers of its maximal ideal. The residue field has odd characteristic, a standing assumption in the work.

The authors sort out which characters are real-valued and which conjugacy classes are real. Such questions sound narrow, but they shape how representations of the groups behave. Real characters link to symmetry inside the group's own structure. The results serve representation theorists who work with groups over local rings, a key case in number theory.
arxiv-2601-10770:
Runyuan Cai, Yu Lin, Yiming Wang, Chunlin Fu, and Xiaodong Zeng present GPA, a single speech model for many tasks. Speech systems have long used separate models for text-to-speech, speech recognition, and voice conversion. Split pipelines limit scale, efficiency, and transfer between tasks. GPA instead uses autoregressive transformers for all three jobs at once.

The name plays on the school grade average: the goal is solid results across all audio subjects. One shared model can pool what each task teaches the others. Recognition may sharpen synthesis, and conversion may sharpen both. The work speaks to teams that want one speech engine for products instead of three narrow ones.
arxiv-2601-10870:
Guo-Niu Han and Lihong Yang add a doubly refined count of alternating sign matrices. These matrices, filled with zeros, ones, and minus ones under strict rules, have a famous counting story. The alternating sign matrix conjecture of Mills, Robbins, and Rumsey, from 1982, was proved by Zeilberger and by Kuperberg. Since then, refined counts that track extra parameters have been a steady pursuit.

Behrend and co-authors reached a quadruply refined enumeration by adding parameters. Han and Yang give yet another doubly refined version. Each refinement tests how deep the pattern runs. These counts tie into statistical physics and combinatorics, where the same numbers count ice-type models and plane partitions.
arxiv-2601-10970:
Canwen Wang and co-authors model couples therapy with a multi-agent simulation. Couples therapy helps partners resolve conflict and grow closer. Training new therapists leans on textbooks and roleplay. Those tools often miss the complexity and emotional nuance of real couple dynamics. A simulator could let trainees practice against lifelike partners and a therapist agent.

The system is multimodal and multi-agent, modeling multi-party interaction in the therapy room. Each party is played by an agent with its own stance. Trainees can face hard moments safely and repeat them. The work speaks to clinical training and to the wider study of how AI can model delicate human interaction without putting real couples at risk.
arxiv-2601-11170:
Web crawling for South Slavic tongues is the topic of this 2026 preprint. The authors are not named in the record held here. Their team built the CLASSLA-web text sets by crawling whole country domains. That method works well for tongues with few digital texts.

An early round of crawling gave the largest sets yet for this group. Those sets were called CLASSLA-web 1.0 in the first release. The new work looks at a fresh round of crawling, named 2.0. It weighs what repeat crawls add in new text. It also weighs the costs and flaws that come with each new round.
arxiv-2601-12270:
Reshabh K Sharma, Dan Grossman, and David Kohlbrenner build a compiler defence against a new class of side channels. Classic side channels leak secrets via unsafe instructions, memory access, or branch choices. Constant-time code rules block those patterns and are in wide use.

Data memory-dependent prefetchers open a fresh leak path that those rules miss. Their tool, named in the work, splits secrets at compile time to block that path. A compiler fix can guard much code at once. The work is in systems security.  The defence is built in at compile time for all runs.
arxiv-2601-12670:
Yuxuan Du and five co authors hunt for exotic dibaryon states in nuclear physics. A dibaryon is a system of two baryons bound or resonant together. The famous deuteron is the simplest case, made of a proton and a neutron. The team look for deuteron like states with one bottom quark and set values of strangeness.

They work inside the chiral quark model, a standard frame for such searches. They study strangeness values of minus one, minus three, and minus five. Their scattering calculations yield two resonance states at strangeness minus one. Predicted states give experiments a target to confirm or rule out. The work adds to the map of exotic hadronic matter.
arxiv-2601-12870:
Lazlo Bleker and five co authors present Text2Structure3D, a model that generates structures from text prompts. The model is graph based and aims at equilibrium structures, designs that balance their loads. It supports intuitive design exploration in the conceptual phase of structural design. Engineers could sketch ideas in words and see candidate forms at once.

The approach combines latent diffusion with a variational graph auto encoder and graph transformers. It generates structural graphs close to an equilibrium state. Close matters, since a pretty form that cannot stand is useless. Their work was published in an engineering results journal. Generative tools like this may reshape early stage design work.
arxiv-2601-13170:
David Lipshutz and Robert J. Lipshutz prove calm for a self sorting neural net. Real brain nets reshape their own links by local rules. One rule grows links that fire in sync, a Hebbian step. Its twin shrinks such links, an anti Hebbian step. How local steps yield sound whole net acts is still open.

An past model used both steps to do principal subspace work, a way to find the main axes of data spread. But no one had shown that the bent link flows stay calm from all starts. The pair now prove that whole calm. For brain and learning staff, the proof firms up a model of how nets can sort data on their own.
arxiv-2601-13270:
Matteo Acclavio and Roberto Maieli join two tools that rarely meet, Bayes nets and logic code. A Bayes net maps how chance facts lean on each other. It is a stock tool for chance sense. To fold it in a logic code frame is hard, since the net's web is rich.

Their tongue is called probLO. It grows the LO tongue of Andreoli and Pareschi, built on linear objects. In it a Bayes net can be both stated and run as code. That join lets chance sums be run by proof steps. For AI and logic staff, the work opens a path where chance nets gain the clear rules of logic code.
arxiv-2601-13470:
Gabriel Avanzi Ubiali, Jose Carlos Marinello Filho, and Taufik Abrao share the load of a huge antenna array for 6G nets. Extra large MIMO uses vast antenna grids to give fast links with even grade. Its resource work is huge if it leans on fresh channel reads for each pick.

The team picks three things at once. They pick which subarrays to use, which users to serve, and which pilots to assign. They give closed form marks for signal to noise plus clash in both central and spread uplink forms. Closed forms let picks be made with no fresh full reads. For 6G teams, that cut is what makes huge grids real.
arxiv-2601-13570:
Tingting Dan, Jiaqi Ding, and Guorong Wu model brain acts with a geometric state space net on curved manifolds. State space models track how hid neural states shift over time and yield the signals we read. Deep nets add flex to that frame. Pairs of the two have fit brain scan data well.

Brain state spaces are not flat, though. Their true shape bends, as on a Riemannian manifold. The team's net, GeoDynamics, holds states on such a curved space by build. That build may fit brain paths that a flat model warps. For brain teams, a model whose space matches the data's shape can read acts with less twist.
arxiv-2601-13870:
Yanbing Zhang, Ruifeng Yuan, Liyan Luo, and Lei Wu speed up simulations of rarefied gas flows in 2026. Rarefied gas is thin gas where wall effects rule the flow. Heat-flux boundary conditions are hard to apply in a fast way. The wall-reflected gas temperature and density must be found as the computation runs.

Their work sits in the general synthetic iterative scheme, or GSIS. That scheme solves the Boltzmann kinetic equation in an outer loop. Macroscopic synthetic equations run in an inner loop. An efficient heat-flux treatment could cut cost for aerospace and vacuum work.
arxiv-2601-14270:
Liangming Pan and a team at Peking University survey a young field in this 2026 paper. Large language models can solve problems that take many reasoning steps. Yet the inner workings behind that skill stay unclear. Past surveys mostly cover engineering tricks that raise scores. This one takes a distinct path.

The survey maps the mechanisms inside multi-step reasoning. It asks what parts of the model do the work, and how. The title calls this opening the black box. For readers, the paper offers one full view of what is known so far. It sorts a fast-growing set of studies into a clear frame.
arxiv-2601-14370:
Alessandro Trinca and six co-authors study the first giant black holes in this 2026 paper. Supermassive black holes appear very early in the universe. Their rapid emergence challenges current models of black hole growth. One proposed path is the direct collapse black hole scenario. In it, gas in pristine, low-metallicity halos forms supermassive stars first.

Those stars then collapse into massive black hole seeds, under specific environmental conditions. The team hunts such objects around high-redshift quasars. Their focus is both formation and detectability: how these seeds arise, and whether telescopes could spot them. Readers get a guide to one leading answer to the early giants problem.
arxiv-2601-14470:
Mohamad Salim, Jasmine Latendresse, SayedHassan Khatoonabadi, and Emad Shihab count token use in AI coding teams in this 2026 paper. LLM-based multi-agent systems now automate complex software engineering tasks. The work spans requirements engineering, code generation, and testing. Yet their operational efficiency and resource use stay poorly understood.

That gap hinders practical adoption, since costs and environmental impact are unpredictable. Tokenomics, the authors' term, quantifies where tokens are used in agentic software engineering. Tokens are the text units models read and write, and each one costs money and compute. Readers get a breakdown of where the spend goes when agent teams build software.
arxiv-2601-14570:
Xiaojie Yang and six co-authors forecast crowds at a world expo in this 2026 paper. Accurate forecasting of daily attendance is vital for managing transportation, crowd flows, and services at large-scale international events. Their case is Expo 2025 Osaka, Kansai, Japan. Existing approaches often rely on multi-source external data, such as weather, traffic, and social media, to improve accuracy.

That reliance often leads to unreliable results, because the available historical data are insufficient. The team's study is an empirical attendance predictive study, as its title says. Its subtitle is Place with Intention. The team kept the plan lean. It works with the kind of data a host can get in real life. Readers get a forecast method tested on a real mega-event, built to work when rich side data cannot be trusted.
arxiv-2601-14770:
Tobias Raichle, Erfan Amini, and Bin Yang adapt speech enhancement at test time in this 2026 paper. Adapting speech enhancement models to unseen environments is crucial for practical deployments. Speech enhancement removes noise from recordings. Test-time adaptation for it remains largely under-explored, though. A lack of understanding of how these models degrade under domain shifts is one cause.

The team observes that mask-based enhancement models lose confidence under domain shifts. Their predicted masks become flattened, losing decisive speech preservation and noise suppression. Their method works via mask polarization, pushing masks back toward firm decisions. Readers get an adaptation scheme that fixes a named failure mode, not just a score.
arxiv-2601-15270:
Hirotaka Onuki studies smooth surfaces over a ring that mixes two worlds of arithmetic. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with regular del Pezzo surfaces in mixed characteristic. The base ring is the Witt vectors over a closed field of prime characteristic above two.

The surface sits inside a flat, projective three-fold over that ring. Its anticanonical sheaf, a key bundle for this class of surfaces, is ample. Onuki proves a global regularity result for these surfaces. The plus sign in the title marks the strong form of that global regularity claim.
arxiv-2601-15370:
Maciej Kilian, Oleg Mkrtchyan, and co-authors stack two kinds of sparsity to make expert models cheaper. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with mixture-of-experts layers. Weight sparsity is their usual trick: each token wakes only a few experts.

Data sparsity is the mirror trick: each expert handles only a few tokens. Expert-choice routing does this, but it breaks causality in autoregressive models. Training and inference then mismatch. The authors compose both sparsities in one design. The aim is much better compute efficiency without the causal flaw sneaking back in at inference time.
arxiv-2601-15670:
Fan Gao and Runze Wang study representations of covering groups in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their objects are genuine Iwahori-spherical representations of central covers. Each carries positive real Satake parameters. For these, they prove an upper bound for geometric wavefront sets. The bound was formulated for general genuine representations in earlier work by Gao and co-authors. Wavefront sets measure the size and shape of a representation in geometric terms.

The pair also show the bound is sharp in key cases. Equality holds for covers of type A groups. It also holds for some representations of covers of exceptional groups. An upper bound plus cases of equality gives a firm picture. Representation theorists use such results to classify and compare representations.
arxiv-2601-15770:
Jue Xu and four co-authors mimic quantum motion on normal computers in a 2026 arXiv paper. Clean quantum dynamics are hard to mimic. Tensor-network methods slow down as entanglement grows and fills the system. Pauli-truncation methods cope, but they lean on noise or chance. Neither fits clean, quiet dynamics well. The team proposes the Low-weight Pauli Dynamics algorithm, or LPD. It tracks local observables for short-time dynamics with no noise.

Local observables are what most tests in the lab measure. A fast classical method for them helps check quantum hardware. It also lets theorists test ideas with no quantum device at hand. The title stresses that the method uses no randomness. Fixed, repeatable methods are easier to check and reproduce. In benchmarking disputes, that is a real virtue.
arxiv-2601-16470:
Yonatan Ashenafi lifts state space to a high size to track wild chance paths. His 2026 preprint deals with Bayes grain tracks of chance moves. Wild curves in the move maths make tracks hard to keep true. Grains spread, clump or miss the true path in such cases. Ashenafi maps the wild model to a high size straight model.

The map can be turned back, so no facts are lost. Straight Gauss form in high size is far more easy to track. Tracks then hold true through wild bends in the path. Firm tracks serve drive, flight and fund path tools. The work gives a fresh frame for hard tracks.
arxiv-2601-16570:
Leonardo Zambrano and three coauthors certify quantum traits with flawed reads. Their 2026 preprint deals with checks that a state is as claimed. Such checks back all claims made for quantum gear. Reads in real labs are never free of flaws. Past proofs oft take reads as if they were exact.

The team gives a proof path that takes read flaws in count. It works for bent sums of state traits, a wide class. Flaw aware proofs keep claims true on real lab data. They stop teams from claims that rest on false exact reads. The work firms up quantum gear checks.
arxiv-2601-16670:
André Brandão, Diogo Matos, Miguel Guimarães, Simão Cunha, and João Saraiva look at the energy cost of code. Their 2026 preprint centers on Lua, a small and loved script tongue. World plans urge cuts in the carbon cost of tech. The tongue a program uses shapes its power draw. Tongues that run line by line tend to use more power.

Fast tongues like C sip power by contrast. Lua trades speed for ease and small size. The authors weigh that trade with care. They ask what the green cost of Lua truly is. Their work can guide teams that want light code. It also feeds the wider push for clean tech.
arxiv-2601-17270:
Max McKinnon, Samir Khaki, Chandan KA Reddy, and William Huang test voice activity detectors. These tools tell speech from silence in audio. They feed speech recognition and many voice apps. The team asks a plain design question. How much does window size change detector accuracy? Window size is the span of sound judged at once.

They test three known detectors: Silero, WebRTC, and a root mean square method. Tests run on varied real-world audio streams. They also try hysteresis, a trick that stops fast on-off flicker. Clear answers help builders pick settings with proof, not habit. Small choices here shape how well voice tools hear real speech.
arxiv-2601-17470:
Chia-Ming Lee and five co-authors present PhaSR, a method to remove shadows from images. Shadow removal must split light effects from true surface color. That split fails when physical priors are off line. PhaSR aligns priors at two levels. It aims for robust work from one light source to many. Ambient light from mixed sources is the hard end.

Aligned priors keep colors true once shadows lift. Bad removal can bleach or tint a scene. Good removal aids photo tools, robots, and self-driving sight. The dual-level design targets the root cause, not just the look. It gives vision systems cleaner inputs under real light.
arxiv-2601-17570:
Hadi Salloum and three co-authors speed up Monte Carlo reinforcement learning. That method learns from sampled episodes of play. It suffers high sample complexity. Sparse rewards, large state spaces, and correlated paths make it worse. The authors reformulate episode selection as a QUBO problem. QUBO is quadratic unconstrained binary optimization, a compact math form.

Quantum-inspired samplers then solve that selection problem. Picking the right episodes should cut wasted learning. Each episode costs time and compute to run. Smarter picks mean faster training for the same budget. The work joins quantum-style optimization with classic learning. It treats data choice as an optimization task in itself.
arxiv-2601-18070:
Jinwu Chen and co-authors tune a chip design that computes inside its own memory. Their 2026 preprint deals with SRAM computing-in-memory accelerators. These chips promise high energy efficiency and throughput for AI work. The catch is balance. Many design variants and mapping choices make it easy to mismatch the compute side and the storage side. A bad match can drag performance down a great deal.

The team's tool, CIM-Tuner, explores hardware and mapping together. Joint search finds pairings that one-sided tuning misses. The goal is a chip whose memory and logic pull in the same direction. As AI models grow, such in-memory designs are a leading hope for cheaper inference.
arxiv-2601-18470:
Silvio Candido and many colleagues design a part to soak up a fierce beam of light at a planned CERN ring. The ring will smash bits of matter with their anti-twins to probe deep laws. At each smash point, stray light flies out with great heat. That light must be caught and its heat shed in a safe way, or it would harm the ring.

Their plan runs lead in a flow, like a stream of thick soup. Lead can take the heat load the team must shed, which runs to a huge rate per unit. The stream takes the heat on and then gives it up as it loops. The paper sets out the form of the dump and the checks on its flow. A sound dump is a must for the ring to run at full strength.
arxiv-2601-18870:
Hans Dang and six colleagues show by a lab test a core rule of quantum theory that had not been shown head on till now. The rule sets how two traits of a light field trade: to read one trait shifts the next by a set sum. That rule sits at the root of the famed cap on how sharp both traits can be known at once. Past tests checked the cap, not the rule at its root.

The team read the rule from two kinds of joint count on the light field. Each count is a chart of how oft two reads land as a pair. The two charts, set side by side, give the rule's sum with no room for doubt. A head-on show of such a root rule is a rare gain. It firms the base on which much of light-based quantum work stands.
arxiv-2601-18970:
Alex Berian and four co-authors improve photo making from just a few input views. Novel view synthesis builds a new photo of a scene from a fresh angle. With only a few shots to start from, older methods treat each input view as if it counts the same toward the target view.

That flat treatment leads to weaker results, since some views plainly help more than others. The team adds attention that weighs where the model looked, giving key views more say. Sharper few shot views help uses like product shots, scene previews, and robot sight where extra photos cost time.
arxiv-2601-19170:
Wangyang Ying and seven co-authors turn plain text procedures into workflow graphs with the help of model teams. A procedural graph lays out steps and their order, which software can check and run. Language models can draft such graphs, but they often build broken structures or misread the logic of the steps.

The team uses several agents that refine the graph for both structure and logic. One pass fixes form, another checks that the flow makes sense. Sound workflow graphs are the bridge from written procedures to automation that firms can trust.
arxiv-2601-19270:
Banghui Hua and Jiang Zhu derive a missing piece of a theory that predicts gravitational wave signals. The theory models how quark matter confines, using a loop quantity called the Polyakov loop. Its kinetic term, how the loop changes in space and time, was often set by hand in a simplified way.

For the first time, the pair derive that term from first principles in hot pure Yang-Mills theory, with a field dependent scaling factor. They extend the math to theories with more colors as well. A derived, not guessed, term makes wave forecasts from such phase changes far more trustworthy.
arxiv-2601-19370:
Kaushlendra Pandey, Harpreet S. Dhillon, and Abhishek K. Gupta study car platoons as communication networks on highways. Platooning means vehicles travel close together in a coordinated line along a shared route. It promises lower fuel use, lower emissions, and smoother traffic flow.

Highways suit platoons, with their long shared stretches, yet the communication side is underexplored. The team analyzes connectivity for platooned users: who can reach whom, and how reliably. A platoon is only as safe as its links. So coverage math like this underpins the whole idea. It backs the fuel savings claims and the safety case regulators will demand.
arxiv-2601-19570:
Krzysztof M. Gogol, Manvir Schneider, Jan Gorzny, and Claudio J. Tessone study an attack on crypto trading. A sandwich attack traps a victim's trade between two trades by the attacker. The attacker buys first to push the price up, lets the victim buy high, then sells for profit. The team asks whether this trick works on Ethereum rollups, the scaling networks that keep their order books private.

Private mempools hide pending trades, which should block the attacker's view. The authors build a formal model of the best front-run and back-run sizes. Profit in the model depends on trade volume, pool depth, and slippage bounds. They add a second model for whether both attack trades can land in the same block. The study shows where privacy protects users and where it does not.
arxiv-2601-19770:
J.-P. Rivet and a large team of astronomers report quick observations of a near-Earth asteroid named 2025 FA22. The asteroid passed close to Earth in September 2025, at about twice the Moon's distance. Its size is estimated at a few hundred metres across. It ranks among the largest near-Earth objects seen at such close range.

The flyby triggered a rapid-response campaign by the International Asteroid Warning Network. The team gathered spectropolarimetric and broadband polarimetric data during the approach. Polarised light reveals facts about an asteroid's surface, such as grain size and composition. Practising on a real visitor tests the warning system end to end. The data also add to the record of a potentially hazardous class of objects.
arxiv-2601-19970:
Nourin Shahin and Izzat Alsmadi benchmark the security of Llama language models. As these models move from research into enterprise systems, their weaknesses threaten data privacy and system integrity. The authors evaluate several Llama variants against the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, a standard catalogue of language model risks.

They measure threat detection accuracy, response safety, and computational overhead together. A model that is safe but unusably slow fails deployment just as an unsafe one does. The comparison shows how variants trade these properties off. Enterprises choosing a model get evidence rather than vendor claims. The work supports safer rollout of open-weight models.
arxiv-2601-20270:
Holly Trikilis, Pasindu Marasinghe, Fariza Rashid, and Suranga Seneviratne use least-to-most reasoning to detect phishing URLs with large language models. Phishing is still one of the most common attack routes, so sorting real links from fake ones matters. Language models have shown promise at this task, but how they reason about a link is little studied.

The authors' framework breaks the judgment into smaller steps, from least to most complex. Stepwise prompting may make the model's decision process clearer and more accurate. Stronger link detection protects users who must judge an address quickly, often on a phone.
arxiv-2601-20370:
Paolo Baldan, Roberto Bruni, Francesco Ranzato, and Diletta Rigo introduce APPL, a program logic for abstract properties. Program logics are rule systems for proving facts about code. APPL is a unifying Hoare-style logic that subsumes standard Hoare logic, incorrectness logic, and several forms of hyper Hoare logic.

The logic is parameterized by an abstract domain, which sets how properties are approximated. One framework then covers many existing logics and new ones built from fresh abstractions. A common base could simplify the design of verifiers that must prove both correctness and security properties of programs.
arxiv-2601-20770:
Pamela Harris and four co-authors study a special family of number lists in this 2026 math paper. A parking function is a list of choices that lets every car find a spot. A prime parking function keeps that property even after any one entry of one is removed. The authors view these objects from several angles at once.

One lens comes from Lukasiewicz paths, step-by-step walks with set rules. Another comes from quasisymmetric functions, a tool from algebra. By moving between views, the team can count and compare these lists in new ways. The paper is combinatorics: the study of counting and structure. It adds links between three topics that are often taught apart.
arxiv-2601-20870:
Matteo Gianferrari and six co-authors teach spiking networks to learn new classes without forgetting old ones. Their 2026 paper presents STAER, a rehearsal method for spiking neural networks. Spiking networks pass signals as brief pulses, like real neurons. Their event-driven timing suits continuous learning well. Class-incremental learning, though, has been blocked by two problems. One is catastrophic forgetting; the other is misaligned spike timing.

Rehearsal stores old examples and replays them during new training. STAER aligns that rehearsal in time, matching the temporal code of spikes. That alignment is the heart of the method's name. Better alignment should let old memories survive new lessons. The work targets brain-like hardware that learns on the job. Such chips could adapt in the field without a data center.
arxiv-2601-21070:
Daniel Rodriguez-Cardenas and seven co-authors argue that testing code models needs better infrastructure. Their 2026 paper looks at benchmarks for large language models in software engineering. Code models advance fast, yet evaluation lags behind. Current benchmarks focus on narrow tasks and single metrics. That hides gaps in robustness, interpretability, fairness, and efficiency. It also hides questions of real-world usability.

The authors cite deeper problems too. Data engineering practices are inconsistent across benchmarks. Software engineering context is often limited. Contamination issues are widespread, with test data leaking into training. Their paper works toward comprehensive benchmarking infrastructure. Better yardsticks would let the field trust its own progress claims. The work appears at a 2026 conference on AI foundation models and software engineering.
arxiv-2601-21170:
Augusto Santos and three co-authors hunt for early warnings hidden in causal structure. Their 2026 paper proposes a machine learning method to detect emergent events early. The cases span seizure onset, sudden customer churn, and pandemic outbreaks. Such events arise from hidden causal links in complex systems. The core challenge is to unveil a system's latent causal structure. The process that makes the data is unknown and partly observed.

The title names the theme: the powers of precision. A structure-informed detector uses the learned causal web to spot trouble early. Precision matters, since false alarms train users to ignore warnings. The method aims to detect onsets across unlike domains with one idea. That breadth is the paper's bet. It serves hospitals, firms, and health teams that fear the same shape of surprise.
arxiv-2601-21470:
Ruicheng Ao, Hongyu Chen, Haoyang Liu, David Simchi-Levi, and Will Wei Sun merge two variance-cutting tricks for learning with scarce labels. Labeled data may be rare while a trained model can label the rest cheaply. Prediction-powered inference uses those cheap labels with a control signal to cut noise.

A classic optimization trick, SVRG, cuts noise with reference gradients. The authors show the two tricks are the same idea in different dress. Their combined method uses both signals at once. The result is steadier training for semi-supervised problems, where each true label is precious.
arxiv-2601-21670:
Zixuan Xia, Hao Wang, and five co-authors add geometric regularizers to multimodal learning. Joining data types like image, text, and sound should give richer models. Strong optimization alone, though, does not guarantee well-shaped representations.

Even with careful balancing, multimodal models often suffer two flaws. Features inside one modality can collapse together, and paired samples can drift apart across modalities. The authors add dispersive and anchoring terms to fight both flaws directly. Healthier geometry should make each single-modality skill sturdier and the fusion between them more faithful. It should also help when one input stream is noisy or missing at test time. The paper treats the shape of these learned spaces as a problem in its own right, not a side effect of training.
arxiv-2601-21970:
Dmitriy Zhigunov and Jacob Page study turbulence through its hidden skeleton. Exact unstable solutions of the Navier-Stokes equations are thought to underpin how turbulence behaves. These exact coherent structures are usually computed only in tiny domains, the smallest boxes that can sustain turbulent motion.

Real flows, though, sprawl across large domains with many interacting substructures. The team's 2026 preprint extends the dynamical systems approach to such extended flows. They show how new, simple invariant solutions can be built by combining smaller pieces in space. If large-scale turbulence really is assembled from these blocks, the picture could guide both theory and smarter flow control in engineering.
arxiv-2601-22370:
Nicholas Di, Eric Chi, and Samy Wu Fung widen the reach of a workhorse method for hard optimization. Operator splitting breaks a big task into small ones, each solved by a proximal step. Their 2026 preprint notes that most functions lack a neat form for that step, which has long fenced the method in.

The team build proximal steps from Hamilton-Jacobi equations, a classic frame from physics. That source yields steps for a far wider set of functions. Wider reach could speed tasks in imaging, control, and learning. The work joins two old fields in a new way. It gives solvers a bigger toolbox.
arxiv-2601-22570:
Aditya Sarkar, Jiacheng Cheng, Shlok Mishra, and Nuno Vasconcelos let a predictor say no, backed by a memory of past data. Selective prediction gives a model a reject option for low-trust calls. Their 2026 preprint notes that past work sticks to closed tasks with fixed answer sets.

Their plug-and-play method adds memory to judge trust on open tasks too. A model that can abstain is safer in the wild, where odd inputs abound. The work targets settings like open visual questions. It aims for fewer bold, wrong answers. Knowing when to stay silent is a skill.
arxiv-2601-22970:
Jeong Woon Lee and three co-authors seek smoother control policies from actor-critic learning. Policies learned this way often jitter with rapid, erratic swings, which physical machines cannot follow safely. Common fixes smooth the policy's output directly, treating the symptom rather than the cause.

The authors instead stabilize the Q-gradient field, the signal that guides the policy. A calmer guiding signal should yield calm motion without bolted-on smoothing. Smooth control matters for robots, drones, and other systems that act in the physical world. Treating the cause, not the symptom, is the argument: a jittery gradient field will keep producing jittery policies downstream.
arxiv-2601-23270:
Takashi Tsuchimochi and Benjamin Mokhtar improve a cheap quantum chemistry method for ground and excited states. Configuration interaction singles is efficient for excited states, but it overshoots excited-state energies. It also struggles with strongly linked systems, partly because it lacks orbital settling.

Their add-ons add state-mixing, linear response, and spin projection to the basic method. These fixes aim for rough accuracy at singles-level cost. Affordable excited-state methods help screen dyes, solar materials, and similar candidates. State-mixing, linear response, and spin projection are the three add-ons layered onto the singles framework in this work.
arxiv-2603-01470:
When each test of a design is costly, smart search methods try many options at once to save time. Shuhei Sugiura, Ichiro Takeuchi, and Shion Takeno improve that parallel search in this 2026 study. Past parallel methods either work poorly in practice or lack firm proof that they will not waste tests.

Their method, randomized kriging believer, grows from a known simple heuristic for batch search. It keeps low compute cost, simple code, and use with many base methods, even when tests finish out of order. The team proves bounds on expected regret, a formal sign that wasted tests stay limited. Tests on made-up tasks, standard benchmarks, and emulators of real data back the claim that it works well.
arxiv-2603-01570:
Database teams need hard test queries to judge how well a system runs, yet writing them by hand takes long. Jeffrey Tao, Yimeng Zeng, Haydn Jones, and colleagues automate that search in this 2026 work. Their tool uses Bayesian optimization, a smart search that learns from each trial as it goes.

Instead of fixed sample workloads, the search hunts for queries that leave the most room to speed up. Early tests show the found queries offer more than twice the speed-up headroom of standard benchmarks. That extra headroom matters more as learning-based parts enter database systems and need stern tests. Less hand work plus harder tests could help builders spot weak spots in query planning much sooner.
arxiv-2603-01670:
Hugo Jaquard and Nicolas Keriven study how finite random sampling schemes approach their continuous limits. Their 2026 work concerns determinantal point processes, which pick spread-out point sets that repel each other. As the pool of candidate points grows without bound, the discrete scheme should mimic a continuous one.

They define a trait called weak coherency that captures when statistics of the two schemes concentrate alike. With that trait, guarantees proved for the limit process transfer back to the finite scheme. Main results give conditions under which weak coherency holds, even when the limit kernel or space is unknown. One use builds data coresets smaller than plain random sampling at the same error. Another samples repulsively on an unknown surface from points drawn from an unknown density.
arxiv-2603-01870:
Francisco Mateus Rocha Filho, Ajalmar Rego da Rocha Neto, and Thiago Alves Rocha widen logic-based explanations for machine learning classifiers. Their 2026 work tackles opaque predictions: users need reasons they can trust, not just a label. Logic-based explanations guarantee correctness, yet they often cover too few cases to be useful.

Prior methods grow explanations step by step, one feature bound at a time, which trades cost against coverage. Small steps cost heavy compute, while large steps shrink how many instances an explanation covers. Their Onestep method builds each bound in a single pass, which cuts the iterative overhead. Twostep takes a more gradual route and pushes coverage much higher in tests. Average coverage gains over prior work are large across data sets, which makes guaranteed explanations more practical.
arxiv-2603-01970:
Stephen Blackstock, Amaro Tuninetti, Dieter Vanderelst, and colleagues model frequency-swept waveforms with a new polynomial family. Their 2026 work serves sonar, radar, and communications, plus the study of bat and dolphin calls. Polynomial phase signals are staples in all those fields for design and analysis.

Their CPSFM family builds frequency modulation from Chebyshev polynomials and their special traits. Orthogonality, recurrence relations, and links to trigonometric functions make the math compact. Fourier transforms, convolution, correlation, and the ambiguity function all get closed analytic forms. Those forms ease both waveform design and the study of non-polynomial sweeps like hyperbolic chirps. The team applies the model to biosonar calls of Mexican free-tailed bats, a natural test of fine frequency control.
arxiv-2603-02070:
Guilhem Fouilhe, Rebecca Eifler, Antonin Poche, and colleagues let users probe plan choices through chat with an AI guide. Their 2026 work serves plan making for real tasks, where the human should steer the tool, not be swapped out. Likes and know-how come out bit by bit through questions, so the tool must explain on demand.

Their setup uses more than one language model agent and stays neutral to the style of account it serves. Any account method can plug in, while the agents run the chat in light of the user and the case at hand. One built case deals with clashing goals in a plan, where two aims pull in opposed ways. A user study pits the chat front end against a fixed-form account tool. The aim is to draw out user likes fast and to build trust in the plans shown.
arxiv-2603-02170:
Jintao Zhang, Marco Chen, Haoxu Wang, and colleagues study fast, low-precision attention in this 2026 paper. Attention is the core step that lets a model weigh which inputs matter most. Using eight-bit numbers speeds it up, but training with them lagged full precision. Their earlier system, SageBwd, kept fine-tuning quality yet trailed in early training.

Here the team tracks down why that early gap appears. A norm step on some vectors proves vital for stable training at large batch sizes. Most errors trace to one gradient in the backward pass. Smaller batches let the eight-bit method match full precision in early training. Smoothing one vector set also stays key for stability.
arxiv-2603-02270:
Vasiliy Kudryavtsev, Kirill Borodin, German Berezin, and colleagues build a pet identification system in this 2026 study. Reuniting lost pets with owners needs fast, accurate matching from photos. Photo-only systems struggle, and past data sets were small. The team adds fake text descriptions as extra identity clues.

Their training corpus holds almost two million photos of near seven hundred thousand animals. Careful tests picked the best image and text backbones for the job. A gated fusion step, which weighs each source before merging, worked best. The full system reached top accuracy well above photo-only baselines. Fake text descriptions sharpened the line between similar animals, the results show. The work points to richer profiles for lost-pet searches.
arxiv-2603-02370:
Phillip Howard, Xin Su, and Kathleen Fraser measure cultural bias in vision-language models in this 2026 paper. Such models can show harmful bias, but past tests focused on visible traits like race or gender. Cultural traits, like religion or wealth, hide in scene context, not faces. No good data set marked those context cues, until now.

Their data set holds nearly sixty thousand synthetic counterfactual images. An editing model places the same person into many real cultural settings. Religion, nationality, and wealth status vary while the person stays fixed. That design isolates the effect of context on model outputs. Any output shift then traces to context alone, not appearance. The authors show the set can quantify cultural bias in popular models.
arxiv-2603-02670:
Jing Wang, Xuchen Lin, Ze-Zhong Liang, and a large team map how thin hydrogen gas is spread around nearby galaxies. Their 2026 paper combines data from the FEASTS and MHONGOOSE surveys, using sharp radio images of the 21-centimeter line. They build the first present-day count of gas clouds by column density, reaching far thinner gas than before.

At high densities their count matches older work, but with about one hundred times better sensitivity. Next to counts from distant quasars, nearby dense gas looks slightly scarcer, while the thinnest gas barely changed over cosmic time. Thin gas also sits closer to galaxies than older studies and simulations suggested. That gap warns that matching faint absorbers to galaxies, and modeling thin gas, remain hard problems.
arxiv-2603-02970:
Eliott Van Dieren, Tommaso Vanzan, and Fabio Nobile mix two search styles so an optimizer explores widely yet finishes fast. Their 2026 algorithm, LAGO, pairs Bayesian optimization, which learns a rough map of the whole space, with trust region methods that polish a promising spot using gradients. Many hybrids let one style starve the other.

Here both sides propose candidates each round, and a predicted-improvement contest picks the next evaluation. The global search works outside the current trust region, while local results feed the global model only when spaced far enough apart to stay numerically safe. The split gives fuller coverage of the design space than plain local methods. Local convergence near good regions stays fast.
