Her devotion to the heart of Jesus stands here near its source, centuries before it spread through the church. The nuns who loved her finished the book from her notes. It remains a summit of medieval women's writing on prayer.
goethe-faust-part-1-taylor-1870:
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe wrote Faust over much of his long life. Bayard Taylor gave Part One to America in 1870, keeping the original meters. His version made Goethe's masterpiece a classic in English as well as German.

Faust, a scholar sick of book learning, strikes a pact with Mephistopheles. The devil shows him youth, pleasure, and the world beyond his study. Faust woos Gretchen, whose ruin gives the tale its deep pathos and pain. Love, guilt, and striving clash in scenes of song and dread. Taylor's verse keeps the shifts of mood that made Faust famous.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_CH:
In 1970 the CIA ran a plot to block Salvador Allende from taking office in Chile, and it failed. Kissinger Briefed Nixon on Failed 1970 CIA Plot tells how Henry Kissinger reported that failure to President Nixon.

The briefing book, part of the Chile's Coup at 50 series, publishes the records of that briefing and the plot behind it. A kidnapping scheme ended with Chile's army chief murdered, and Allende took office anyway. Three years later a coup succeeded where the plot had not. The documents connect those two attempts in the words of the men who ran the first one.
grimoire-pope-honorius-1670:
The Grimoire of Pope Honorius appeared under that startling name in 1670. No pope wrote it; the attribution is a forgery meant to lend the black art a blessing. The French manual teaches conjurations of spirits in a form dressed as authorized ritual, which made it both notorious and sought after.

Its pages mix prayers with commands to demons in a single working system. Priests, the fiction runs, may lawfully bind what others must fear. The book became central to the French grimoire canon. Copies circulated in seminaries and villages alike, whispered about for centuries. Black magic wearing a forged blessing explains its fame and its danger in the eyes of the church.
harte-luck-roaring-camp-1870:
Bret Harte was a young San Francisco editor when his California stories made him famous almost overnight. The Luck of Roaring Camp and Other Stories appeared as a book in 1870. Harte drew on the gold-rush camps of the Sierra foothills, where he had worked as a teacher and express messenger.

In the title story, rough miners adopt a baby born in their camp and soften around him, until tragedy strikes. The Outcasts of Poker Flat banishes a gambler, a prostitute, and others into a deadly snowstorm. Harte mixed sentiment with grit and created the California myth for readers worldwide. The book founded the American local color movement in fiction.
holbach-system-of-nature-1770: The System of Nature, Holbach's 1770 materialist bible. The atheist's system. This book preserves that philosophy. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
huxley-lay-sermons-1870:
Thomas Henry Huxley, the biologist known as Darwin's bulldog, gathered his popular talks in Lay Sermons, Addresses, and Reviews in 1870. Huxley wrote for working people and students, not just scholars. He believed science belonged in public life.

The essays defend evolution, praise clear thinking, and argue for science in schools. One famous piece compares the physical basis of life in all living things. Another urges readers to sit down before facts like a child. Huxley's plain, fighting style carried Darwin's ideas to a wide Victorian public. The pieces were first printed in journals and given as public talks.
jennings-the-rosicrucians-1870:
Hargrave Jennings told a wild tale of the Rosy Cross in The Rosicrucians, his book of 1870. Its full name adds Their Rites and Mysteries. Jennings mixed scraps of fact with rich dreams of fire cults, phallic signs, and hid bands that rule the ages from the dark.

Scholars scoffed, yet crowds ate it up. The book made the Rosy Cross a fad in its age. Later bands took its dreams as fact, which gave it odd real force. It is less a true tale than the spark of a myth. Jennings had a poet's eye for fire, gold, and strange rites. That eye makes his wild claims read like a vivid dream of the past.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lubliner-oziasz:
Oziasz Louis Lubliner (1809–1868) was a Polish writer, and a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman gives his life. After the Polish revolution of 1831 he settled in Brussels. He died at Warsaw, where in 1862 he had been appointed librarian at the university.

In Brussels Lubliner published a French study of the Jews in Poland, viewing their condition in Russia through history, law, and politics. His Polish “Obrona Zydow” of 1858 defended Jews living in Polish lands, and he wrote many articles on the Jewish question. A later Brussels book of 1861 attacked Emperor Nicholas I’s confiscations in Poland and his harsh treatment of Polish Jews. The entry preserves the record of a writer who argued the Jewish case in two languages and two capitals.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mannheimer-isaa:
Isaac Noah Mannheimer, the preacher who united Vienna's Jews, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Copenhagen on October 17, 1793, he was a cantor's son. He studied Talmud alongside philosophy and Oriental languages at university. When Denmark emancipated its Jews in 1814, he became the state's first Jewish catechist. He died at Vienna in 1865.

The article follows his call to Vienna in 1821. The community there was split into two parties, and Mannheimer pleased both. He organized one congregation with a program and ritual on a traditional basis. Berlin and Hamburg pulpits followed, until Vienna called him to its new synagogue in 1824. His sermons were models of their time. His German prayer-book translation shaped many communities' services. In 1848 Brody sent him to the Austrian Reichstag, where he spoke against the Jew-tax. The entry honors a preacher who made moderate reform hold together.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-massel-joseph-1:
Joseph Massel, a Russian Jewish Hebraist who carried Hebrew printing to Manchester, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Joseph Jacobs and A. S. Waldstein. Born at Ujasin, in the government of Wilna, in 1850, he emigrated to England in the 1890s, settled in Manchester, and opened a printing and publishing office there.

Nearly everything the entry records is translation work, English and German literature carried into Hebrew. His books include a novel rendered from the German, Milton's "Samson Agonistes" as "Shimshon ha-Gibbor" in 1895, the ancient tale of Ahikar the Wise, and Longfellow's "Judas Maccabeus" in 1900. He also published original poems with translations from English, and in 1903 an anthology of Hebrew poets spanning 1725 to his own day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-ben-elijah:
Meir ben Elijah, an English poet who flourished at Norwich about 1260, is entered in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by Joseph Jacobs. England's medieval Jews left little poetry, and this notice is built on one manuscript: a Vatican codex holding a single long elegiac poem by Meir and fifteen smaller ones. A. Berliner published the poems from that manuscript at London in 1887, with an introduction arguing that Meir may have been a son of Elias Levesque.

The entry itself is three sentences long. It fixes the man's city and century, names the manuscript that preserves him, and points the reader to Berliner's edition and to the Anglo-Jewish bibliography for the case about his father. For the history of Hebrew verse in medieval England, where so little survives at all, even this much is a landmark.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendes-francisc:
Francisco Mendes was a Portuguese Marrano physician. Richard Gottheil and Meyer Kayserling give him a short and dramatic notice in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was physician to Don Affonso, brother of the cardinal-infante. He lived at Lisbon in the sixteenth century. There the shoemaker Luis Diaz proclaimed himself the Messiah. He persuaded Mendes, at thirty-seven, to undergo circumcision and openly confess Judaism. That was about 1541, and other converts did the same.

The awakening ended at the stake for its prophet. Diaz was burned at the first auto-da-fé held at Evora. That burning came toward the end of 1542. Mendes escaped the same fate only by flight. The entry draws on a contemporary Italian summary reprinted by Grätz. It draws on a Lisbon history of the Inquisition too. In five lines it preserves a whole messianic episode, and one man's escape from it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meza-christian-:
Christian Julius Frederik de Meza, born Solomon de Meza at Amsterdam on September 4, 1727, was a Danish physician of Portuguese Jewish descent. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. The son of Rabbi Abraham de Meza, he studied medicine at Amsterdam and Utrecht and settled in Copenhagen in 1753.

For a long time Meza was Copenhagen's only Jewish physician, popularly nicknamed the Jew doctor, yet widely respected and a member of its new medical society from 1772. He published a French treatise on raising children in 1769 and a history of medicine in 1795 that German critics savaged. After his wife's death in 1783, he embraced Christianity together with his son and daughter.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-miranda-lalla-1:
Lalla Miranda, an Australian singer born in Melbourne in 1876, is profiled in a brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry by Joseph Jacobs and Martha Washington Levy, published in 1906. Both her parents were singers, and she sang in public at thirteen. Europe finished her training, under teachers that included Madame Richard of the Paris Grand Opera.

Her career, as the entry traces it, ran three straight years at the opera houses of Amsterdam and Rotterdam, then to the Théâtre de la Monnaie in Brussels. In 1900 she sang in Rigoletto at Covent Garden in London, the summit the article records. A single source is cited, Harris's Jewish Year Book for 1901-2, which fits the entry's brevity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-montreal-10970:
Montreal, Canada's metropolis on its island in the St. Lawrence, was the chief Jewish center of British North America, as Cyrus Adler and Clarence I. de Sola report in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The census of 1901 counted 6,790 Jews; eastern European immigration had roughly doubled that to about 13,500 by 1904, in a city of 370,000.

The community was old and suddenly young at once. Its first congregation, the Spanish and Portuguese Shearith Israel, dated to 1768, yet a second synagogue waited until 1858 and a third until 1882. Then growth exploded: eleven more congregations formed by 1904, some already large with commodious buildings, some barely organized. The entry refers readers to its Canada article for the earlier history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mosler-henry-11:
Henry Mosler was an American genre painter born in New York City on June 6, 1841. Cyrus Adler and Florence N. Levy wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Taken to Cincinnati as a child, he began art at ten and went to Düsseldorf in 1863. After study there and in Paris, he came home to portraits and small genre pictures.

In 1874 Mosler returned to Europe and spent twenty years in Munich and Paris. His Return of the Prodigal Son took an honorable mention at the Paris Salon of 1879. The French government bought it for the Luxemburg gallery, the first such purchase from an American artist. More medals followed, and his pictures entered museums from Sydney to Philadelphia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nagawkar-samuel:
Samuel Moses Nagawkar was a Beni-Israel soldier born at Bombay about 1810. Joseph Jacobs and J. Hyams wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He enlisted in the Tenth Regiment of Native Infantry in 1832. He served on foreign service at Aden from 1840 to 1844.

His record runs through the southern Mahratta war and the Central India campaign of 1858 and 1859. The entry lists his battles: Kotah, Padoon, Chanderi, the Serai, Gwalior, Pawrie, Bijapur, Jhansi, and more. He finished with the Abyssinian campaign of 1867 and 1868. He retired at the end of 1871 after nearly forty years in uniform.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neumann-eleonor: Eleonora Neumann was a German violinist of brief, bright fame. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote her short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. She was born at Lissa in 1819. She learned music at Warsaw, where her father lived for years. His expulsion for political reasons ended that home. In March 1838 she played at Milan with great success. A tour of northern Italy won every critic's praise. She died at Triest in January 1841.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-notkin-note-nat:
Nathan Notkin was a Russian contractor and financier. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Shklov in the mid-1700s. He died at St. Petersburg in 1804. He lived there though law barred Jews from it.

Potemkin thought well of him in his lifetime. Dealings with Derzhavin shaped the Jews' fate through him. Derzhavin's Opinion on the Jews echoed Notkin's plans. Farming and factory colonies for Jews he proposed. He pressed them on Paul I through Kurakin. Schooling the young stood high in his scheme. Nevachovich called him the champion of his people. When Kovno sought expulsion, he pleaded their cause. His work fed the reforms granted in 1804.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-paley-john-1187:
John Paley was an American newsman from Russia. Joseph Jacobs and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born on February 6, in 1871. His birth town was Radoszkowice, in the Wilna land. He had the usual schooling of a Jewish boy there.

John read at Talmud schools at Minsk, Volosin, and Libau. In 1889 he crossed the sea to New York for good. There he became the editor of Der Volksadvokat. In 1891 he moved to Philadelphia for new work. He joined the Jüdische Presse, then the Volkswächter, there. Back in New York, he took a bigger post in 1893. He ran the Jüdisches Tageblatt and the Jüdische Gazetten. The piece calls it the most read Jewish paper on earth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pear-pirus-comm: The pear gets only a brief note in this entry. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The fruit shows up in the Talmud, the entry says. It does not seem to have been widely grown. The note adds one text warning for readers. The Septuagint wrongly used the Greek word for pear. It used it where the Hebrew speaks of baka trees.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pinne-12170:
Pinne was a small German town in the province of Posen. Gotthard Deutsch and Louis Lewin wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews appear there first in a charter of 1553. The charter curbed their buying of leather.

Dues squeezed from Jews left the community deep in debt. Churches and hospitals held the notes on that debt. A divorce case of 1764 caused a famous stir. The husband claimed he was another man entirely. Responsa argued the case for years afterward. A charter of 1789 set thirty-four rules for Jewish life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pontremoli-hiyy: Hiyya Pontremoli was a Turkish writer on rabbinic law who died at Smyrna in 1832. Isidore Singer and M. Franco wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a son of Benjamin Pontremoli of Smyrna. Among his works is a book called Zappihit bi-Debash. That book gathers his rulings on one part of Jewish law. The part is Orah Hayyim, which treats daily rites and prayer. Little more of his life is told in the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raba-b-ada-1247: Raba bar Ada was a Babylonian teacher of the third set of amoraim. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a pupil of Judah ben Ezekiel at Pumbedita. He passed on sayings of Rab that he had heard at home. Some came from his father and some from his teacher. He passed on sayings of Isaac as well. None of his own sayings has come down to us.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-raphael-12570:
Raphael is one of the archangels in Jewish tradition. Joseph Jacobs and Ludwig Blau wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. His name does not appear for an angel in the canonical books. Michael and Gabriel are named there, but Raphael is not.

The article finds Raphael instead in older apocryphal books. In Tobit he is one of seven angels before God. In Enoch he ranks second among the archangels. Jewish calendars link him to the sun and to Sunday. Later lists place him with Michael, Gabriel, and Uriel. The entry traces how a major angel grew outside the Bible itself. His rank stays high across many sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-remak-ernst-jul:
Ernst Julius Remak was a German physician born on May 26, 1849. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Berlin, son of Robert Remak. He studied at five universities across Germany.

The article says he earned his medical degree in 1870. He then served in the Franco-Prussian war. From 1873 to 1875 he assisted in nervous diseases at Berlin's Charité. He set up as a nerve specialist in the capital. He became a lecturer in 1877 and professor in 1893. He wrote more than fifty essays for medical journals. His books treat electric diagnosis and nerve inflammation. A biographical lexicon by Pagel is the cited source.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-riquetti-joseph:
Joseph Shallit Riquetti was a scholar of the seventeenth century. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He spent his youth at Safed. He subsequently settled at Verona in Italy.

The article says he published Gerondi's Yihus ha-Zaddikim at Verona in 1646. He then published a map of Palestine at Amsterdam. That map carries the title Hokmat ha-Mishkan. It is also called Iggeret Meleket ha-Mishkan. In 1676 he went to Mantua on a second edition. His Yihus was later published in that city. Three scholarly sources support the brief entry. Readers should note a twin entry under Richetti. It covers a Safed born editor with the same works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-josep:
Joseph Rosenthal was a Russo-Jewish scholar born at Suwalki, in Russian Poland, on February 14, 1844. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He taught himself Talmud, languages, and sciences with no teacher's aid.

From 1866 Rosenthal wrote learned pieces for Hebrew papers such as Ha-Maggid. One noted article set out the religious system of the Sefer Yezirah. His Derek Emunah, from 1894, holds four essays on religious philosophy. In the 1890s he settled at Warsaw and practised law there. He was also a strong chess player, a tournament winner in 1885.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samoscz-david-1:
David Samoscz was a German author of Hebrew books for the young, born at Kempen in 1789. Isidore Singer and Gotthard Deutsch wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He tutored at Breslau, entered business, and returned to writing late.

Samoscz wrote story after story in Hebrew, adapted mainly from the German. He retold Campe's moral tales and his Robinson the Younger in Hebrew. A book on the discovery of America followed the same German source. He also built textbooks: a primer and catechism, a Hebrew grammar, poems. His aim was Jewish children learning through their own tongue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schiffers-emanu:
Isidore Singer and A. Porter wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Emanuel Schiffers. He was a Russian chess master. Schiffers was born of German parents at St. Petersburg on May 4, 1850. He died there on December 12, 1904. He studied at the gymnasium of his native city. In 1871 he became a private tutor.

Schiffers took up chess at about fifteen. Within five years he was beating strong Russian players. In 1873 he first met Tchigorin, then his pupil. He even gave the young man odds of a knight. For seven years the pupil grew stronger than the teacher. In 1880 Schiffers lost the Russian championship to Tchigorin. He still won matches against Alapin, Chardin, and Mitropolsky. At Hastings in 1895 he took sixth prize among twenty-two masters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-second-day-of-f:
Kaufmann Kohler and Wolf Willner wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on the second day of festivals. The rabbis added that day to every holy day except Yom Kippur. Distant Jews learned the new moon's date from messengers. Those messengers left Jerusalem on set days of each month. They rested on Sabbaths and on Yom Kippur itself.

Diaspora Jews could not be sure which day was correct. A month might run twenty-nine days or thirty. Guessing wrong could shift a whole festival. Keeping two days removed all doubt. When Hillel fixed the calendar in the fourth century, the doubt vanished. Palestinian teachers still warned Babylon to guard the fathers' custom. A future decree, they said, might breed confusion again. Reform leaders in 1846 let congregations drop the second day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shetadlan-lit-p:
Shetadlan, literally persuader, was the Jewish community's envoy to hostile governments. Isidore Singer and Joseph Jacobs wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the office. The role lasted from medieval Germany into modern Russia. When a decree threatened Jews in some place, they sent him.

The shetadlan traveled to the seat of power to plead. He worked to soften or reverse harmful legislation. The Council of Four Lands sent such envoys to Wilna. Custom gave these men unusual freedom under Jewish law. Being near the government, they might break rules to save life. Often the envoy was the community's richest member. Lower taxes helped him too. The entry shows diplomacy as a survival tool for Jewish towns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-silverman-josep:
Joseph Silverman was an American rabbi born at Cincinnati, Ohio, in 1860. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He studied at Cincinnati's high school, university, and Hebrew Union College. He graduated as rabbi there in 1884.

Silverman served congregations at Dallas and then Galveston in Texas. From 1888 he was rabbi at New York's Temple Emanu-El. Until 1899 he assisted Gustav Gottheil in that pulpit. He presided over the Central Conference of American Rabbis for three years. He also organized the Emanu-El Brotherhood for his congregation. Twice he gave the opening prayer in Congress's House. His catechism for learners appeared at Galveston in 1885. The entry presents a Reform leader of national standing.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-singapore-13770:
Singapore was the capital and seaport of a British dependency. Joseph Jacobs and N E B Ezra wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Jews began to settle there in 1840. For years they met in a rented house near the business quarter. That street is still known as Synagogue street today.

About 1877 the community bought better ground for worship. It built the synagogue Maghain Aboth, opened on April 4, 1878. Both Sephardic and Ashkenazic Jews used that house. A second, larger synagogue, Chaised-El, was built in 1904. About 700 Jews lived among 160,000 people in all. Most had come from Bagdad, India, or Germany.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-ben-jud:
Solomon ben Judah of Dreux, surnamed the Holy, was a French tosafist. Gotthard Deutsch and S Mannheimer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He also worked as a Bible commentator in his time. He studied under Isaac ben Samuel the Elder of Dampierre. He headed the school of Dreux in the early thirteenth century.

He was among the rabbis who received a famous letter. Meir ben Todros Abulafia wrote to protest against Maimonides. His name appears in the Tosafot and in Or Zarua. His brother Jacob was also a Bible commentator of note. A son of his, Joseph, likely corresponded with Isaac of Dampierre. The entry traces this whole learned family circle in brief.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spitz-isaac-eiz: Isaac Spitz, called Eizig, was ab bet din in Bunzlau, Bohemia. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He was born in 1764 and died at Bunzlau in 1842. He wrote Mat'amme Yizhak, a work of songs and sayings. His son Yom-Tob published that work at Prague in 1843, the year after his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-strashun-mathia:
Mathias Strashun was a Russian Talmudist and writer born in Wilna in 1817. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Julius Gottlieb wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. He was born on October 1 of that year. He studied under Manasseh of Ilye and Isaac of Volozhin. He died on December 13, 1885.

Alongside Talmud, Strashun learned several languages and sciences. He also ran businesses, failing once before prospering. He spent much of his fortune building a great library. His house became a meeting place for scholars across Europe. He corresponded with Zunz and Rapoport on hard questions. For years he led the Hebrew charities of Wilna. The state bank named him an adviser. The entry portrays a scholar who joined wealth with learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-taw-14270:
Taw is the twenty-second letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Crawford Howell Toy and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. Its name connects with a Hebrew word for sign. The letter carries two different sounds in tradition. Context and a dot decide which sound is meant.

Soft taw lisps like the th in English thin. Hard taw sounds like a plain English t. A dagesh mark signals the hard pronunciation. Sefer Yezirah classes taw among the lingual letters. Modern phonetics calls it a voiceless dental stop. It can swap places with tet or shin in roots. As a numeral, later usage gives taw the value 400. The short entry packs a letter's sound, class, and number.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ullmann-alexand:
Alexander de Ereny Ullmann was a Hungarian deputy and political economist. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Born at Budapest in 1850, he died there in 1897. His father founded Hungary's first insurance company. Alexander took his law degree in 1872 at Vienna.

He entered the bar the following year. His father's death brought the family Hungarian nobility. From 1884 to 1892 he sat in Hungary's parliament. He represented the district of Also-Arpas there. His books treat stockholders' rights to sue in court. Others cover compulsory settlements and industrial law reform. A late work addressed legal regulation of Jewish affairs. Essays filled the Pester Lloyd and other journals.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-venture-mardoch:
Mardochée Venture was a French Jewish scholar of the seventeen hundreds. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Venture lived at Avignon in the late seventeen hundreds. With Isaiah Vidal he made a book of liturgical chants. It served the Jews of the county of Venaissin.

That book, printed at Avignon in 1765, holds a poem by Venture. The poem mixes Hebrew and Provençal lines. Pedro II of Brazil later translated it into French. Venture himself translated prayer books into French. His versions cover daily prayers, the High Holy Days, and fast days. Editions of his festival prayers kept appearing into 1845.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-walls-14770:
Walls in the ancient Near East were built of stone or brick. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Canaanite farmyard walls used great unhewn blocks. Some of those walls still stand east of the Jordan. City walls followed the same rough pattern.

Digs at Lachish found brick walls ten feet thick. At Megiddo, stone bases carried layers of brick. Such size explains Israel's fear in the Bible. Spies reported huge walls in the land. Solomon's palace wall used hewn stone instead. That choice was rare and costly. Tyrian builders, famed for cut stone, likely shaped his design.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wesel-baruch-be:
Baruch Bendet ben Reuben Wesel was a German rabbi and scholar. Gotthard Deutsch and Schulim Ochser wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was also called Benedict Reuben Gompertz. He was born at Wesel in the late sixteen hundreds. He died at Breslau about 1753. His family spread across Germany, Austria, and Holland.

In 1724 Wesel joined Breslau's rabbinical court. The Council of Four Lands named him rabbi in 1728. He served the Polish congregation at Breslau. An inherited fortune first left him independent. Poor business choices soon lost that fortune. The congregation then granted him a salary. A tax fight cost him his title and freedom briefly.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolf-hebr-ze-eb:
Wolf, called zeeb in Hebrew, is the wild beast named in the entry by Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz. They wrote it for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The piece notes that wolves still roam the land of Israel. They hunt in pairs or packs near sheepfolds at night.

In the Bible the wolf stands for bold force and blood lust. The entry lists the key verses that use it so. One is the blessing of Benjamin in Genesis. Others come from Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. The Talmud adds plain facts about the beast. It says the wolf looks much like a dog. Its bite leaves a long and ragged wound. Old tales with the wolf as a figure close the piece.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zappert-israel-:
Israel L. Zappert (1795-1865) was an Austrian friend to the poor of Prague. Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was the elder brother of George Zappert of note. He was the grandsire of Bruno Zappert as well.

His own grandsire was Wolf Zappert, the root of the line. Wolf was twice court jeweler to great lords of his day. He spent one whole fortune to save Jews from a ban. That ban would have cast them out of Trebitsch town. When Jews were driven from Prague, he alone could stay. His will set up twenty-two funds for good works in Prague. His son ran those funds, and then Israel in his turn. Israel led more than one aid group in that town. He set up a fund for poor brides and one for the sick.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zippor-15270: Zippor was the father of Balak, king of Moab, in the Bible. Emil G. Hirsch and Bernhard Pick wrote this brief entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Every passage that names Zippor names Balak with him. Balak hired the prophet Balaam to curse Israel as it neared his land. The entry also notes a possible hint at Zippor in the phrase 'the former king of Moab' in Numbers.
lectures-and-essays-pg6570:
Goldwin Smith collected his Lectures and Essays from periodical papers. A prefatory note says friends asked for the reprints. He jokes that the great public is sick of reprints, with reason.

Smith suggests the book might be called Contributions to Canadian Literature. Much of it first appeared in Canadian journals. History, politics, and literature share the table of contents. Smith wrote as a liberal critic on both sides of the Atlantic. His essays preserve sharp nineteenth-century argument in polished form. Cheap series like this changed who could own serious books. Huxley's presence in it signals science claiming popular ground.
lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-literat:
Lippincott's December 1873 number continues The New Hyperion. Edward Strahan asks whether auld acquaintance should be forgot. Fannie R. Feudge's sketches of eastern travel reach Bangkok. Life at the national capital anchors the nonfiction.

A day's sport in East Florida follows for outdoor readers. K. Cornwallis narrates a history of the crisis. William Black's Princess of Thule advances through chapter twenty-four. Monthly gossip recalls Bulwer and Salvini's Othello in notes. Saint Martin's temptation and the long fellow of Ti appear. Notes and books received close the December number's back pages.
lubbock-origin-of-civilisation-1870:
John Lubbock's Origin of Civilisation, published in 1870, is the companion to his Pre-historic Times. This volume turns from tools and mounds to the mental and social condition of early man. It asks where language, religion, marriage, and law began.

Lubbock gathers reports of peoples worldwide and arranges them as stages in one ascent toward civilization. His scheme is the founding text of evolutionary anthropology, and it shows: the rankings reflect his era's confidence in its own summit. Modern readers mine the book for its data and argue with its ladder. Together with its companion, it set the terms of the field for decades.
memoirs-of-louis-xiv-and-his-court-and-o:
Volume eleven of Saint-Simon's memoirs opens at chapter seventy eight. Saint-Simon turns to the outside life of Louis XIV at court. He has told the last twenty two years as he knew them.

Such plain details, he says, soon slip from the memory of posterity. Kings may learn from them how to earn and keep respect. At army meals, all sat covered, and few could claim a seat. Even high rank did not suffice, save for rare men like Vauban. Clergy were barred, save cardinals and bishops who held rank. Such fine rules of the table fill this volume's pages.
newman-grammar-of-assent-1870:
Late in life Newman turned from church history to the workings of belief itself in An Essay in Aid of a Grammar of Assent, published in 1870. The book asks how people can be sure of things they cannot prove like sums. It is his philosophy of religious belief and conscience.

Newman splits assent into kinds, from loose opinion to the firm grip of certitude, meaning settled sureness of mind. He argues that conscience and a trained sense, which he calls the illative sense, guide real reasoning more than formal logic does. Catholic readers treat the book as the classic account of how faith assents to doctrine.
noyes-history-american-socialisms-1870:
John Humphrey Noyes knew America's communes from inside, and his History of American Socialisms of 1870 surveys them all. Noyes founded Oneida, the most daring experiment of the age. From that vantage he writes the documentary history of Shakers, Owenites, Fourierists, and his own community alike.

Scores of experiments rise and fall in his pages, most of them dead within a few years. Noyes asks why some endured, and his answers carry the weight of a man who staked his life on the question. The book remains a primary source on nineteenth-century communalism, written by a participant.
openalex-w1793796070:
Tanmoy Mondal, Chandrasekhar Kanduri, and co-authors wrote this study. It appeared in Nature Communications in July 2015. Long noncoding RNAs help control which genes stay active. How they find their target genes was poorly understood. The team mapped hundreds of such RNAs in repressive chromatin.

One RNA, called MEG3, shared targets with a gene-silencing protein. Those targets included genes of the TGF-beta pathway. MEG3 binds far-off control sites on the DNA. Its binding spots carry GA-rich letter sequences, they found. Those sequences guide MEG3 through RNA-DNA triplex forms. Such triplexes may be a general targeting method, they suggest.
openalex-w1968635670:
S. Chatrchyan and the CMS Collaboration studied the new boson. Their paper appeared in Physical Review Letters in February 2013. A new particle had been seen near a set mass range. The team tested its mass and its spin-parity nature. They used its decays into pairs of Z bosons.

Data came from proton collisions in two LHC run years. The sample abstract confirms a measured mass was obtained. It does not state the value in the hosted text. Spin-parity shows how the particle behaves under mirror flips. Those traits decide if it matches the Higgs boson. The study was a key identity check for the discovery.
openalex-w2033146070:
Daniel Furtado Ferreira wrote a guide to a statistics program called Sisvar. His paper appeared in Ciencia e Agrotecnologia in 2014. Sisvar is widely used by researchers in Brazil. It runs many standard statistical analyses. One less-used feature compares group means using bootstrap methods.

Bootstrap methods resample the data many times. They can replace classic tests for comparing treatment means. Ferreira reviewed how these procedures work in Sisvar. He covered tests such as Tukey and Scott-Knott in bootstrap form. The bootstrap versions showed greater power in his review. They also controlled error rates better on skewed data. The guide aims to spread use of the stronger methods.
openalex-w2118849770:
Antoine Rabatel, Bernard Francou, Alvaro Soruco and colleagues reviewed the state of glaciers in the tropical Andes. Their paper appeared in The Cryosphere in 2013. Tropical glaciers are sensitive climate indicators. They also store water for dry seasons. Decades of studies now allow a long view.

The overview traces glacier change over centuries. Records combine old photos, moraines and modern monitoring. Glaciers across the range have lost area and volume. Retreat sped up in the late twentieth century. Small low glaciers face the fastest disappearance. Warming air temperatures drive much of the loss. The authors warn of water supply effects downstream.
openalex-w2129191970:
S. W. A. Naqvi, H. Bange, L. Farías, and colleagues published this review in Biogeosciences in 2010. They gathered what is known about two greenhouse gases, methane and nitrous oxide, in ocean zones that hold little or no oxygen. Many such zones sit along coasts, and some grow larger because human pollution feeds them extra nutrients.

The review finds that the supply of dead organic matter to the seafloor mainly controls methane made in sediments. Low oxygen in bottom water plays only a smaller, adjusting role. Methane builds up most in enclosed basins and over rich shelves. Bacteria that consume methane block much of its escape to the air, limiting the climate effect.
openalex-w2586485670:
María Fernanda Nieto-Jacobo, Johanna M. Steyaert, and Fátima Berenice Salazar-Badillo, with colleagues, published this 2017 study in Frontiers in Plant Science. It examines Trichoderma, a group of fungi that help plants grow. The team asked how the fungi's growing conditions change the signals they release. Those signals include indole acetic acid derivatives and volatile compounds that travel through air and soil.

Earlier work showed one Trichoderma scent compound makes roots branch sideways in test plants. Not all species make that compound, yet most still promote growth, so the link looked weak. This study compares ten strains, three well-studied models and seven screened on willow and impatiens. Arabidopsis plants serve as the test host. By varying growth conditions, the authors track which signals appear and how plants respond. The goal is to pin down how these helpful fungi talk to plants.
openalex-w2849537270:
Richard P. G. ten Broek, Pepijn Krielen, and Salomone Di Saverio lead the 2018 Bologna guidelines update in the World Journal of Emergency Surgery. Adhesive small bowel obstruction chokes the intestine with scar tissue, usually from earlier abdominal surgery. It is a common emergency with real mortality. The World Society of Emergency Surgery's working group first issued these guidelines in Bologna. This paper revises them with fresh evidence.

The group systematically searched the literature on epidemiology, diagnosis, and treatment. Each recommendation was graded by the strength of its supporting evidence. New sections cover preventing obstructions and handling special patient groups. The guidelines standardize decisions that emergency teams make under time pressure. When to operate, when to wait, and how to image are all addressed. The update aims to cut both deaths and unnecessary operations worldwide.
openalex-w3042266870:
Alicia Hillert, Yair Anikster, Amaya Bélanger-Quintana, and colleagues published this review in The American Journal of Human Genetics in 2020. It maps the genetic landscape and epidemiology of phenylketonuria, an inherited disorder of metabolism. The hosted copy is the authors' own manuscript version of the journal article.

Phenylketonuria, often shortened to PKU, is one of the classic inherited metabolic diseases screened for in newborns. Its pattern varies across populations, and its genetic causes span many variants in the responsible gene. The authors gather worldwide data on how common the condition is and where its variants concentrate. Such a map supports screening programs, counseling of families, and fair access to the special diets and drugs the condition requires.
openalex-w4414971670:
Fumio Nemoto, Nobuyuki Koike, Daichi Sato, and colleagues build a quantum generative model for bicycle-sharing demand. Their paper appeared in the Journal of the Physical Society of Japan in 2026. Sharing systems suffer when bikes pile up at some stations and vanish from others. Good demand forecasts help rebalance them.

The model uses quantum time evolution to encode correlations between stations. It then generates realistic demand scenarios. Against two classical forecasting methods, it performed competitively with far fewer parameters. It also recovered the links between stations well. The authors show how the generated scenarios can guide efforts against shortages. The work tests whether quantum machine learning can beat heavier classical models on a real city problem.
openalex-w7204247170: Acne does not always end with the teens; many adults battle it past 25. This paper reviews adult acne: its hormonal drivers, its toll on self-image and social life, and current treatments. The authors note how adult cases differ from teenage ones. A dermatology review for the millions who thought they had outgrown pimples.
openalex-w7204994470: Cats get skin cancer too, and squamous cell carcinoma is one of the most important feline tumors, striking the skin and mouth. This narrative review gathers what veterinary medicine knows about its causes, clinical signs, diagnosis, and treatment. The authors consolidate scattered knowledge into one reference. Written for veterinarians and informed cat owners, it covers a disease where early recognition can save a pet's life.
openalex-w7207825270: High school Portuguese textbooks decide how millions of students learn to write, and this article inspects how they handle text genres, from news articles to essays. The authors review contemporary textbooks for their theory, classroom practices, advances, and shortcomings in teaching genre. Grounded in dialogical linguistics, the paper asks whether textbooks truly prepare students to write for real situations. Useful for teachers, editors, and curriculum designers.
paul-christian-histoire-de-la-magie-1870:
Paul Christian, the pen name of Jean-Baptiste Pitois, published his Histoire de la magie in French in 1870. The full title promises a history of magic, the world beyond nature, and fate across the ages and peoples. Christian worked among the books of the Arsenal library in Paris, a famed store of old lore.

His history runs from the ancient world through the long tradition of the grimoires, the spell books of the Middle Ages. He writes as both scholar and believer in the wonder of his subject. The book became a base text for the French occult revival of his century. Its sweep still gives readers a map of how magic was remembered.
phrenological-journal-and-life-illustrat: Phrenological Journal and Life Illustrated, 1870. Another volume. This book preserves that periodical. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The library keeps the document safe for everyone.
plos-pone-0000070:
Iván L. Calderón, Felipe A. Arenas, José Manuel Pérez-Donoso, and their team studied bacterial enzymes in PLOS ONE in 2006. Catalases are enzymes that break down hydrogen peroxide, a toxic by-product in cells. The team found these enzymes can also carry out a second job: reducing tellurite, a toxic compound of the metal tellurium.

That second job needs the cell fuel NADPH to run. An enzyme with two roles blurs tidy textbook categories. It also has practical promise. Bacteria that neutralize tellurite could help clean metal-polluted water or recover rare metals. The finding adds a new function to one of the most studied enzymes in biology, a reminder that even classic proteins hold surprises.
plos-pone-0000170:
Simone Immler, Harry D. M. Moore, William G. Breed, and colleagues published this playful-titled study in PLOS ONE in 2007. By hook or by crook, it asks how the shape of rodent sperm relates to competition and cooperation. The authors use morphometry, careful measurement of form, across rodent species.

Sperm shape varies wildly among rodents, including hooked heads in some species. The authors test whether that variation tracks how hard sperm compete, or whether sperm join forces. The results feed a long debate in evolutionary biology about why sperm look so different when their job is the same.
plos-pone-0000270:
Arne Traulsen and Martin A. Nowak published this theoretical biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007, under the coined heading chromodynamics of cooperation. It studies how cooperation survives in finite populations, where chance events in small groups can help or kill a cooperative strategy. The authors model that process with tools borrowed from physics.

Cooperation is puzzling because cheaters can exploit it, yet it thrives in nature. Finite population maths shows when cooperators can still win. The paper adds a formal framework for that question, one used across biology, economics, and the study of human social behavior.
plos-pone-0000370:
Kumar S.D. Kothapalli and colleagues compared baby formulas with different fat content in a 2007 PLOS ONE study. The fat in question is DHA, an omega-3 fat found in brain tissue. Using newborn baboons, the team measured how moderate and high DHA formulas changed gene activity in the cerebral cortex, the brain's outer layer.

Gene activity profiles, called transcriptomes, show which genes a tissue has switched on. Comparing them across feeding groups reveals how diet in the first days of life can shape the developing brain at the molecular level. The work speaks to debates over how much DHA infant formula should contain.
plos-pone-0000470:
Alexey A. Nabatov and colleagues reported that cholesterol drugs interfere with HIV's entry routes in lab tests, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Statins, widely used to lower cholesterol, disrupted the levels of CCR5 and its partner RANTES in CD4 T lymphocytes in vitro. CCR5 is the doorway most HIV strains use to enter immune cells.

The team found statins preferentially decreased infection by R5 viruses, which use CCR5, over X4 viruses, which use another doorway. An approved, cheap drug with even a modest anti-HIV effect would interest researchers, especially for settings where standard therapy is scarce. The work is laboratory evidence, an early step that later clinical studies would need to test.
plos-pone-0000570:
Ulrich Abel and colleagues built a statistical yardstick for genome events, described in PLOS ONE in 2007. Genomic events, such as gene gains, losses, or breakpoints, scatter along chromosomes. Their method gives a real-time definition of non-randomness in how genomic events are spread. It tells clustering that means something from clustering by chance.

Hotspots of change can mark fragile DNA or sites of selection, but only if the clustering is real. A fast, principled test lets researchers scan whole genomes and trust the hotspots they flag. The paper contributes a tool to the era when genome-wide data first outran the statistics used to judge them.
plos-pone-0000670:
Ramon Reig and Maria V. Sanchez-Vives studied synapses in cortex that never sits still, writing for PLOS ONE in 2007. The cerebral cortex stays active around the clock, in waking and in sleep. That ongoing activity shapes how synapses transmit and how they change in the short term, a property called plasticity. One network pattern is a slow rhythm that alternates up states and quieter phases.

Most synapse studies use quiet slices of tissue, which may miss how real cortex behaves. Working in an active network keeps the background rhythm in the picture. The findings speak to how the brain processes signals amid its own noise, and how sleep-like rhythms affect communication.
plos-pone-0000770:
Raymond K. Auerbach, Apichai Tuanyok, William S. Probert and colleagues compared whole genomes of the plague bacterium from North America, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Yersinia pestis caused several devastating epidemics in history and remains important to public health and biodefense. The bacterium is widespread in the western United States, in wild rodent cycles. It arrived there only recently in evolutionary terms.

Comparing whole genome sequences on a small timescale shows how fast this pathogen changes once established. Small differences can trace spread between regions and hosts. For a bacterium with plague's record, tracking its micro-evolution is both basic science and practical surveillance for health agencies.
plos-pone-0000870:
Drew Purves, Jeremy Lichstein and Stephen Pacala built a new forest model covering 250 North American tree species, published in PLOS ONE in 2007. A forest canopy is the sum of crown sizes, shapes and places within a stand. Canopy form shapes light, growth and nearly every part of forest life, yet there was no agreed way to work it out from basic tree data.

Their model is spatially implicit, meaning it captures crowns without mapping every tree. It also allows crowns to shift shape as trees compete for space and light. A tool like this helps link simple field measures to the structure of whole forests.
plos-pone-0000970:
Min Ni and Jae-Hyuk Yu identified a regulator that links spore making with sugar storage in a fungus, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Trehalose is a sugar that shields cells from stress. Fungal spores, the bodies fungi use to survive and spread, need large trehalose stores to last.

In Aspergillus nidulans, a model fungus, the authors describe a novel regulator that couples sporogenesis, the making of spores, with trehalose biogenesis, the making of the sugar. Coupling the two ensures spores are packed with protection as they form. The finding tidies two fields, development and stress biology, into one control point.
plos-pone-0001070:
C. Mary Schooling, Tai Hing Lam, G. Neil Thomas and colleagues used Hong Kong's migrant history to study sex differences in body risk, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Gaps between the sexes in blood fats and body shape widen at puberty, while diabetes risk does not follow the same pattern. Hong Kong Chinese are mostly first or second generation migrants who grew up in very different conditions.

That history lets the team separate growing up environment from adult environment. Adults shared a developed setting for years, but their childhoods differed sharply. Their analysis asks how much of the adult sex gap was set early. The answer bears on when prevention should start.
plos-pone-0001170:
Sixteen neurodegenerative disorders are linked to expanded trinucleotide repeats, stretches of DNA where a three-letter unit repeats too many times. Tanay Ghosh and colleagues explored how such repeats kill neurons in the polyglutamine group of these diseases, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They focused on a channel protein called Vdac1, which sits in the membrane of mitochondria, the cell's power plants.

The authors report a role for Vdac1 in polyglutamine-mediated neuronal cell death. The molecular chain from repeat expansion to dead neurons has long been elusive. Placing a mitochondrial channel in that chain gives researchers a new place to intervene.
plos-pone-0001270:
A dairy cow's liver must switch its chemistry abruptly at calving, when milk production begins. Cansu Agca and Shawn Donkin studied one liver enzyme, pyruvate carboxylase, at that moment, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The bovine liver makes six versions of the enzyme's RNA transcript, differing only in their leader region while sharing the same coding region.

The authors determined the profile of these mRNA variants in liver at calving. Which variants dominate may affect how the cow makes glucose for milk. The work belongs to the practical science of keeping high-producing dairy cattle metabolically healthy.
plos-pone-0001370:
Steven Giles and colleagues wrote a 2007 PLOS ONE study on a fungus that can cause grave lung illness. The fungus lives in soil and air, and it most harms people with weak immune systems. A lung protein that helps the body fight germs was the focus of the work. The team asked whether that protein can hold back this fungus.

The authors report that the fungus stands up well to the lung protein. In their tests, the protein did not curb the yeast as it does with many other germs. The result helps explain why this fungus is so hard to clear. It also points drug work toward other lines of defense.
plos-pone-0001470:
Lauren Stewart and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE brain scan study on how we hear tunes. A tune has two levels: the broad up and down shape, and the exact gaps between notes. An old model held that the brain handles these levels in a set order. The team tested that order with scans.

Their scans back a ranked flow, with broad shape handled before fine gaps. The brain areas lit up in a sequence that fits the model. That order helps explain why some brain harms spare tune shape but blur fine pitch. It also guides work on how music skill is built in the brain.
plos-pone-0001570:
Yingyao Zhou and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on guessing jobs for malaria parasite proteins. Genome reads name many proteins whose jobs stay unknown. The gap is worst for proteins found in just one group of species. The team used gene use patterns across species to infer those jobs.

By matching use patterns to proteins of known job, they tagged many unknowns with likely roles. Proof based tags beat pure sequence guesses for odd proteins. Each new job call gives drug teams a lead to test. The method can be reused for any germ with a fresh genome.
plos-pone-0001670:
Paola de Candia, Ran Blekhman, Adrien E. Chabot, and their co-authors combined several genome methods to study one gene regulator in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Many traits that set humans apart from chimpanzees may stem from changes in how genes are regulated, yet few proven cases were known. The regulator in focus is FOXO1a, a transcription factor that switches target genes on and off.

By layering genomic approaches, the team traced how FOXO1a helps run a pathway that responds to oxidative stress. That is the cell damage caused by reactive oxygen forms. The full text gives the data sets they merged and the pathway members they found. Studies like this show how small changes in gene control, not just in genes, can push species apart.
plos-pone-0001770:
Shu-Bai Liu, Ying-Ying He, Yun Zhang, and their co-authors isolated an unusual protein complex from amphibian skin in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Non-lens beta-gamma-crystallins occur widely in vertebrate tissues, but their functions were unknown. Trefoil factors start mucosal healing and are involved in tumor formation, yet their mechanisms were also elusive.

From frog skin the team purified a naturally existing 72-kilodalton complex joining a non-lens crystallin with a trefoil factor. The full text gives the purification, the structure, and functional tests. Two mystery proteins found holding hands in skin secretions is the kind of clue that can crack both of their jobs at once.
plos-pone-0001870:
Nadia Tinto and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a form of diabetes that runs in families and starts young. The form, called GCK MODY, comes from faults in the glucokinase gene, which helps the body sense blood sugar. The team worked with children from South Italy who were thought to have this type of diabetes.

The group read the gene in full for thirty young patients. They then studied how each fault found might change the shape of the gene product. By matching gene faults to signs of illness in each child, the study shows how a fault can be tied to a case. That helps doctors give families a firm cause for early diabetes.
plos-pone-0001970:
Jacqueline Boultwood and co-authors studied a gene's role in a rare anemia, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The illness, refractory anemia with ring sideroblasts, is a bone marrow disorder. In it, iron piles up in the power units of young red blood cells, forming rings. Why the iron lands there was unknown.

The team focused on ABCB7, a protein that ferries iron-related cargo out of those power units. A fault in that ferry is a prime suspect for the iron build-up. Work on this gene may explain the odd iron pattern and point to care for a little-known blood disorder.
plos-pone-0002070:
Robert van Beers wrote a theory study in PLOS ONE in 2008 on why our eyes jump the way they do. Saccades are the fast jumps the eyes make between fix points, and their duration and path are strikingly stereotyped. We have no voluntary control over those traits. They are set by how far the eye must move, and a bit by direction and starting pose.

Van Beers argues that this fixed pattern is not a flaw but a solution. It minimizes the consequences of motor noise, the random error in our muscles. If noise grows with speed, a set speed profile keeps the eye on target. The work reframes a quirk as smart design.
plos-pone-0002170:
Anna Rita Zuena, Jerome Mairesse, Paola Casolini, and co-authors studied how stress before birth shapes rat pups, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Restraining a pregnant rat is a standard model of early stress, and it leaves lasting marks on the behavior and brain chemistry of her young. For more than 30 years, scientists had guessed that the effects differ between males and females.

Few studies had compared the sexes head-on. This team did, and found two distinct profiles: male and female offspring showed unlike patterns of behavior and brain chemistry after the same prenatal stress. The result argues that early-stress research must always reckon with sex.
plos-pone-0002270:
Alienke Monsuur, Paul de Bakker, Alexandra Zhernakova, and co-authors found a cheaper genetic test route for celiac disease risk, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Celiac disease is an autoimmune reaction to gluten. Genes in the HLA region on chromosome 6 shape the risk of celiac disease. They also shape the risk of many other autoimmune disorders, including type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, and multiple sclerosis.

Testing HLA variants directly is costly and slow. The team showed that tag SNPs, a small set of marker variants that stand in for the risky HLA types, can detect them effectively. A cheap, accurate screen can sort patients far faster in clinics and in large genetic studies.
plos-pone-0002370:
In 2008, Schooling and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits C. Mary Schooling, Sun Wenjie, Sai Yin Ho, and others. Its subject is moderate Alcohol Use and Mortality from Ischaemic Heart Disease: A Prospective Study in Older Chinese People. Moderate alcohol use is generally linked to lower ischaemic heart disease (IHD) death.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002470:
A research team led by Yu reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Keming Yu, Jian Ge, James Bradley Summers, and others. Its subject is tSP-1 Secreted by Bone Marrow Stromal Cells Contributes to Retinal Ganglion Cell Neurite Outgrowth and Survival. Bone marrow stromal cells (BMSCs) are pluripotent.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002570:
Work from Fox and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Andrew S. Fox, Steven E. Shelton, Terrence R. Oakes, and others. Its subject is trait-Like Brain Activity during Adolescence Predicts Anxious Temperament in Primates. Early theorists (Freud and Darwin) speculated that extremely shy children, or those with anxious temperament, were likely to have anxiety problems as adults.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002670:
Hong Qin led a team whose 2008 PLOS ONE article deals with genomic instability is associated with natural life span variation in saccharomyces cerevisiae. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Hong Qin, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Increasing genomic instability is associated with aging in eukaryotes, but the connection between genomic instability and natural variation in life span is unknown. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002770:
Simon Hong led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was interaction between purkinje cells and inhibitory interneurons may create adjustable output waveforms to generate timed cerebellar output. The catalog record names Simon Hong first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. We develop a new model that explains how the cerebellum may generate the timing in classical delay eyeblink conditioning. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002870:
Françoise Dromer, Claire Bernede-Bauduin, Didier Guillemot and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on severe cryptococcosis, a serious fungal infection. Guidelines from the year 2000 backed care with drugs such as amphotericin B, but those plans had not been fully tested across real clinical settings. The authors set out to check how well treatment choices held up in practice.

Much of the paper weighs the paired use of amphotericin B and flucytosine, named in the title as having a major role. It reviews cases where trial rules had left gaps in the evidence. For clinicians, the value is a closer look at drug choice for a hard and risky infection.
plos-pone-0002970:
Neeraj Raizada, Lakbir Chauhan, Ajay Khera and co-authors surveyed HIV among tuberculosis patients in India for 2006 to 2007. Little was known about the HIV burden in this group, and no population-based surveys had been reported before. The two infections often worsen each other.

Their community-based survey tested tuberculosis patients treated by the national control program. Seroprevalence here means the share with HIV markers in blood. Published in PLOS ONE, the numbers help Indian health services plan joint testing and care for two linked epidemics. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003070:
Motoki Azuma, Yasuaki Kabe, Chikanori Kuramori and co-authors found a transporter moving haem building blocks into mitochondria in 2008. Haem is the iron-holding group in proteins for oxygen transport, respiration, signaling, and detoxification. Its precursor, protoporphyrin IX, must cross into the mitochondrial matrix to finish haem synthesis.

The adenine nucleotide translocator transports those precursors, the title reports, assigning a second job to a well-known carrier. Published in PLOS ONE, the result closes a gap in the haem pathway. Faults in that pathway cause the porphyria diseases, so each step matters. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003170:
Md Jaber Hossain, Danielle Hickman and Daniel R. Perez track changes in a duck flu virus in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. H9N2 avian influenza viruses keep circulating worldwide, and in Asia they have caused outbreaks and set lineages in land-based poultry. Some strains are classed as potentially pandemic because they have infected humans and caused mild respiratory disease.

The team report evidence of expanded host range and mammal-linked genetic changes in a duck H9N2 virus after adaptation in quail and chickens. Readers see how passage through farm birds can shift a virus toward mammals. That is central to judging pandemic risk from animal flu.
plos-pone-0003270:
Tamar R. van Raalten, Nick F. Ramsey, Jeff Duyn and colleagues track brain change with practice in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Practice can have a profound effect on performance and brain activity, especially if a task can be automated. Tasks that allow automatization typically involve repeated encoding of information paired with a constant response. Much remained unknown about the effects of such practice on the brain.

The title reports that practice induces function-specific changes in brain activity. Readers learn that learning does not quiet the brain in one uniform way. Different task parts change differently, which refines how training and rehabilitation effects are interpreted.
plos-pone-0003370:
Jean-Philippe Lavigne and colleagues asked a basic question about mixed infections in this 2008 study. Two gut bacteria, Enterococcus faecalis and Escherichia coli, often show up together in sick patients. Doctors still debate how much harm the first one does on its own. The team tested the pair in tiny worms called Caenorhabditis elegans.

The worms were exposed to each bacterium alone and then to both at once. Together, the two microbes killed far more worms than either one did alone. That joint effect is called synergy, and it was strong in these tests. The results suggest mixed gut infections can be worse than the sum of their parts.
plos-pone-0003470:
André Altmann and co-authors compared prediction methods for HIV therapy in this 2008 paper. Doctors read the HIV genome to spot drug resistance mutations. Those mutations change viral proteins so drugs bind less well. Choosing therapy from that reading is now standard care.

No single algorithm reads resistance data best, so the team fused classifiers. They compared ways of merging several predictors into one call. The fused methods aimed to forecast drug response more accurately. Better forecasts help match each patient with drugs that still work. Drug resistance is the main reason HIV treatment fails over time.
plos-pone-0003570:
Balaraj B. Menon and co-authors tested bacterial enzyme vaults in this 2008 paper. The carboxysome is a protein shell inside certain bacteria. It is packed with RubisCO, the enzyme that first fixes carbon dioxide. That fixation feeds the Calvin-Benson-Bassham cycle of the cell.

The team placed foreign and chimeric RubisCO forms inside these shells. The carboxysomes of Halothiobacillus neapolitanus sequestered them successfully. Programmable compartments could one day boost carbon capture in microbes. The study tests how flexible that natural vault is. Bacterial shells like these are now a model for building tiny reactors.
plos-pone-0003670:
Juliette Colinas, Scott C. Schmidler, Gil Bohrer, and colleagues published this genome study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Most of a eukaryote's DNA does not code for proteins, and its role is still unclear. The team studied how the length of DNA stretches relates to how active genes are.

They found opposite patterns for two kinds of length. Longer gaps between genes tracked with gene activity one way, while longer gene bodies tracked with it the other way. The split hints that noncoding DNA is not filler. Its lengths may form part of the system that tunes gene use.
plos-pone-0003770:
Anthony J. Robertson, Alison Coluccio, Peter Knowlton, and colleagues published this embryo study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Runx proteins are regulators that control gene activity in animal development and are linked to cancers in mammals. In the sea urchin, the Runx gene SpRunt-1 is active through the early embryo.

The team studied blastula-stage embryos and found Runx expression drives cell division there. Its activity is also mutually linked with Wnt signaling, another ancient growth pathway. The pairing shows old growth circuitry already working together in the earliest stages of animal life.
plos-pone-0003870:
Gino Miele, Harald Seeger, Denis Marino, and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on prion infection. Prions can pass between people through blood, so health services need ways to spot carriers. At the time, tests done during life relied on tissue samples taken by biopsy. Such tests do not suit screening large groups of people.

The authors point to a protein called alpha-1 antichymotrypsin found in urine. Raised levels of that protein marked people carrying prion infection. A urine test would avoid biopsy and could be used on many samples at once. The work offers a path toward screening blood supplies and finding carriers early.
plos-pone-0003970:
Monica Borgatti, Roberta Rizzo, Maria Beatrice Dal Canto, and co-authors measured a molecule released by early embryos in 2008. Earlier work tied soluble HLA-G from embryos to better IVF implantation. That link made labs watch HLA-G closely in embryo cultures. Other released molecules might carry similar signals.

Their PLOS ONE article reports release of soluble ICAM-1 by human embryos. Samples came from oocytes and embryos fertilized in vitro. A measurable release gives clinics another possible marker of embryo quality. Better markers could raise IVF success by guiding embryo choice. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004070:
Michela Garofalo, Cristina Quintavalle, Ciro Zanca, and co-authors hunted for partners of a survival kinase in 2008. Akt is a kinase that carries survival signals in cells. It regulates several proteins involved in apoptosis, the cell death program. The team screened yeast for new proteins that interact with Akt.

Their PLOS ONE article reports Akt controls drug-induced death through Bcl-w. Akt lowers Bcl-w, a protein that normally holds death back. That link gives drug-induced death a clearer path in cancer cells. It also suggests targets to make chemotherapy kill more surely. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004170:
Jonathan Lin and colleagues published this cell study in PLOS ONE in 2009. When proteins misfold inside the endoplasmic reticulum, cells switch on the unfolded protein response, a set of signals that cuts the load of bad proteins. If balance cannot be restored, the same system can push the cell to die.

Two branches of this response, named PERK and IRE1, were thought to act alike. The team shows their effects on cell survival pull in opposite directions. That split matters for diseases of misfolded proteins, where tipping the response toward survival or death could change the outcome.
plos-pone-0004270:
Jennifer Taylor-Cousar and colleagues published this cystic fibrosis study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The lung disease seen in cystic fibrosis varies widely between patients, so surroundings and other genes must shape its severity. The team proposed that inherited differences in ABO histo-blood group antigens, which alter sugar coatings on proteins, could be one such modifier.

They tested whether variants in histo-blood group genes track with infection and with lung disease severity in cystic fibrosis. Modifier genes explain why the same main mutation can leave one patient much sicker than another. The hunt for such modifiers is now a standard part of cystic fibrosis research.
plos-pone-0004370:
Ming Zhao and colleagues published this tuberculosis study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Multidrug-resistant and extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis are global health problems. The team studied these resistant forms in Shanghai, one of the largest cities in Asia. They measured their features, prevalence, and how often they are transmitted.

Tuberculosis there is diagnosed and treated through a large municipal system, giving the study broad coverage. Knowing how much resistant TB is transmitted, rather than newly generated by failed treatment, changes the control plan. Their data tell Shanghai whether to hunt transmission chains or fix treatment first.
plos-pone-0004470:
Drugs that freeze the cell's internal tracks may pick out the most dangerous cancer cells, argue Newaj Abdullah, Gus Rosania, and Kerby Shedden in PLOS ONE in 2009. For cancer therapy, what counts is killing the cells with the highest power to grow tumors. Those cells may be only a small share of the tumor.

The team used a standard panel of sixty human cancer cell lines, a workhorse test set for drug screening. They examined how microtubule inhibitors, drugs that jam the tracks cells use to divide and move, hit tumorigenic lines in particular. Their analysis asks whether these drugs are selective for the worst cells, not just toxic to all. Selectivity like that is what separates a smart cancer drug from a blunt one.
plos-pone-0004570:
Illegal and unreported fishing worldwide is measured for the first time by David Agnew, John Pearce, Ganapathiraju Pramod, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Illegal fishing contributes to overexploitation of fish stocks. It also hinders the recovery of fish populations and the ecosystems around them.

Earlier estimates were national or anecdotal. This study undertook a world-wide analysis, reviewing the situation in fifty-four countries and regions. Putting a number on the hidden catch changes the policy debate: quotas built on reported catches alone understate the pressure on stocks. The estimate gives governments and fisheries bodies a shared starting figure for enforcement and for setting catch limits that reflect what is really taken.
plos-pone-0004670:
Lee Byrne, Diana Cole, Brian Cox, and colleagues counted prion seeds in yeast for a PLOS ONE study in 2009. They worked with a yeast prion that spreads well when cells divide. New seeds form over time and pass to daughter cells, which keeps the trait stable across many cell rounds.

The team focused on how many seeds each cell holds and how they move at division. They also used a drug that blocks a helper protein to watch seed loss and gain. Counts like these help explain how a protein shape, not a gene change, can act like a lasting trait in yeast.
plos-pone-0004770:
Miriam Matamales and colleagues used nuclear staining to identify striatal spiny neurons and their subgroups in transgenic mice, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Precise identification of neuron types is a major challenge in brain science. In the striatum, most neurons are one broad class, the medium spiny neurons, which split into two intermingled groups.

The groups differ in where they send fibers and which proteins they carry. The team used a staining method and engineered mice to tell them apart. Reliable labels let researchers link each group to movement and habit learning. They also aid Parkinson and Huntington studies.
plos-pone-0004870:
Mariana Piuri, William Jacobs, and Graham Hatfull developed fluoromycobacteriophages for rapid antibiotic susceptibility testing of tuberculosis, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Rapid susceptibility testing of Mycobacterium tuberculosis is paramount as multiple and extensively drug resistant strains emerge and spread. The virus based assay uses fluorescent phages to deliver a reporter gene into live tuberculosis cells. Producing light only when cells remain viable after drug exposure.

Results arrive in days instead of weeks. Faster answers guide correct regimens sooner. Phage assays suit low resource laboratories. Drug resistant tuberculosis control could improve markedly. The work also raises clear questions that targeted studies can now address.
plos-pone-0004970:
Most genes come in two copies, one from each parent. The copies usually duplicate at the same time. Some genes break that rule. Only one copy works, and the copies replicate out of sync. Devkanya Dutta and colleagues examined this pattern in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used human embryonic stem cells.

Such exceptional genes include odorant receptors and immune genes. The study found the asynchronous pattern across many genes in the stem cells. It also found non-equivalence between the two autosome copies. Our paired genomes are less equal than they look. The work matters for how scientists read gene activity in early development.
plos-pone-0005070:
Cells control protein building with a brake called 4E-BP. The brake blocks cap-dependent translation, one main route of protein synthesis. Phosphate tags switch the brake off. Nathalie Oulhen and colleagues built a mimic of the tagged state. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They tested it in a cell-free sea urchin system.

The variant mimics hyperphosphorylated 4E-BP. In the system, it inhibited protein synthesis. A faithful mimic gives researchers a precise tool. They can hold translation in one state and study the consequences. Sea urchin systems are classic for this work. The study sharpens tools for a basic question: how cells tune the making of proteins.
plos-pone-0005170:
A blood parasite called Trypanosoma congolense is one of the main limits on cattle farming across Africa. In cattle, low red blood cell counts are the key sign of the disease. Noyes and colleagues used infected mice in PLOS ONE in 2009 to ask what controls that anemia.

Anemia in cattle can linger even after parasite numbers fall to very low levels. The mouse work traces the processes that keep red cell counts down during and after infection. Knowing those controls could help vets protect herds and guide new treatments. It also helps explain why sick animals stay weak for so long.
plos-pone-0005270:
Asthma narrows children's airways, and doctors track it with breathing tests. Blowing tests give flow measures, while a body box measures airway resistance directly. Mahut and colleagues compared those two families of measures in asthmatic children in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Early obstruction shows up as a bigger drop in mid-breath flow than in total breath volume, and as raised specific airway resistance. Mapping how the two measures relate shows which test catches early change best. That helps clinics choose tests for young patients. Young lungs change fast, so a test that catches the first signs of blocked air flow gives a child a head start on care that keeps the lungs strong.
plos-pone-0005370:
Does obesity caused by a rich diet persist after the diet ends? Guo and colleagues tested that question in male C57BL/6 mice in PLOS ONE in 2009. Groups of mice got free access to two different obesigenic diets, then switched back to plain chow.

The title gives the result: the obesity persisted after the temporary diets ended. Weight gained on the rich diets was not fully reversed by returning to normal food. Lasting effects of short feasts matter for how diet history is judged in obesity research. Mice are not men. Yet a weight gain that will not lift in mice is a strong hint to look for the same lock-in in men and women who diet and then regain.
plos-pone-0005470:
