Ting-Ting Liu and colleagues built a fast test for bacteria in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Doctors need to know quickly which germ a patient has and which drugs will kill it. Old tests rely on growing the germ, which can take days.

Their method uses scattered laser light, boosted by tiny metal particles, to read the chemical make-up of the germ's wall. When an antibiotic harms the wall, the light pattern changes within a short time. A test this fast could help doctors pick the right drug sooner and use antibiotics more wisely.
plos-pone-0005570:
Viviana Moresi and co-authors studied muscle repair in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Muscle stays healthy by making new fibres after damage. A signal called TNF, raised in many wasting diseases, blocks that repair and shrinks muscle.

The team tested how a hormone, vasopressin, and TNF affect a family of enzymes called caspases during repair. Adjusting caspase activity changed how well muscle rebuilt itself and worked after damage. That balance could be used to help muscle recover in disease and after injury. The work also shows that repair signals can help or harm depending on dose and timing.
plos-pone-0005670:
Oscar Ramírez and colleagues used new gene-reading tools in 2009 to study an extinct goat that once lived on a Mediterranean island. Isolated islands in that sea bred odd dwarf forms of elephants, hippos, deer, and goats. Most of those forms died out in the recent past, leaving only bones behind.

The team tried shotgun sequencing, a method that reads many short scraps of DNA at once, on the old remains. Warm climates break DNA down fast, so success was far from sure. Their work tests whether rich gene data can still be pulled from fossils kept in mild, temperate settings.
plos-pone-0005770:
Aristides Hatjimihail tackled a lab quality problem in 2009: how often should control checks run in clinical chemistry? Labs measure control samples to catch errors before patient results go wrong. Checking too rarely risks harm; checking too often wastes money.

Hatjimihail frames the timing choice as a risk problem and offers a way to estimate the best interval. The method uses a residual risk measure, weighing the chance an error slips through. Labs can adapt it to their own tests and error rates. Better timing means safer results at a fair cost, a quiet but real gain for patients.
plos-pone-0005870:
Shona Kirk and co-authors showed in 2009 that a mother's diet-driven obesity can permanently reset how her offspring's brains handle appetite. Brain circuits that govern eating are wired early in life. The group had already seen overeating and fat gain in adult offspring of rats fed a rich diet through pregnancy and nursing.

Here they traced lasting changes in the offspring's central food-intake controls. Those changes persist into adulthood, long after the diet ends. The work adds to evidence that early nutrition programs later weight. It carries a clear message for pregnancy care and obesity prevention across generations.
plos-pone-0005970:
One fish in South America sees the world in two halves at once. Gregory Owens, Diana Windsor, Justin Mui and colleagues began the gene-level study of that trick in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper covers Anableps anableps, the four-eyed fish, whose eyes split so it can watch above and below the water at the same time.

As a first step, the team cataloged ten visual opsins, the light-catching proteins that set what colors an eye can sense. A full opsin list shows the raw material the fish's odd vision is built from. The work opens the way to asking how one eye serves two worlds, in air and in water, at once.
plos-pone-0006070:
Hibernation slows a body to a crawl, and breeding is usually shut down for its length. Gemma Morrow and Stewart Nicol found an animal that breaks that rule in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies the echidna in Tasmania, an egg-laying mammal that sleeps through several cold months and then mates in mid-winter.

Hibernation and reproduction overlap in these echidnas, the title reports. Mating begins while the animals are still in their hibernation season. The overlap rewrites a basic assumption about what a sleeping body can do, and it shows how a mild-climate hibernator can bend rules that hold firm in harsher lands.
plos-pone-0006170:
Birds that travel long distances face heavy demands, and Donata Kalthoff and colleagues asked whether travel also changes flu risk. Their 2009 PLOS ONE study tested stonechats, small birds that eat insects, for weakness to the H5N1 bird flu virus. Three groups were compared: strong migrants, weak migrants, and birds that stay put.

As the title states, migratory status was not related to how sick the birds became. Strong travellers and stay-at-home birds fared alike in the tests. The result helps separate the act of migration itself from other causes of flu spread. It also gives wildlife health workers a firmer base for tracking risk in wild birds.
plos-pone-0006270:
Repeating made-up words like blonterstaping predicts how well someone learns language, but nobody knew why. Johanna Barry, Mervyn Hardiman, and Dorothy Bishop measured brain responses to such nonwords in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. They used the mismatch response, a brain signal that fires when a sound breaks a pattern.

That signal serves as a neurophysiological signature of language learning capacity, per the title. Three rival explanations for the nonword link are weighed against the brain data. A measurable brain marker could flag children who need language support early. The study connects a classroom observation to brain function.
plos-pone-0006370:
Mitochondria power the cell and also help run programmed death, so their DNA might influence cancer risk. Edith Mueller and colleagues tested mitochondrial haplogroups against prostate cancer in middle European Caucasians in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Mitochondria are also the main source of harmful reactive oxygen species.

No association was found between the mitochondrial variants and prostate cancer, per the title. A clean negative result still sharpens the field's aim. Research effort can move to likelier genetic factors. The study shows the value of publishing well-tested null findings. Clear no-result work like this is a real, if quiet, gain for the field.
plos-pone-0006470:
Pauli Amornkul and colleagues surveyed HIV in rural western Kenya for PLOS ONE in 2009. They aimed to estimate how common HIV is among young people and to describe the risk factors involved. The study focused on residents aged thirteen to thirty-four in Asembo. It was a community-based cross-sectional survey, a snapshot of a whole population at one time.

From a demographic surveillance system, the team drew a random sample of residents. Staff contacted people at home to take part. Random sampling makes the rates more trustworthy than clinic-based counts. Knowing who is most at risk helps target testing and prevention where they count most.
plos-pone-0006570:
Huijie Hou, Lei Li, Younghak Cho, and colleagues built tiny microbial fuel cell arrays in PLOS ONE in 2009. Microbial fuel cells are remarkable green energy devices that exploit microbes to generate electricity from organic compounds. Devices in use were mostly large and slow to test. The team microfabricated arrays of small fuel cells.

Their title reports the arrays reveal electrochemically active microbes. Many samples can be screened at once for electricity-making ability. Finding the best microbes is the bottleneck for this technology. Miniaturized arrays speed that search greatly. The work blends microbiology with clean energy engineering.
plos-pone-0006670:
Richard E. Jacob and colleagues published a methods comparison in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their subject was lung damage caused by long-term cigarette smoke. They worked with mice exposed to smoke over an extended period. The question was how best to measure widening of the air spaces in the lungs.

The team prepared, sliced, and imaged mouse lung tissue using standard stereology methods. They then ran two different quantitative approaches on that same material. Comparing the results showed how each method judged the enlargement. Widened air spaces are a hallmark of emphysema, so measurement choices matter. The work helps other researchers pick a reliable way to score smoke damage in animal studies.
plos-pone-0006770:
Alexis Menteyne and his team studied the brain's guard cells after long seizures in PLOS ONE in 2009. The guards are called microglia. Their working state shifts with the illness that wakes them. Woken microglia can switch on sets of potassium channels. Those channels carry slow electric currents in the cell.

The team worked in the hippocampus after status epilepticus, a state of non-stop seizures. One channel part, Kv1.3, stood out in the woken cells. It was by far the main one they used. Knowing which channel rules the cell gives drug makers a clear target. A drug that calms these guards could help treat seizure-linked swelling in the brain.
plos-pone-0006870:
Bart Ferwerda and colleagues studied an inflammation brake and the plague bacterium in PLOS ONE in 2009. The brake is caspase-12, an enzyme that calms inflammation. It inhibits caspase-1 and a pathway called NOD2/RIP2. People with working caspase-12 face higher sepsis susceptibility. A stop mutation removed the enzyme and replaced the ancient type in many populations.

The team asked how caspase-12 shapes responses to Yersinia pestis. That bacterium causes plague. Losing an inflammation brake may help fight some infections while harming in others. The trade-off could explain why the broken version spread. The work ties a human gene variant to plague defense.
plos-pone-0006970:
Rodrigo Publio, Rodrigo Oliveira, and Antonio Roque modelled the retina in PLOS ONE in 2009. Sensory systems must respond to both faint and bright signals. Gap junctions between cells may widen that range by preventing early saturation. The team built a small conductance-based model of the rod pathway in the vertebrate retina.

They varied gap junction strength and a rod current called I h. Then they measured how the model's response range changed. Their results support a real widening role for these connections. Understanding this range helps explain how eyes keep working from starlight to daylight.
plos-pone-0007070:
Clara Elbers, Carolien de Kovel, Yvonne van der Schouw, and colleagues studied appetite genes in Europeans in PLOS ONE in 2009. People differ greatly in how much they eat and which foods they prefer. These patterns run in families, so genes are involved. Farming began about eleven thousand years ago and changed diets fast.

The team tested variants in two neuropeptide Y receptor genes, NPY1R and NPY5R. Variants tracked with nutrient-specific food intake. The genes also showed signs of recent selection in Europeans. That pairing hints that new farm diets reshaped human appetite genes as they spread.
plos-pone-0007170:
David Root, Anthony Fabbricatore, David Barker, and colleagues probed cocaine relapse in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cocaine addiction is a chronically relapsing disorder. Cues present during drug taking become learned triggers. Facing them in abstinence raises the chance of relapse. How habit and goal-directed behavior share that control was the question.

The team devalued cocaine and observed the animals' behavior afterward. They found evidence for both habitual and goal-directed control. Pure habit models cannot explain the full picture. Treatment may need to address both systems, since relapse can be driven by either route.
plos-pone-0007270:
Jean-Robert Ioset and Harparkash Kaur presented simple field tests for antimalarial drug quality in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Malaria remains a major public health problem in Africa, Asia, and Latin America. Artemisinin-based combination drugs are the most effective antimalarials available, built from a plant-derived compound family.

Poor quality formulations can fail patients and fuel drug resistance. The authors describe simple assays that can be run in the field. The assays check current artemisinin-based combination products without advanced lab equipment. Their methods give regulators and clinics a practical way to spot bad medicines early.
plos-pone-0007370:
Dana Willner, Mike Furlan, Matthew Haynes, and colleagues surveyed viruses in the airways of cystic fibrosis patients in 2009. The human respiratory tract is constantly exposed to viruses, microbes, and particles from air, water, and food. Airway mucus and immunity decide which organisms persist in the lungs of healthy and sick people.

The authors use metagenomic analysis of respiratory tract DNA viral communities. They compare cystic fibrosis and non-cystic fibrosis individuals. Their PLOS ONE inventory shows how viral communities differ when thick mucus traps material. Such differences may influence the chronic infections that damage cystic fibrosis lungs.
plos-pone-0007470:
Narasimhan Venkatachari and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how HIV-1 infects dendritic cells. Dendritic cells are immune scouts that carry antigens to T cells. Earlier work showed they can trap HIV particles and hand them to T cells, spreading infection. Whether dendritic cells themselves acquire virus from infected T cells was the open question here.

The team found evidence that dendritic cells acquire whole virus particles from infected T cells. The route is an antigen uptake mechanism, the scouts' normal way of sampling material. That means the virus can move from T cell to dendritic cell, not only the reverse. The finding revises part of the picture of HIV spread in the body. Blocking that handoff is one more target for prevention research.
plos-pone-0007570:
Raul Torres and Juan Ramirez published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on a signaling molecule found in an unexpected place. Chemokines are messengers that usually work outside cells, guiding cell-to-cell communication. The chemokine Cxcl12 comes in several forms, called isoforms. Most work has focused on the widespread alpha and beta forms. The team studied the gamma isoform in the adult mouse heart.

The gamma form does not stay outside the cell. It localizes to the nucleolus, the dense core inside the nucleus where ribosomes are built. A communication signal with a seat inside the nucleus suggests an entirely separate job. That job likely involves the cell's protein-making capacity. The finding redraws what a chemokine can be. It also opens a new line of questions about signals that moonlight as nuclear residents.
plos-pone-0007670:
Bih-Rong Wei and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on a blood marker for ovarian cancer spread. Epithelial ovarian cancer often spreads across the peritoneum, the abdominal lining. Gauging that tumor burden usually requires surgery or imaging. The team measured a protein called S100A6 in the blood of mice with the disease. They then checked the same marker against disease stage in patients.

In mice, serum S100A6 concentration predicted the peritoneal tumor burden. In patients, higher levels were associated with advanced stage. A blood test that tracks abdominal spread could help monitor treatment without repeated surgery. Ovarian cancer is usually caught late, so every monitoring tool counts. The study moves S100A6 from a laboratory observation toward a clinical candidate. It must still prove itself in larger patient groups.
plos-pone-0007770:
Sanda Ljubicic and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It studies a switch protein called RalA in the insulin-making cells of the pancreas. RalA and its sibling RalB are GTPases, molecular switches used in many cell tasks. They help control growth and membrane traffic.

Beta cells release insulin through a secretory process of many steps. The team traced how Ral proteins get switched on in these cells. They then analyzed which secretory steps RalA regulates. Precise control of insulin release is central to blood sugar health. Each switch in the chain is a possible drug target.
plos-pone-0007870:
Yiu-Wing Kam and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It shows how airway enzymes help the SARS coronavirus enter human cells. Enveloped viruses must activate their surface glycoproteins to get inside. That activation often comes from a cut by a protease.

The SARS virus's spike glycoprotein is the key that must be cut. The authors found that proteases found in the airways perform that cleavage. The cut enhanced entry into human bronchial epithelial cells in the lab. Airway proteases thus act as accomplices in infection. Blocking them is one idea for antiviral treatment.
plos-pone-0007970:
Andrea Doeschl-Wilson and colleagues modeled a sheep disease puzzle in PLOS ONE in 2009. Scrapie is a fatal brain disease of sheep, and a single gene, the prion protein gene, sets how prone each animal is. New data tied that same gene to lamb survival as well.

Older models had treated the gene as if it only set disease risk. Adding its link to lamb fitness changed how long scrapie should last in a flock, and why prone types persist. The work warns breeders that culling for one trait can tug on another, with effects that play out over years.
plos-pone-0008070:
Xiaoning Qian and Byung-Jun Yoon used a classic statistics tool to find shared circuits across species in PLOS ONE in 2009. The tool, hidden Markov models, excels at finding patterns in noisy chains of data. Interaction maps between proteins are noisy and differ by species.

Their method hunts for pathways that stay alike across species despite the noise. Shared circuits are likely the vital ones, kept by evolution while spare parts changed. Finding them helps focus lab work on the wiring that matters most, in microbes and in human cells alike.
plos-pone-0008170:
Anne Mette Fisker Hag and colleagues read vessel genes in rats carrying HIV genes in PLOS ONE in 2009. People with HIV suffer clogged arteries at higher rates, but the cause is tangled with drug effects and lifestyle. A rat that carries HIV-1 genes gives a cleaner test of the virus alone.

Three genes tied to vessel lining and cell grip were read along the aorta, the body's main artery. Their activity varied by region in the virus-carrying rats. Regional highs point to where virus-driven artery harm begins, and to the molecules a preventive drug might target.
plos-pone-0008270:
Andrew J. Sachs and colleagues studied a mutant mouse brain in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. The weeble mouse carries a frameshift fault in the Inpp4a gene. Affected mice develop early cerebellar ataxia and lose nerve cells. Purkinje cells of the cerebellum are hit especially hard. Yet some areas of the cerebellum are spared in a pattern.

Protection in those spared areas correlated with expression of the Eaat4 gene. A patterned match like this hints at what shields some neurons. Understanding selective survival could inspire treatments for degeneration. The study uses a mutant to probe why some cells live and others die.
plos-pone-0008370:
Holger Kühn and colleagues studied ribosome assembly proteins in yeast in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Noc1p, Noc3p, and Noc4p are essential for building ribosomes. They share a stretch of about forty-five amino acids called the Noc-domain. The function of that domain was unknown. Noc4p forms part of the small subunit processome, an assembly machine.

The team showed the Noc-domain of Noc4p mediates submodule formation. It also governs incorporation into the processome itself. Without it, a building block of the ribosome cannot join the line. The work clarifies an early step in ribosome biogenesis.
plos-pone-0008470:
Li-Jun Yang and co-authors simulate a cancer drug leaving its targets in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The drug imatinib blocks kinases, enzymes that switch proteins on. Two targets are called c-Kit and Abl. Drugs that lock the inactive form of a kinase draw much interest. They tend to be strong and selective. The team use steered computer simulations of molecules.

They pull imatinib away from each kinase in the model. They compare which exit path is likelier for each target. The paths help explain why the drug binds one target more tightly. Such detail can guide design of better kinase drugs.
plos-pone-0008570:
Hong Wu and co-authors solve structures of human methyltransferases in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. SET domain methyltransferases deposit methyl marks on histone tail lysines. Those marks play a major role in epigenetic regulation of gene transcription. One mark, on lysine 9 of histone H3, is called H3K9. It generally signals gene silencing. The team solve structures of catalytic domains of four such enzymes. They are GLP, G9a, Suv39H2, and PRDM2, half of the known human set.

Comparing the four structures reveals shared and unique features. Those features explain how each enzyme selects its target. Structural biology of this kind guides drug design. Inhibitors of these enzymes are of interest in cancer and other diseases.
plos-pone-0008670:
Francesca Silvagno and co-authors locate the vitamin D receptor in blood cells in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Like other steroid hormones, vitamin D elicits transcriptional events and rapid non-genomic effects. Receptor localization and mechanisms of rapid responses are still controversial. Vitamin D also shows anticoagulant effects in some studies. The team examine human platelets and differentiated megakaryocytes, the cells that make platelets. They search for the vitamin D receptor in mitochondria, the cell's energy units.

They find mitochondrial localization of the receptor in both cell types. A mitochondrial receptor could mediate rapid, non-genomic vitamin D actions. Platelets lack nuclei, so a mitochondrial site explains vitamin effects there. The finding reframes vitamin D signaling in blood clotting cells.
plos-pone-0008770:
Saurabh Mehta, Edward Giovannucci, Ferdinand Mugusi, and colleagues linked vitamin D levels to HIV outcomes in women. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Vitamin D shapes many immune defenses beyond bone health. Whether low levels speed HIV disease was untested in large studies. Data from resource-limited settings were especially scarce. The cohort gave a chance to test the link properly.

Women with low vitamin D faced faster disease progression. They also showed more anemia and higher death rates. The links held across the follow-up period. If causal, cheap vitamin D supplements could aid HIV care where drugs are scarce.
plos-pone-0008870:
Tomoji Mashimo, Akiko Takizawa, Birger Voigt, and colleagues created immune-deficient rats with gene-targeting scissors. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Rats are favorite lab animals, yet making knockout rats was long blocked. Rat embryonic stem cells suitable for classic methods were unavailable. Zinc-finger nucleases cut DNA at chosen spots, offering a bypass. Knocking out one gene produced the X-SCID immune defect.

The engineered rats lacked mature immune defenses, as intended. Such rats can host human cells and tissues for study. A working rat knockout route expands genetic research beyond mice. Transplant and infection science gain a larger model animal.
plos-pone-0008970:
JiaJia Dong and co-authors challenged a standard belief about radiation and cell death, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The old view held that more radiation exposure always means more cells dying. It also assumed a safe threshold dose below which nothing happens. The team tested those ideas on frog embryos exposed to X-rays.

Short bursts of harder X-rays set off early cell-death events in the embryos. The effect depended on the energy of the rays, not just the total dose. Even brief exposures could start the death programme sooner than expected. The result warns against judging radiation risk by dose alone.
plos-pone-0009070:
Hector Guillen-Ahlers and co-authors removed a death switch from tumour-prone mice and counted gut tumours, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fas, also called CD95, starts cell suicide when its partner binds it. Faults in that suicide path have been reported in colorectal cancer. The mice used, Apc Min/+, grow many intestinal tumours by design.

Adding Fas deficiency made the tumour burden heavier. Without the death signal, more abnormal gut cells survived to form tumours. The count rose compared with mice that kept Fas working. The result supports Fas as a genuine guard against bowel tumours.
plos-pone-0009170:
Carlene Starck and Andrew Sutherland-Smith showed a muscle-growth brake can fold into toxic clumps, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Myostatin limits muscle growth throughout life. It is implicated in sporadic inclusion body myositis, a wasting disease of ageing. That disease resembles amyloid disorders like Alzheimer's in its pathology.

The precursor form of myostatin aggregated in the team's experiments. Its clumps took amyloid form and proved toxic to cells. A growth regulator turning into cell poison fits the myositis picture. The result may link muscle wasting to the wider amyloid story.
plos-pone-0009270:
Nikolai Axmacher and co-authors published this memory study in PLOS ONE in 2010. What other people claim to remember can bend what we think we remember. Earlier studies of this social conformity effect gave mixed answers. One puzzle was whether false alarms and correct recognitions are swayed equally.

The team varied how many group members gave the same wrong answer. Memory conformity grew in graded steps with the size of the agreeing group. Old and new items were not affected in the same simple way. The study shows social pressure tunes memory by degrees, not as an all-or-nothing switch.
plos-pone-0009370:
Christophe Fuerer and Roel Nusse published this methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2010. The Wnt pathway guides embryo development, adult tissue upkeep, and stem cell control. Studying it in specific cell types needs tools that report or tweak the pathway. Lentiviruses, which slip genes into cells permanently, are ideal carriers.

The authors built lentiviral vectors that read out Wnt activity in living cells. Others in the set manipulate the pathway up or down. A shared toolkit lets labs compare results across cell types and experiments. It lowers the barrier for any group wanting to probe this central pathway.
plos-pone-0009470:
Hongguang Liu and co-authors merged two kinds of medical imaging in PLOS ONE in 2010. Optical imaging tracks glowing probes inside a living body. Nuclear imaging tracks probes that give off radiation. Each method has strengths the other lacks. The team asked whether a radioactive probe could also be seen with optical tools.

They showed that such probes give off a faint light that optical cameras can pick up. One probe could thus serve in both kinds of scan. That could cut cost and simplify work that tracks tumors or infection. The study is a proof that the two worlds can be joined in practice.
plos-pone-0009570:
Susan Baker and co-authors asked a surprising question about fatty liver disease in PLOS ONE in 2010. The severe form of the disease is called NASH. It strikes people who drink little or no alcohol, and it is tied to obesity. Earlier work found that gut bacteria in obese mice make extra alcohol. The team tested whether that home made alcohol plays a role in the liver damage.

If gut microbes brew alcohol, the liver would face it just as it faces drink. Their work explores that link in the setting of obesity. The idea adds a new suspect to a common disease. It suggests that calming the gut's microbes might help protect the liver.
plos-pone-0009670:
Kei-ichiro Mishiba and co-authors studied gene silencing in gentian plants in PLOS ONE in 2010. Plants can silence foreign DNA by adding methyl tags to it. The 35S enhancer is a strong switch borrowed from a plant virus and used in much genetic work. The team introduced DNA carrying that enhancer into gentian, an ornamental flower. They tracked how the plant tagged the new sequence.

The enhancer was methylated strictly and from scratch, a process called de novo methylation. That tagging can switch the introduced genes off. The result shows how firmly plants police new DNA. It matters for anyone engineering flowers or crops with introduced traits.
plos-pone-0009770:
Quitting smoking is hard, and treatment costs keep many smokers from getting help. Thomas Land and colleagues studied what happened when Massachusetts Medicaid began covering tobacco dependence treatments. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Medicaid is the public health insurance program for people with low incomes. After coverage began, smoking prevalence among the covered group fell. Treatments include counseling and medicines that ease withdrawal. The decreases linked a policy choice to a real change in behavior. The results gave other states evidence on what coverage can achieve. The study tracked the change over time.
plos-pone-0009870:
Multiple myeloma is a cancer of blood cells that also weakens bone. Kyoko Takeuchi and colleagues tested whether blocking one growth signal could do both jobs at once. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The signal is TGF-beta, which keeps osteoblasts, bone-building cells, from finishing their growth. Blocking it restored terminal osteoblast differentiation, letting the builders mature. Myeloma often grows inside the bone marrow itself. With bone building restored, myeloma growth was suppressed as well. One intervention that heals bone and slows cancer would be doubly valuable. Bone loss is one of myeloma's worst effects.
plos-pone-0009970:
In major depression, brain genes may fall out of step with each other and with hormones. Chris Gaiteri and colleagues looked for that broken timing in gene activity data. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

Gene synchrony is how closely genes rise and fall together. Altered synchrony suggested a combined hormone-mediated dysregulated state in depression. Hormones like cortisol set daily rhythms that genes normally follow. The idea links two systems long studied apart. A dysregulated state could help explain depression's mix of mood and body symptoms. Depression affects mood, sleep, appetite, and drive.
plos-pone-0010170:
Lewis Halsey and Craig White fitted cane toads with motion sensors in a 2010 study. Cane toads were brought to Australia to control pests, but became invaders themselves. Their invasion front advances fast, damaging each new habitat they enter. Models that predict spread from energy use and feeding grounds could help plan a response to that advance.

Using accelerometry, sensors that record movement, the team measured toad energetics and behavior together. Their PLOS ONE report shows the method works in this species. Better energy data can sharpen forecasts of how far and fast the front will move.
plos-pone-0010270:
The authors were Ibrahima Baber, Moussa Keita, Nafomon Sogoba, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study counted malaria mosquitoes in Mali. They ran two mark-release-recapture surveys in 2008, in wet and dry seasons. Villages studied included Fourda, a fishing village by the Niger River, and Kenieroba, both with many Anopheles gambiae mosquitoes.

From recaptures, they estimated population size and how far mosquitoes migrate. Those numbers decide how vector control, like spraying or bed nets, should be spaced and timed. Efficient control of the malaria mosquito depends on knowing how populations move between villages.
plos-pone-0010370:
Ravit Arav-Boger and colleagues compared malaria-drug relatives against cytomegalovirus in PLOS ONE in 2010. The virus, called CMV, can cause grave illness in people with weak immunity. A plant-derived drug, artesunate, had been reported to slow CMV growth. The team tested several single-unit forms of the drug family. They also built and tested new double-unit forms, called dimers.

In lab tests, the dimers fought the virus far better than the single forms. Doubling the molecule greatly raised its strength. That kind of jump can revive a drug family once set aside. More testing would be needed for safety and dosing. For now, the study marks dimers as the form worth pursuing against CMV.
plos-pone-0010470:
Eric Sayre and colleagues asked whether where arthritis strikes changes how much work people lose, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Osteoarthritis wears down joints and often pushes people to cut hours or quit. The team compared effects across six sites: knee, hip, hand, foot, lower back, and neck. They drew a random sample of six thousand patients for the analysis.

Not all joint sites should cost the same in working life. A bad hip and a sore hand threaten different jobs differently. Knowing the differences helps target support and treatment where work loss is worst. It also helps employers and insurers plan fairly. The study treats arthritis as an economic issue, not only a medical one.
plos-pone-0010570:
Pierre Sellier and colleagues varied treatment start times in monkeys infected with SIV. Their PLOS ONE study, from 2010, asked how timing shapes early spread. In human HIV, the moment of infection is rarely known. So the cost of delaying therapy is hard to measure directly. Monkeys infected with the related SIV virus offer a timed model. Six groups started antiretroviral treatment at different points after infection.

Earlier starts changed both early viral growth and how widely the virus seeded the body. Reservoirs seeded early may persist for life despite treatment. Timing data from monkeys guide thinking about treating very early human infection. They also define windows where intervention could limit reservoirs. This study maps those windows experimentally.
plos-pone-0010670:
Örjan de Manzano and colleagues linked brain chemistry to creativity test scores, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Dopamine helps the brain filter signals, letting some through and holding others back. The team focused on dopamine D2 receptors in the thalamus, a relay hub deep in the brain.

Healthy volunteers with fewer thalamic D2 receptors scored higher on creativity tests. Looser filtering may let in more ideas to combine, at some cost to focus. The authors compare this pattern with traits seen in some mental illnesses. The result supports a shared biology behind creative thinking and certain disorders, without claiming one causes the other.
plos-pone-0010770:
Omar Kabbarah and colleagues compared the genomes of melanomas before and after spread, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Melanoma kills mainly by metastasizing, reaching organs far from the first skin tumor. The genetic steps that turn a local tumor into a spreading one were only partly mapped.

Primary tumors and their matched metastases were profiled together. The spread tumors carried added changes on top of the primary tumor's set. Some changes clustered in pathways tied to growth and movement. An integrated map like this narrows the search for prognostic tests and for drugs aimed at spread itself, melanoma's lethal step.
plos-pone-0010870:
Andreas Pfenning, Tae-Kyung Kim, James Spotts and co-authors published this brain genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. CaRF is a protein that switches genes on in neurons when calcium signals arrive, first found through its grip on a gene for a key brain growth factor. Almost nothing else was known about its targets, so the team mapped where it binds across the genome.

They showed CaRF's DNA-binding part is strongly conserved through evolution and grips DNA on its own, in a sequence-specific way. A genome-wide scan in neuronal DNA found well over a hundred binding sites, most near known genes. Many neighbors take part in signaling between nerve cells. Pfenning and colleagues turn an obscure factor into a mapped regulator, giving neuroscientists a list of genes it may coordinate when neurons fire.
plos-pone-0010970:
Nathalie Burch, Anne-Sophie Arnold, Flurin Item and co-authors published this muscle model study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Exercise protects health through molecular changes inside muscle, but those changes are hard to study without a good laboratory model. The authors tuned electric pulse stimulation of cultured mouse muscle cells until the cells behaved as if they had trained.

They calibrated the pulsing using a master exercise gene, PGC-1alpha, as the benchmark, then compared gene changes in the dish against real mouse muscle after single and repeated treadmill sessions. The stimulated cells reproduced the trained muscle's pattern across metabolic and structural genes. Burch and colleagues deliver a bench model of exercise that needs no animals for first-pass questions. It should speed the search for the signals that make activity so protective.
plos-pone-0011070:
Nicole Schonrock, Yazi Ke, David Humphreys and co-authors published this Alzheimer's study in PLOS ONE in 2010. MicroRNAs, the small regulators that fine-tune gene activity, are abundant in brain and their profiles shift in Alzheimer's disease, but whether those shifts are cause or consequence was unclear. The authors exposed mouse hippocampal neurons to amyloid-beta, the peptide that drives the disease, and watched the regulators respond.

Using sensitive low-density arrays, they found about half of all measured microRNAs fell in response to the peptide, with changes unfolding over time. Schonrock and colleagues show that amyloid itself deregulates the neuronal microRNA network, placing the disruption downstream of the known culprit and potentially upstream of further damage. Silenced microRNAs could unleash harmful genes, making them candidate targets for therapy and markers of early disease.
plos-pone-0011170:
Romano, Carvalho-Mello, Jamal and colleagues traced hepatitis C in PLOS ONE in 2010. This liver virus spreads through blood contact, often within close social groups. The team asked how people's social networks shape the paths the virus takes through a community.

They showed that network structure does guide how the virus spreads and clusters. That means prevention aimed only at single people may miss the real routes of spread. Health action that follows the network can reach those most at risk sooner. The approach suits a virus that often stays silent for years while still spreading.
plos-pone-0011270:
Lay, Davis, Chen-Bee and colleagues protected rat brains with touch in PLOS ONE in 2010. Mild stimulation of the whiskers, given soon after a stroke blocked blood flow, was tested for its effect on the brain's outer layer. The result was striking for such a gentle input.

The mild sensory input completely protected the adult cortex from ischemic damage in their model. A natural protective reflex seems to reroute blood or activity to save tissue. Therapies inspired by this effect could buy time for stroke patients. The finding also challenges the idea that only strong interventions can rescue the stroked brain.
plos-pone-0011370:
Xiaodong Bai and colleagues built a gene resource for the soybean aphid in 2010 by combining newer sequencing methods. The aphid is an invasive pest that drains soybean plants and spreads plant viruses across North America. Without a solid set of its gene sequences, researchers had few molecular tools to study how it feeds, resists sprays, and adapts.

By merging data from complementary sequencing strategies, the team assembled a far richer catalog of the aphid's active genes than either method gave alone. That catalog lets scientists pick target genes for study and for control. Pest managers gain starting material for tools such as gene-based traps or sprays aimed at aphid-specific genes. The paper shows how pairing methods can fast-track resources for a pest that farming cannot wait on.
plos-pone-0011470:
Sundaravadivel Balasubramanian and co-authors measured in 2010 how heart muscle cells remodel their inner skeleton under growth pressure. When the heart must work harder, as in high blood pressure, its muscle cells thicken, a change called hypertrophy. Beta-actin, a core skeleton protein, must move and turn over for that thickening to happen, yet its dynamics had not been timed in adult heart cells.

Working with adult feline heart cells, the team found that growth stimulation speeds beta-actin dynamics, with the protein exchanging and rearranging faster than in quiet cells. That restlessness is part of how the cell rebuilds itself bigger. Understanding the skeleton's behavior during thickening matters because hypertrophy can tip from helpful adaptation into heart failure. A step that only happens during remodeling is a possible point for drugs meant to slow the harmful kind.
plos-pone-0011570:
Colin Steer and co-authors reported in 2010 that a child's genes decide how much breastfeeding lifts that child's IQ. Breastfeeding is linked on average to higher IQ, yet the gain varies. Fatty acid handling is a plausible reason. Milk's value depends on the fats a child's body can build from it. The team tested variants in FADS2, a gene for processing fatty acids, alongside breastfeeding history and IQ.

FADS2 variants modified the effect of breastfeeding on child IQ, so nutrition's payoff depended on the child's DNA. That gene-environment interplay warns against one-size advice and against reading the average effect as everyone's effect. It also points to a mechanism, fat processing, that formula design could one day compensate for in children whose genes make them poor processors. Such studies refine public guidance without overturning it: breastfeeding helps, and genes help explain for whom it helps most.
plos-pone-0011670:
Benjamin Krummel and co-authors tested a blood assay for tuberculosis contact tracing, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Standard immune tests for TB can show that contact happened, but they cannot tell a recent infection from a remote one. That distinction decides who needs prompt preventive treatment when a new case is found.

The team used an IL-2 ELISpot test, which reads a different immune signal, during a contact investigation. Their results assess whether this signal separates recent from remote infection better than existing assays. A sharper timing test would let health teams focus drugs and follow-up where the risk is freshest.
plos-pone-0011770:
Shreya Kanodia and co-authors studied lasting remissions in chronic myelogenous leukaemia, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Interferon treatment produces complete cytogenetic remission in a minority of patients, and in a few the remission persists after the drug is stopped. Interferon partly works by raising killer T cells specific for a leukaemia peptide called PR1.

The team related those PR1-specific T cells to remissions maintained without further treatment. Their findings suggest immune guards keep the cancer down after interferon withdrawal. That link supports therapies that strengthen such T cells to hold leukaemia in check.
plos-pone-0011870:
Carmel McVicar and colleagues compared anemia drugs in 2010 for an unwanted side effect: new blood vessel growth in the eye. The drugs, called erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, boost red blood cell production and are widely used for anemia. Doctors have worried they might also worsen vessel overgrowth in an oxygen-starved retina.

Using a mouse model of ischemic retinopathy, where the retina lacks oxygen, the team tested three agents side by side. The agents did not behave alike in their effect on vessel growth. Such differences matter when choosing an anemia drug for patients who already have fragile eye vessels, since the wrong pick could add harm where sight is at stake.
plos-pone-0011970:
Jayavel Sridhar and co-workers introduced in 2010 a computer tool for finding small regulatory RNAs hidden between bacterial genes. These small RNAs are everywhere in bacteria and help control survival, adaptation, and disease-causing behavior. Existing search tools missed many of them or buried real ones in false alarms.

Their program, sRNAscanner, scans bacterial genomes for intergenic small RNA genes with a method built for that specific hunt. Each small RNA found is a possible control knob for traits like antibiotic tolerance. Better detection widens the target list for understanding, and perhaps one day disarming, bacterial pathogens.
plos-pone-0012070:
Ida Casorelli and co-workers showed in 2010 that a gene for DNA repair also steers the swelling of the gut in mice. The gene, Mutyh, makes an enzyme that fixes DNA bases spoiled by oxygen. Faults in the human form of the gene cause bowel cancer in a rare family polyp ill. Weak repair was also thought to lift the cancer risk that comes with long gut swelling.

In mice bred to stand in for the human gut ill called ulcerative colitis, the team found the gene shaping the swelling itself, not just the cancers that may come years later. A repair gene with a hand in swelling ties two fields that are most often kept apart. The tie may help tell why long-held gut swelling so often ends in bowel cancer.
plos-pone-0012170:
Emanuela Esposito, Emanuela Mazzon, Irene Paterniti, and co-authors tested a heart drug on spinal cord injury in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Olprinone is used in clinics for heart failure, where it strengthens the heartbeat and opens blood vessels. After a spinal cord injury, much of the lasting damage comes not from the blow itself but from swelling and cell death that follow in the next hours.

Given after trauma, the drug calmed that follow-on inflammation and reduced cell death in the injured cord. Repurposing a known drug skips years of safety testing if it works. Results like this mark a candidate worth moving toward trials for an injury that still has almost no drug treatments.
plos-pone-0012270:
Sanghwa Lee, Jinwoo Lee, and Sungchul Hohng improved a single-molecule light technique in PLOS ONE in 2010. The method watches one molecule at a time by energy transfer between glowing dyes, and using three colors at once can reveal complex dances between several moving parts. Older three-color versions suffered from dyes bleeding into each other's channels and from signals that died too quickly to follow.

Their design separates the three colors cleanly and stretches the watching time. Longer, cleaner movies of single molecules show steps that averaged measurements blur away. Better tools of this kind spread fast, because every lab studying molecular machines faces the same limits.
plos-pone-0012370:
Makandwe Nyirenda, Basia Zaba, Till Bärnighausen and co-authors tackled a bias problem in HIV surveys in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper from rural South Africa. Household surveys give the main HIV rate estimates, but many people refuse testing or are away, and those missing people may carry HIV at higher rates. Raw survey numbers can thus understate the true rate.

The team used death rates from a watched population to adjust survey results for the people who did not respond. Their corrected estimates came out higher and matched other local data better. Health planners who rely on survey rates for clinics, drugs, and staff can use this method to avoid planning for too few patients.
plos-pone-0012470:
Hui-Ju Hsu, Chin-Fu Lee, Andrea Locke and colleagues stretched cells at different speeds to watch their skeletons respond, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Cells in tissues are pulled and squeezed as the matrix around them deforms. They answer by reorienting stress fibers, the cables that give them shape and strength, and by firing growth signals named JNK and ERK.

The team found the remodeling and the signals depended on how fast the stretch came, not on a focal adhesion protein called FAK. Rate, not just amount, is what cells read. That rule matters for engineering tissues and for understanding diseases like asthma, where airway cells face abnormal stretch patterns.
plos-pone-0012570:
Michael Daly, Elena Gaidamakova, Vera Matrosova and fellow researchers studied how a near-un-killable microbe guards its proteins, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The bacterium Deinococcus radiodurans can survive blasts of radiation and dry spells that kill almost all other life. The team holds that its trick is not tougher DNA. Small guard molecules shield its proteins from harm, so its repair crews stay alive and can fix the DNA later.

The study details these small-molecule shields and how they keep proteins safe from rust-like damage. If proteins are the true weak point, then guarding them is the master move for surviving radiation. The same chemistry could one day help shield healthy tissue in cancer care, or crews on long space flights.
plos-pone-0012670:
Avogadri, Merghoub, Maughan and co-authors tested a virus-based vaccine against melanoma, the deadliest skin cancer. Melanoma often shrugs off standard chemo and radiation, so immune treatments are a key hope. Their 2010 study loaded alphavirus particles with TRP-2, a protein found on melanoma cells.

The particles trained both antibody and cell arms of the immune system against the tumour. In their mouse tests the vaccine gave a strong treatment effect. Dual immune attack is a sought-after trait in cancer vaccines, making this design worth further study.  Both arms were measured in the same animals for fairness.
plos-pone-0012770:
Abdel Rassoul, Alves, Pantesco and co-authors compared gene activity in the ageing brain of a tiny primate with that in Alzheimer's disease. Ageing is the biggest risk factor for Alzheimer's, yet most of what happens in a normally ageing brain is still unclear. Their 2010 study used the grey mouse lemur, a small primate that ages in ways close to humans.

They read gene activity in the temporal cortex across ageing and in disease-like change. Separating plain ageing from disease signals helps drug hunters aim at the disease alone. The lemur gives that comparison a primate setting.
plos-pone-0012870:
Liu, Meckel and Long separated two jobs of a transport protein in natural killer cells. NK cells kill infected and cancerous cells by releasing granules full of toxic proteins. Their 2010 study used automated imaging to track thousands of granules moving inside living NK cells.

They found Rab27a does one job for granules near the cell surface and a different one for granules deeper in the cell body. Splitting those jobs matters for immune faults where granule release fails. Precise granule tracking itself is a tool other cell biologists can reuse.
plos-pone-0328670:
Daye Yang and colleagues report a 2026 animal study on functional dyspepsia, a lasting stomach disorder marked by a weak gut lining and low-level inflammation. Their focus is a treatment that sends mild electrical pulses to the vagus nerve through the skin of both ears. The team wanted to know whether this stimulation calms the gut by changing the behavior of immune cells called macrophages.

In mice bred to mimic the disorder, two weeks of stimulation improved feeding and lowered a key inflammatory signal in the small intestine. More macrophages shifted into their calming form, and the gut barrier grew stronger. When mice lacked a gene named GATA3 in these cells, the benefits largely faded, showing that this gene helps drive the effect.
plos-pone-0333370:
Lina Xu and colleagues asked how an aging countryside affects greener farming in China. Using national family panel surveys from 2018, 2020, and 2022, they linked the share of older adults in farm households to measures of green agricultural development. Their analysis focused on farm households rather than whole regions.

Households with more older members scored lower on green development, mainly through weaker farm earnings, and the effect was strongest in western China. Hired farm services softened the harm, raising output while cutting chemical use. The results suggest that support services for older farmers can protect both incomes and the environment.
plos-pone-0335670:
Mirjana Čizmović and co-authors studied cigarette prices in Montenegro from 2010 to 2022 in work published in 2026, asking how tobacco firms respond when excise taxes rise. Governments raise such taxes to cut smoking, but firms can blunt the effect through pricing.

Monthly prices for hundreds of brands were analysed across price tiers. Cheap brands absorbed part of each tax rise, staying affordable, while premium brands raised prices by more than the tax. Slim cigarettes stayed especially cheap. This cross subsidy keeps a wide price ladder that taxes alone cannot close, and the authors argue tax design must change to stop it.
plos-pone-0337870:
Kosuke Nakano and colleagues measured, for the first time in walking patients, the actual straightening force a knee brace applies, and how brace design changes the load inside the knee. Their 2026 study fitted sixteen people with inner-side knee osteoarthritis with a sensor-equipped brace and compared no brace against two versions differing only in the length of the brace's inner lower-leg strut.

The longer strut generated stronger corrective force through the whole stride and significantly cut the inward knee load at the moment of foot strike, when damage-relevant stress peaks. Stronger brace force tracked lower joint load across patients. The findings give brace fitters a concrete design dial: a longer inner strut buys measurable unloading for arthritic knees.
plos-pone-0338270:
Kweku Safo-Ankama and co-authors surveyed garment and textile firms in Ghana's Western Region about what pushes them toward greener production. Small clothing firms face real barriers: hard-to-find materials, money pressure, and the practical headaches of cleaner methods. Their 2026 study collected three hundred fifteen valid responses from small and medium firms and modeled the relationships statistically.

Two forces clearly mattered: the sustainability challenges firms face and their limited access to materials both shaped how far they adopted green practices. Money pressure, surprisingly, showed no significant effect. The authors recommend investment in recycling technology and closer cooperation across the industry. They frame greener production as a route to jobs and regional standing in West African textile manufacturing, not just an environmental duty.
plos-pone-0339270:
Mohammady and colleagues fed Nile tilapia a seaweed extract to test health effects in a 2026 study. Groups of young fish received five diets with rising extract doses for seventy days. Growth, digestion, blood measures, gut shape, and defense genes were all tracked.

Fish on supplemented diets grew better and used feed more efficiently than the control group. Digestive enzymes, blood values, and antioxidant defenses also rose with supplementation. Gut surfaces developed in ways that favor nutrient uptake. The extract, called fucoidan, looks like a helpful feed addition for farmed tilapia, a cheap protein source across Africa and Asia, though best dose and cost still need farm-scale checks.
plos-pone-0343670:
Kihun Nam and colleagues studied disaster recovery in South Korea. Official records covered the years 2015 to 2024. Damage sums and recovery spending were split by hazard. Splits also ran by region. A careful comparison used Japan data as well. Japan tracks deaths more than spending. Recovery is often assumed to scale with damage.

Spending tracked damage fairly closely at national level. Hazard types differed in recovery intensity. Regions differed in spending patterns too. Extreme years broke the tidy line. Extra recovery kicked in past asset repair. Recovery plans should expect surges after huge events. A straight ratio will underfund the worst years.
plos-pone-0343870:
Wei Shi and colleagues studied how heat and pressure change the way sand carrying wash fluid leaks into cracked rock during horizontal well cleaning. Leaks waste fluid and delay oil return. Scans rebuilt the crack pore network, particle sizes were tuned by a classic bridging rule, and coupled fluid and particle simulations were checked against lab tests and a field job.

Higher pressure pushed particles deeper and worsened deep pollution. Higher heat swelled particles and thinned fluid, so particles sealed shallow cracks instead and invasion depth fell sharply. Field crews who match fluid to formation heat and control flow rate cut leaks and restart production sooner, the team reports.
plos-pone-0344470:
Jin Gyeong Kim and Jiyeon Kim compare text-mining methods that help investigators find hidden abuse material trading sites on the dark web. Anonymity and scattered pages make such crime hard to track, and searches depend on having the right keywords. Their 2026 study gathers text from more than twenty-four hundred dark web pages and tests three ways of pulling out telling terms.

A graph method that ranks words by how centrally they connect to others proved most precise alone. Pairing it with a meaning-based method expanded early clues best and surfaced the most useful new keywords. The combined approach could help police widen a small early lead into a fuller map of illegal sites faster and with less manual trawling.
plos-pone-0347670:
Xiao Xuefeng and colleagues test whether friendly root fungi can carry a valuable Chinese tree through drought, in this 2026 PLOS ONE greenhouse study. Cinnamomum migao, a medicinal tree found only in southwest China's dry karst country, struggles as droughts grow harsher. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi trade nutrients with roots, but which fungus and mixture work best was unknown.

Seedlings were paired with two fungal species, singly and mixed, then measured for fungal colonization, root vigor, growth, biomass, and soil enzyme activity. All three treatments significantly improved growth and nutrient uptake over the dry conditions. For growers restoring or farming this tree, the results give a concrete inoculation strategy against a drying climate.
plos-pone-0347770:
Julia Brott and Nathalie Bérubé use genetically engineered mice to locate where a gene's loss causes intellectual disability, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Mutations in the ATRX gene cause ATR-X syndrome in people. Earlier mouse work blamed the forebrain broadly, so the team deleted the gene mainly in one hippocampal area, CA1, in two genetic backgrounds.

Those mice became underactive and more anxious but learned and remembered normally, including spatial tasks. Only mice with the gene removed across the wider forebrain showed the cognitive failures. The disability, the authors conclude, arises from disrupted circuits beyond CA1 alone, which redirects the search for mechanisms and therapies.
plos-pone-0347870:
Dan Long and colleagues built a deep learning system to spot major depression from brain scans. Standard network models treat the brain as an unordered graph, losing track of which region is which. Their 2026 framework adds edge-aware processing that respects each region's identity, plus a contrastive learning step that sharpens the features separating patients from healthy volunteers. The data covered more than eleven hundred people.

The system outperformed conventional machine learning and other neural network models, though its accuracy remained modest. It also highlighted familiar depression regions, including parts of the frontal cortex, the thalamus, and the insula, which strengthens confidence in its reasoning. The authors see it as decision support, not a diagnostic replacement.
plos-pone-0348070:
Salih Gürsoy and Aylin Zekioglu compared two ways of teaching wrestling moves in middle school gym class: students teaching each other, or the teacher demonstrating directly. Thirty-six students trained for eight weeks on four techniques, from an arm drag to the double-leg takedown. Independent raters scored performance with standard criteria.

The peer-taught group clearly outperformed direct instruction on the underarm pass and the double-leg takedown, two moves needing fine coordination between partners. The other two techniques showed no real difference. Peer teaching may shine exactly where a move is complex, because explaining and correcting a partner forces deeper learning. The study gives gym teachers evidence for mixing student-led practice into skill units.
plos-pone-0348170:
Amirah Akhtar and colleagues interviewed twelve British South Asians living with depression that keeps returning, for this 2026 PLOS ONE study. This group faces higher depression risk and extra barriers to getting help, so the researchers asked what treatment people had actually experienced and what they would choose.

Participants described weighing the pros and cons of medication in an ongoing, personal way, and most preferred non-drug options, especially creative, art-based therapy. Help that was adapted to their culture and included religion appealed most. Complaints centered on inexperienced therapists and on support ending too abruptly, leaving gains to fade. Services, the authors argue, should build culturally fitted, longer-lasting support.
plos-pone-0348270:
Jianye Gu and co-workers tackle a stubborn problem for learning machines: adding new categories over time without forgetting old ones. As models expand their inner feature spaces, memories of earlier classes drift and blur. Their 2026 method freezes the core network and adds tiny gated adapters for each new task, building separate subspaces that still share information through attention.

A learned mapping then lines old class memories up inside the newest space, all without revisiting old training data. Benchmark tests showed better accuracy and stronger resistance to forgetting than rival approaches. Keeping the core frozen also kept computing costs low. The design suits tools that must keep learning on the job, from photo sorting to medical screening.
plos-pone-0348370:
Fei Fei, Richard J. Siegert, Xiaohan Zhang, and Jonathan Koffman interviewed thirty people living with the chronic lung disease COPD at a Chinese teaching hospital about living with clusters of symptoms. Breathlessness, cough, and exhaustion rarely arrive alone, yet medicine often treats each in isolation. The 2026 qualitative study asked patients what these tangled symptoms mean to them.

Patients described trigger symptoms, such as a cough that sets off breathlessness and then fatigue, in a chain reaction they learn to anticipate. The clusters disrupted work, social life, and identity, and patients managed them by personal priority, not medical ranking. The authors urge clinicians to ask about triggers and meanings, not just severity scores.
plos-pone-0348570:
Yucheng Li and co-workers compare two ways of aiming radiation beams for early left-sided breast cancer while patients hold a deep breath. Holding the breath moves the heart away from the beam and shields it. Their 2026 study builds both plans for twenty patients treated at one hospital and weighs tumor coverage, dose to nearby organs, and time on the table.

One plan shaped the target slightly better. The other plan lowered dose to nearly every organ at risk and finished its beam time faster. Session lengths settled as patients gained practice across visits. For this breath-hold care, the gentler plan looks attractive where heart and lung sparing matter most.
plos-pone-0348670:
Vijay U. Rathod and co-workers propose one flexible deep learning system that can predict several different diseases from table-style medical data. Many prediction tools are built for a single disease and demand heavy computing. Their 2026 framework picks its model parts based on each dataset's size, feature count, and balance, and explains its outputs.

The system was tried on three public datasets covering heart disease, diabetes, and Parkinson's voice recordings. Paired model combinations scored best for heart disease and diabetes, while a simpler network led on voice data. Results sat close to classic methods overall. A shared, explainable toolkit could help smaller clinics predict disease without building a tool from scratch.
plos-pone-0348770:
Florence Wongnaah and colleagues counted how many women in Ghana report a sexually transmitted infection or symptoms that point to one. They used the twenty twenty-two national demographic and health survey, covering nearly thirteen thousand women of reproductive age. Reports covered infections themselves plus genital discharge and sores, symptoms that often signal an untreated infection.

About one woman in four reported an infection or a related symptom in the survey window. Discharge was the most common report. Odds ran lower for women in their forties, for those who first had sex at seventeen or later, and for mothers, while having several partners raised the odds. Because these infections feed infertility and HIV risk, the patterns help Ghanaian health services aim testing and treatment at the women most likely to be missed.
plos-pone-0348870:
Yorino Sato, Yuta Kawagoe, and Kazuhiro Kawamura track a cell-aging marker called p16 in mouse ovaries as the animals grow older. The marker flags worn-out cells, and the ovary's decline drives falling fertility with age. Their 2026 study measures the marker across body tissues at four ages and checks breeding outcomes step by step.

Marker levels climbed steeply with age in ovary support cells, but not in the eggs themselves. Older females released far fewer eggs, and fewer pregnancies ended in live pups, while fertilization in the dish stayed normal. The failure point seems to come after implantation. Reading this marker in support cells could become a way to judge ovary aging without harming eggs.
plos-pone-0348970:
Ainura Moldokmatova and colleagues built a math model to test why HIV infections keep dropping in Kyrgyzstan among people who shoot drugs. Local experts had three hunches: strong prevention work, shifts in drug use, or cases that go uncounted. The model split the group into health states and let each hunch play out on its own.

In the model, much of the drop came from there being fewer people who shoot drugs at all. Prevention work and drug treatment helped, but on their own they did not match the fall. Telling the true driver from the rest matters: a land that credits the wrong cause may cut the very work that holds the line.
plos-pone-0349170:
Angkon Roy and Showmitra Sarkar assess the health of Bangladesh's coastal ecosystems in this 2026 study. The coast there spans nineteen districts and is home to tens of millions of people, while facing rapid building, habitat loss, and more frequent natural disasters. Checking such a huge area on foot is impractical, so the authors turned to satellite data and computer mapping.

Using a machine learning method together with a pressure-state-response framework, they scored ecosystem health for two years, a decade apart. Health had clearly worsened: areas of low health grew substantially, while medium and high health areas shrank. The strongest district in the earlier year was Satkhira and the weakest was Chittagong, but by the later year different districts held those spots. The authors offer the maps as a basis for decisions about protecting the coast.
plos-pone-0349370:
Xia Huang and colleagues examined more than thirty-three thousand Chinese adults for a nonlinear link between waist size relative to height and an early sign of kidney damage, protein leaking into urine. Most research on belly fat and kidneys assumes more is simply worse. Their analysis used flexible curve models to let the relationship bend, and searched for turning points.

The association formed a U shape, with risk lowest in a middle band of waist-to-height values and rising at both extremes. Subgroup checks kept the pattern robust. The finding warns against treating thinness as automatically protective for kidneys and gives clinicians a target range rather than a one-sided limit. Large, population-spanning data make the bend in the curve hard to dismiss as noise.
plos-pone-0349570:
Alexis Archambeaud and colleagues reviewed the records of patients treated with the drug dapsone at a university hospital in Tours, France, between 2005 and 2021. Dapsone is used for infections and immune diseases, and it can break down red blood cells. Doctors wondered whether a particular danger sign, shredded red cell fragments called schistocytes, appears with this drug and what it means.

Of nineteen patients with blood smears taken during treatment, about half had detectable schistocytes, and those patients had deeper drops in hemoglobin, showing stronger blood breakdown. Ordinarily this fragment pattern points to a clotting emergency, so finding it with dapsone complicates diagnosis. Clinicians reading such a smear need to weigh the drug before assuming the worst.
plos-pone-0349670:
Cora O'Leary, Margaret Curtin, and co-authors published a 2026 protocol for mapping the research on sending technology-dependent children home from hospital. Children who rely on breathing machines often wait long past medical readiness for discharge because training carers, housing, and home nursing must align. The planned review will search four databases for English-language studies since 2015 on the discharge process for these children.

Two reviewers will screen and extract findings independently, organizing the evidence from the child's level up to policy. As a protocol, the document fixes the method in advance rather than reporting results. The authors expect the finished review to expose where discharge pathways break down and to inform family-centered planning and policy for care closer to home.
plos-pone-0349770:
Han Thi Ngoc Nguyen and colleagues surveyed two hundred twelve primary healthcare workers in a district of Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, about stress at work and how they cope. Frontline clinics carry wide duties with limited resources, a recipe for strain. Workers completed standard scales for perceived stress and for coping styles, from problem solving to avoidance, in early 2025.

The analysis mapped how common high stress was and which personal, family, and job traits traveled with it, using models that trimmed weak factors step by step. Coping patterns matter because the same workload can break one worker and not another. District health managers can use the identified risk factors to target support, staffing changes, or training where stress concentrates most.
plos-pone-0349870:
Maria Loconsole, Elisa Tedaldi, and Lucia Regolin tested how newly hatched chicks judge quantities, a window into the earliest roots of number sense. Earlier work showed two different strategies: chicks sometimes just approach the bigger group of familiar objects, and sometimes they react to whether a group can be split into two equal halves. The team reran both setups under matched conditions.

One group of chicks was imprinted on identical objects and chose between sets of five and nine. Another group grew used to even-numbered sets, letting the researchers test reactions to sets that cannot split evenly. Both known patterns were successfully reproduced. Showing the two strategies coexist clarifies that young brains use more than one route to quantity.
plos-pone-0350270:
Gizachew Tadele Tiruneh and co-authors evaluated Ethiopia's move to digitize its community health information system, which health workers use to track mothers and children in rural villages. The government rolled out the electronic system in 2018, but its effect on service use was unproven. Their 2026 survey compared households in areas with and without the system, matching similar communities to make the comparison fair.

Areas with the digital system did better on nearly every measure. Contraceptive use, births in facilities, and childhood vaccination coverage all ran higher, with gains of roughly nine to fifteen percentage points after adjustment. The authors call the results evidence that digitizing frontline records can transform maternal and child health, while noting the survey design cannot fully rule out other explanations.
plos-pone-0350670:
Ruby Hornuvo and colleagues held group talks with eighty seven waste workers in Greater Accra, Ghana, and Kisumu, Kenya, comparing plastic only collectors with mixed waste collectors. Informal workers fill huge gaps where city services fall short. Talks sorted barriers, helpers, and fixes for each business type across both cities.

Both groups lacked crushers and trucks, faced harassment, met faecal hazards in waste, and got little public respect. Paths diverged by city: Accra had moved toward rigid plastic sorting, while home sorting in Kisumu stayed low. Fair pay, gear, and recognition for informal collectors are prerequisites, the authors argue, for any clean city plan to work.
plos-pone-0350770:
Eui Jun Lee and co-authors in Korea tested whether a small language model could help sort sick children in an emergency department in 2026. Triage, judging who needs care first, is safety critical, and big models are hard to run inside hospitals.

They trained the model on tens of thousands of past visits, rewarding it for safe choices. It matched the recorded triage level in well over half of test cases and was nearly always within one level. Dangerous under-triage was rare. A model using only structured data scored higher overall, so the authors present the language model as support, not a replacement, for nurses.
plos-pone-0351070:
Kang and colleagues read the full genomes of two scrub typhus bacteria from South Korea in a 2026 study. Scrub typhus is a mite-borne fever common in Asia, and the strain studied matches a Japanese reference type also found in Korea. Two archived patient isolates were sequenced with a mix of long and short reading methods.

Both genomes formed single circular chromosomes packed with repeated stretches, a known trait of this bacterium. Their surface and typing markers matched the Japanese reference exactly, and family trees placed them in its group. Complete local genomes help track how this fever's strains relate across borders and guide future vaccine and test design.
plos-pone-0351170:
Daniel Perez-Garcia de los Salmones and colleagues studied personal ornaments, beads and pendants, from Llonin Cave in Asturias, Spain. Layers span roughly twenty two thousand to eleven thousand years ago, the largest such set in the region. Tests covered animal source, size, wear, and making marks to trace where pieces came from and how they were made and used.

Patterns shifted over time in whether the cave group made ornaments or brought them in, and in what the pieces signalled socially. Shell and material links tie coastal and inland groups together. Ornaments were not mere decoration: they carried identity and mapped movement and alliances among Ice Age hunter groups in northern Iberia.
plos-pone-0351470:
Yong Zhang and Runming Zhao present a vision system tuned to find small faults on power lines from small field computers. Lines cross busy scenes, faults vary hugely in size, and edge gear has little power to spare. Their design guards fine detail early, then uses focused attention to pick out key defects while shuffling channels to keep the model lean.

On a cable inspection data set, the system beat its base model on both correct calls and overall detection scores. Extra tests showed it also handled insulators, dampers, and bolts well. For power firms, a compact detector that stays accurate on tiny faults could mean faster drone patrols and fewer missed risks.
plos-pone-0351670:
Life-threatening complications in pregnancy are rare but telling events for a health system. Ye Xu, Peimin Hua, and Ye Shen analyzed more than one hundred fifty-six thousand deliveries in Wuxi, China, across four years of citywide monitoring, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

About three hundred fifteen critical cases were found, roughly one in five hundred births. The rate held steady for three years, then rose in the final year. Mothers aged thirty-five and older grew to about a quarter of cases, driving much of the increase. Risk group patterns shifted too, from mostly high-risk toward more moderate-risk mothers, a warning the authors send to local planners.
plos-pone-0351870:
Four health problems now show up early and often in Chinese schoolchildren: poor eyesight, obesity, tooth decay, and curved spines. Yun Shao and co-authors built a shared risk checklist covering all four, described in this 2026 PLOS One paper aimed at children aged seven to nineteen.

Guided by national child health plans, the team drafted a three-level framework from past research and expert meetings. Specialists then rated and trimmed the items through two rounds of structured consultation. The result is a single tool meant to flag risky habits and conditions before disease sets in, helping schools and clinics aim prevention where it counts most.
plos-pone-0351970:
Irena Danilovska and three colleagues built a new scale in this 2026 PLOS One study for spotting what sets successful startup founders apart. Most older tools judge the firm, or use broad personality tests made to explain why people start businesses at all. They say little about which founders actually succeed. The team wrote a thirty-one item scale covering six traits, among them resilience, curiosity, bold decision making, and leadership that changes teams.

They tested the scale on more than ten thousand people: proven founders, company managers, and would-be founders. The six traits held together well as a measure. They also separated successful founders from the other two groups by wide margins, far wider than broad personality tests usually manage. Backers and coaches could use such a scale to judge founder potential earlier.
plos-pone-0352170:
Hirsch and colleagues, in a 2026 paper, catalog what neighborhood data exist inside a giant American COVID-19 research alliance. The alliance joins fourteen long-running health cohorts, more than fifty thousand people in all, so their stored addresses can reveal how place shaped pandemic outcomes. The paper is an inventory, meant to make later studies possible.

Together the cohorts cover areas holding about half the United States population, though only about a quarter of its land, since people cluster. Compared with the country, covered areas were more urban and wealthy, with more residents born abroad and fewer cars per household. Twelve cohorts had recorded neighborhood traits, most often local income and education. Food access and walkability were the commonest built-environment measures, while nature data, such as air quality and green space, were rarest. The authors say harmonizing this patchwork is the next step.
plos-pone-0352270:
Gregory Kearney and four colleagues map COVID-19 deaths across North Carolina in this 2026 study. They ask whether the places with the most deaths were also the most socially vulnerable. Vulnerability here covers poverty, age, housing, and similar hardships. The data cover more than twenty-five thousand deaths from March 2020 to April 2022.

Using mapping software, the team located clusters where deaths ran high. Those hot spot areas scored higher on overall social vulnerability than the rest of the state. The gap was real but modest, and clustering patterns were mixed rather than uniform. Vulnerability therefore explains part of the uneven death map, not all of it. The authors offer the approach as a template for fairer responses to future respiratory outbreaks.
plos-pone-0352670:
Sherraine Della-Moretta and six colleagues test what happens when a primary care doctor joins the sickle cell team itself. Their 2026 retrospective study covers adults at one American tertiary centre from 2020 to 2025. Sickle cell disease fragments care badly. Patients see haematologists for crises but miss ordinary prevention. The centre embedded a board-certified generalist inside the comprehensive clinic. She attended its meetings and practised beside the specialists. Of nearly four hundred patients, about one hundred seventy-four received her care.
