Prevention gaps closed sharply for her patients. Cervical cancer screening odds were roughly four and a half times higher. Depression screening odds were higher still. Tetanus vaccination and sickle-specific annual checks also improved. Acute care use was tracked alongside. Fragmentation is usually blamed on patients missing appointments. This study relocates the fix: put the missing doctor inside the team the patient already trusts, and the routine care finally happens.
plos-pone-0352870:
Lanjie Wu and seven co-authors present this 2026 PLOS One study of chronic hepatitis B. Many patients on long-term antiviral pills fully suppress the virus's DNA. Yet their blood still carries viral RNA. That RNA is a sign the virus stays active inside the liver. The team reviewed one hundred fifty-five patients who had liver biopsies before treatment. They hunted for baseline traits that predict the lingering RNA signal.

Just under half the patients cleared the RNA. Two baseline traits predicted persistence on their own. One was higher starting viral DNA. The other was the absence of a viral core protein in the liver sample. The pair predicted better than either trait alone. The authors suggest the pairing could help doctors tailor treatment and monitoring. It suits patients whose virus refuses to go fully quiet.
plos-pone-0352970:
Williams, Riley, and Baxter-Gilbert studied what an invading salamander eats in Newfoundland in a 2026 paper. The island had no native amphibians, yet several introduced kinds now thrive, including this small woodland salamander. The team examined stomach contents and judged which prey were native and which were earlier invaders.

Comparing island diets with mainland diets tested whether broader eating helped the salamander settle. Feeding on prey that arrived earlier as invaders may also have eased its path. Invaders that eat flexibly can slip past competition that stops pickier newcomers. The case shows how one invasion can pave the way for the next.
plos-pone-0353070:
José Miguel Hernández-Agudelo and seven colleagues survey this 2026 PLOS One study of bats living in and around rural homes in southern Chile. Habitat fragmentation pushes some bat species into houses, raising contact with people and pets and the chance of disease spread. The team visited sixty-nine dwellings in two regions, documenting the houses and asking residents about bat contact and perceived risk.

Nearly half the homes reported bats, most houses were wooden, and two-thirds had unsealed openings bats could use. Households with dogs, cats, children, or older residents had significantly more contact. Most residents knew bats can transmit disease, mainly rabies, yet preventive habits were inconsistent and risks to livestock were underappreciated. The authors recommend joined-up education covering people, animals, and environment together.
plos-pone-0353170:
Untracht and colleagues, in a 2026 study, test whether light-based scans plus machine learning can judge how well a cancer drug works in lab-grown tumor balls. Most new drugs fail in human trials, often because early lab tests predict poorly. Three-dimensional tumor models grown with several cell types are more realistic, but fast, standard ways to grade them are scarce.

The team scanned tumor balls treated with three doses of a chemotherapy drug using optical coherence tomography, a method that builds depth images from reflected light. Two reader models were compared: one that views flat slices from many angles, and one that reads the full volume at once. The volume model sorted the dose groups far more accurately. The authors also point to the image features that drove the volume model's choices. Their results support using these scans for fast screening of drugs in realistic tumor models.
plos-pone-0353270:
Burchardi and colleagues set out a mixed-methods study in 2026 on care for post-COVID syndrome in Germany. Many patients manage lasting symptoms with little support. The study blends insurance records from dozens of insurers, a patient survey, interviews, and home visits for the most severely ill.

An expert panel will turn the findings into concrete steps for better care. Routine records show real care paths, while interviews reveal where patients feel abandoned. Combining both views should expose fixable gaps, such as missing referrals or unclear responsibility. The design treats patient experience as evidence alongside billing data.
plos-pone-0353470:
Woo Bin Park and four colleagues track how a dog-infecting bacterium rewires the chemistry of the immune cells it invades, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Brucella canis causes canine brucellosis, a growing concern as pet dogs live ever closer to people. Mouse immune cells in culture were infected and their small-molecule chemistry measured at several time points, with the biggest upheaval a day after infection.

Key building blocks tied to energy, defence chemistry, and cell membranes dropped sharply as infection took hold. The time-ordered map shows which pathways the bacterium bends first. The authors offer the atlas as a guide for future work on how this pathogen survives inside its host — and where it might be vulnerable.
plos-pone-0353570:
Aslan and Yılmaz explored brain signals for imagined swallowing in a 2026 study. Swallowing problems affect many people after illness or injury, and brain-based controls could one day help with therapy. Thirty volunteers wore scalp sensors while picturing swallowing saliva and picturing swallowing water, without actually moving.

Signals were cleaned, measured in many ways, and narrowed to the features that differed most reliably. Tests left one person out at a time, so the system had to read a brand-new person's signals, as a clinic tool must. Checking luck-based results guarded against false success. The work is an early step toward therapy tools that respond to mental practice alone.
plos-pone-0353970:
Mee Hoong See led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of BREAST-E, a low-cost method for measuring breast volume before reconstructive surgery using ordinary photographs alone. Software turns photos into three-dimensional models. The team tuned marker numbers, camera angles, and offsets across four levels of breast droop, then checked the estimates against removed tissue in twelve patients.

Estimates ran somewhat low on average, and accuracy was best for breasts without droop, growing shakier as droop increased. See offers the method for hospitals that cannot afford advanced imaging.
plos-pone-0354170:
Rawand Khasawneh and co-authors survey in 2026 dialysis patients in northern Jordan on skill with online health information, confidence in managing illness, and quality of life. Patients at four hospitals completed Arabic versions of three trusted scales. Chronic kidney disease and its treatment weigh heavily on daily life, so what lifts life quality matters for care design.

Life quality linked in simple checks to both online skill and confidence, yet those links faded once social and medical factors were counted. Holding a graduate degree and having a job predicted higher life quality, while diabetes predicted lower. Support may need to target work and schooling gaps first.
plos-pone-0354270:
Ryosuke Katayose and five colleagues study how patchy oxygen in a Japanese lake reshapes where fish and their prey live, in this 2026 field study. Warming surface water and oxygen-starved depths squeeze cold-water fish such as kokanee salmon and rainbow trout into a narrowing band. The team compared two open-water sites in a small lake whose unusual shape creates uneven oxygen conditions, using environmental DNA to locate the fish.

Kokanee DNA concentrated where oxygen stayed favorable in summer, when heat above and low oxygen below pinched their living space. The authors infer that this crowding changes where the fish feed, which in turn may pattern the zooplankton they hunt. Because the evidence is correlational, they phrase the food web effect as a possibility, but the study shows how invisible oxygen landscapes can quietly reorganize a lake's ecology.
plos-pone-0354370:
Maaidah Algamdi and Ali Alghamdi test whether computer models can predict how intense back pain will feel, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study from a Saudi hospital. Sixty-one patients with severe pain from lumbar disc problems provided personal details, lifestyle answers, and MRI scans of their spines. Two popular machine-learning methods were trained to separate strong pain from very strong pain.

Both models struggled. One missed every case of the strongest pain, while the other caught only a third, largely because most patients clustered in the worst category. The number of damaged disc levels mattered most among the clues. The authors are frank: the tools are not ready for clinic use and need far larger samples.
plos-pone-0354470:
Lama El Haj Sleiman and Linda Abou-Abbas published this 2026 mixed-methods study of screening new mothers for depression in a Lebanese public hospital. Postpartum depression often goes unscreened in Lebanon. Nurses and managers there answered surveys and joined discussion groups about what they know and what routine screening would require.

Most nurses recognized the condition and the baby blues, but few knew the standard screening questionnaires or all the risk factors. The obstacles looked organizational rather than resistant staff. The authors recommend training, clear referral routes, and building screening into routine after-birth care.
plos-pone-0354670:
Maryam Ghadimi led a team of eight authors on this 2026 protocol for a review of preventing a rare but blinding infection after eye injections. Injections into the eye treat many retinal diseases, yet clinics mix prevention steps in varied combinations that past reviews judged one at a time. Their plan uses network meta-analysis to compare whole strategies against each other across trials and observational studies.

Evidence will be graded for certainty using a standard framework. As a protocol, the paper promises a map of which prevention bundles work best, once the review is done.
plos-pone-0354870:
Hamidreza Ahmadasadi leads a team of eight testing whether a hormone passes a mother's diabetes risk to her pups, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Asprosin, a fasting hormone that pushes blood sugar up, was their suspect. Twelve pregnant rats were split into diabetic and healthy groups. Blood was sampled from mothers and, at sixteen weeks of age, from their male offspring, to see whether the hormone tracked sugar and fat problems across the generation.

Diabetic mothers carried clearly higher asprosin, and in them the hormone marched with unhealthy fat patterns and glucose measures. Their pups told a different story. Offspring asprosin levels were nearly identical between the groups, and no meaningful links to sugar or fat measures appeared in the young animals. Whatever carries diabetes risk from mother to child in this model, the authors conclude, it is not a simple inheritance of raised asprosin.
plos-pone-0354970:
Iffath Syed and co-authors investigate in 2026 what stresses workers in long term care homes, where burnout, injury, and quitting are common. In depth interviews and a survey gave both stories and counts. Stress at work can spill into health and family life, so naming its sources is a first step toward fixing them.

Time pressure, the work situation itself, and money worries topped the list. Family duties, personal health problems, and caring for children added more strain. Many workers leaned on friends, family, and colleagues for support, and used prayer or mindfulness to cope. The authors present support networks as a real buffer worth strengthening.
plos-pone-0355170:
Dalong Zhang and seven colleagues published this 2026 teaching study from an emergency department in Zhengzhou, China. Thirty resident doctors rotated through two teaching styles in a crossover plan: standard lectures and an immersive role-play method borrowed from a popular scripted murder-mystery game, where trainees act out clinical cases.

Residents reported higher satisfaction with the role-play lessons, and their hands-on clinical scores improved more than with lectures. Test scores and patient feedback showed no clear gap between the two styles. Because the group was small and from one hospital, Zhang presents the game format as a promising extra, not a replacement, for standard training.
plos-pone-0355370:
Wenhua Pu and coauthors published a 2026 cell study in PLOS ONE on a tiny RNA that may throttle muscle building. The work has implications for the muscle wasting seen in lung disease and cancer. Scanning blood from patients with chronic lung disease, the team had spotted this microRNA sharply changed. In mice healing from a muscle toxin injury, miR-191 and a gene called Wwp1 moved in opposite directions, hinting at a control pair.

Adding extra miR-191 to growing mouse muscle cells blocked their maturation: the master muscle gene and the contractile proteins of mature fibers fell, and a growth pathway's genes quieted. The mechanism proved direct: the microRNA latches onto Wwp1's message and suppresses it. The authors name this axis as a control point in muscle differentiation. If the same axis drives wasting in patients, blocking the microRNA could become a strategy against atrophy, though that is future work.
plos-pone-0355470:
Rinseo Park and co-authors tracked how social ties formed and dissolved among students working together inside virtual reality. Immersive classrooms are spreading, but group dynamics inside them are hard to observe with ordinary surveys. Their 2026 study logged interpersonal distances session by session during a university virtual reality course and modelled tie changes statistically.

Each extra connection a student held cut the odds of forming or keeping another tie by more than half. A shared friend, by contrast, more than doubled those odds. Students drifted toward isolation overall, yet their subgroups persisted. Tie changes also reduced lopsided group identification and raised familiarity within pairs. Park and colleagues offer the framework for studying small-group life in virtual spaces.
plos-pone-0356070:
Cas Goos and colleagues audit how well psychology papers report the quality of their measuring tools. When a study copies a questionnaire or task, readers need to know whether it was reliable and sound, and whether the copying team changed anything. The team reviewed dozens of measures used in a large set of repeat studies and their original papers, then re-checked the tools using open response data.

Full detail on how to reuse a measure appeared in about half of the repeat studies and in only a tiny share of originals. Many tools also passed checks for consistency unevenly across labs. Goos and colleagues urge authors and journals to report measurement quality plainly, since weak reporting can hide weak tools.
plos-pone-0356170:
Md Mahfuz Uddin and three colleagues compare eight machine learning methods for predicting cardiovascular disease in this 2026 study. Working from an open clinical dataset, they ranked risk factors with four different selection techniques and tested each algorithm under several cross-validation schemes, scoring accuracy, sensitivity, and overall discrimination. The goal was a fair head-to-head rather than another single-model claim.

One gradient boosting method, LightGBM, gave the most balanced performance, pairing the best discrimination score with strong sensitivity, while a rival edged it on raw accuracy but missed more true cases. Systolic blood pressure dominated the predictions, with age and cholesterol close behind; every trait except gender differed clearly between groups. The authors are measured: performance was respectable but not clinical-grade, and outside validation is required before any real deployment.
plos-pone-0356270:
Mingze Sun and seven colleagues translated a well-known sleep questionnaire into Chinese and tested whether it still works, reporting their results in 2026. The questionnaire, a short screening tool covering several common sleep problems, had not previously been validated for Chinese-speaking patients. Just over two hundred adults being treated for sleep disorders filled in the eleven-question version.

Statistical checks showed the translated questions hung together sensibly, sorting into four groups linked to sleep apnea, insomnia, restless legs, and unusual sleep behaviors. Scores lined up reasonably well with clinical measures such as the severity of breathing pauses during sleep. The authors also worked out cutoff scores for each problem area. They conclude the Chinese version is reliable enough for evaluating adult patients, giving clinics in China a quick shared screening tool.
plos-pone-0356370:
Andrea Pietravalle, Francesco Cavallin, Giovanni Putoto, and Daniele Trevisanuto used simulated data to test a published shortcut for dating a pregnancy after birth. The shortcut measures the width of a newborn's cerebellum by ultrasound and converts it to gestational age. Their 2026 simulation study was aimed at poor countries, where early prenatal scans are rare. It generated four datasets matching real low-income studies. It scored the equation's bias across pregnancy stages.

The equation wobbled with age. It overestimated in the late second trimester by about six days on average. It underestimated near term. Its error bands everywhere spanned weeks, too wide for decisions that hinge on days. The authors conclude this shortcut, as published, is not accurate enough to replace better dating methods where prematurity care depends on the answer.
plos-pone-0356470:
Jing Yu and four colleagues build and validate a questionnaire measuring what Chinese clinical nurses know, feel, and do about caring for older patients' feet, in this 2026 study. Foot problems in the elderly are common and consequential, yet no tailored instrument existed for nurses. The team drafted items from the literature and nurse interviews, refined them through two rounds of expert consultation, then surveyed more than three hundred nurses at two large hospitals.

The finished tool holds forty-eight items across knowledge, attitude, and practice sections. Statistical testing showed a clean structure, strong agreement among experts on the items' relevance, and high reliability, including when nurses retook it later. The authors offer the questionnaire to nurse educators and managers who need to find specific gaps in geriatric foot care and target training accordingly.
plos-pone-0356770:
Wenyi Qin and colleagues sequenced the gut microbes of twenty papillary thyroid cancer patients. Samples came just before and three days after their thyroid surgery. The microbial census was paired with thyroid hormone levels. Their 2026 paired study used full metagenomic sequencing. It compared diversity and composition across the operation. It also hunted for microbe and hormone correlations.

Surgery clearly reshuffled the gut. Diversity and composition shifted significantly. A Clostridium species stood prominent beforehand. Several Bacteroides species, among others, rose after. The authors frame the gut and thyroid as an axis. Removing the gland and starting hormone treatment changes the terrain microbes live in. Microbes in turn may shape how patients absorb and respond to hormone therapy. Targeting the gut could become part of aftercare.
plos-pone-0356870:
Bing Yang, Jiaying He, and Yuncheng Shen designed a pavement crack mapping network small enough to run on a phone. It still had to be accurate enough for road maintenance crews. Their 2026 paper rebuilds the classic U-Net design with three additions. A feature module exploits skip connections. A multibranch module reads cracks at several scales at once. An aggregation module weights features adaptively before the final outline is drawn.

Across four public crack datasets, the model posted the best overlap scores among rivals. It used a tiny fraction of their computing power. It traded a little recall for precision on some sets, missing faint cracks rather than inventing them. The authors released code and data, aiming at real-time inspection from ordinary mobile devices.
plos-pone-0357070:
The PLOS One Editors issued this Expression of Concern in 2026. It concerns an earlier study of a possible heart treatment. That study tested intravenous injections of extracellular vesicles. These are tiny parcels shed by cells. The target was chronically under-supplied heart muscle. An Expression of Concern is a formal warning. It says questions hang over a published article while the record is sorted out, short of a full retraction.

Editors flagged two figure panels that look alike. They flagged supporting images that do not match the published figures. They also flagged missing details about animal welfare approvals and humane endpoints. The corresponding author acknowledged one panel was wrong and supplied a correction. The approval code, the authors said, is no longer available. Readers should treat the original study's findings as unverified until the journal resolves the case.
plos-pone-0357270:
Mehdi Nourzadeh Hadad and Mojtaba Kordrostami test whether zapping a soil booster with gamma rays makes tomatoes grow better, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Humic acid, a dark organic extract, is widely sold as a plant stimulant, but its structure varies and so do results. The team irradiated the acid at two doses, applied each at two field rates alongside untreated controls, and measured growth, leaf chemistry, antioxidant status, yield, and fruit quality across the season.

One combination stood out on almost every measure: acid irradiated at the moderate dose and applied at the higher rate. Those plants grew tallest, photosynthesized fastest, carried the richest leaf nutrients, and produced the most marketable fruit, with better sugars, vitamin C, and lycopene. Raising the application rate helped unless the acid had taken the stronger radiation dose, which erased the gain. The study gives growers a specific recipe rather than a vague endorsement.
plos-pone-0357370:
William H Livingston, Adam L Putnam, and Erin J Wamsley used the night of the 2024 United States presidential election to study how dreams shape feelings. Older ideas held that dreaming about an upsetting event softens its sting by morning. Nearly a thousand American adults rated their feelings on election day and again the next day, and reported what they had dreamed during the night between.

Dreaming about the election did not soothe anyone in this sample. Instead, those who dreamed of it woke with stronger negative feelings and a darker view of their own future and the country's. The pattern appeared among Democrats and independents but not Republicans. Livingston and colleagues say dreams may amplify fresh emotion at first, at least after a charged public event.
plos-pone-0357470:
Dung Ngoc Nguyen and coauthors published a 2026 systematic review in PLOS ONE on how the Big Five traits shape emotional reactivity. That covers how strongly people respond, how sharply they react, and how long feelings last. Earlier research fixated on neuroticism, leaving the other traits half-mapped. The review gathered thirty records covering thirty-one studies and fifty samples published across a quarter-century, and combined the findings study by study.

Neuroticism showed the most steadily troubled profile: stronger negative affect, sharper sensitivity to stressors, and slower recovery. Extraversion and conscientiousness leaned adaptive, above all in richer positive feeling. Openness looked mixed, with sharper responses and a split between reported feelings and bodily readings. Agreeableness appeared broadly prosocial, though its negative reactions depended on context. Clinicians and researchers should read feeling profiles trait by trait, they say, rather than treating reactivity as one score.
plos-pone-0357570:
Sogand Sarmadi leads a team of seven examining why emergency nurses in Tehran think about quitting, in PLOS ONE in 2026. One hundred eighty nurses at university hospitals answered validated scales covering quality of professional life, sleep, job stress, and intention to leave, during 2025. Emergency work piles psychological demand onto broken sleep, and managers need to know which strain actually pushes nurses out the door.

Intention to leave rose alongside poor sleep, higher stress, burnout, and secondary traumatic stress, the wear of absorbing patients' suffering. It fell as compassion satisfaction, the reward nurses feel from helping, rose. Statistical modeling confirmed those forces as predictors, joined by financial status, patient load per nurse, and shift type. The authors argue retention plans should protect the satisfying side of the job and fix rosters and ratios, not merely counsel nurses to endure more.
plos-pone-0357670:
Kyungsup Kwon and coauthors published a 2026 cohort study in PLOS ONE following Long COVID patients for a year with a standardized symptom score. Long COVID lacks agreed measurement, making its course hard to describe. Adults with confirmed infection answered symptom questionnaires across twelve domains at one, three, six, and twelve months, with Long COVID defined by a score at or above the proposed threshold.

Just over a quarter of the nearly two hundred participants met the definition at some point. The share above threshold drifted down across the year, but not significantly, and within individuals scores barely moved: those with Long COVID stayed high, others stayed low. People drifting across the category line mostly hovered near it. The burden, they conclude, is more stable than headlines suggest, though missed follow-up questionnaires limit what the trend can prove.
plos-pone-0357770:
Guogang Wang, Hongwei Sun, and Zichao Feng improved robot navigation in messy settings, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Mobile robots need routes through complex environments where obstacles move and spaces are tight. The team fused two planning approaches: an improved global planner based on BI-RRT, and an enhanced local method called DWA that handles immediate dodging.

Wang's hybrid plans routes across the whole space yet reacts locally to surprises, combining the strengths of both worlds. Global planning alone is too slow to dodge a walking person; local dodging alone can trap a robot in dead ends. Warehouse, hospital, and delivery robots all face this split problem daily. The fusion approach offers a practical design others can adapt.
plos-pone-0357970:
Tianyu Zhang and colleagues published a 2026 computational study in PLOS ONE on PFOA, a persistent industrial pollutant nicknamed a forever chemical. The study examines its possible role in fatty liver disease tied to metabolic dysfunction. The team combined toxicology databases, liver gene datasets, and single-cell data, then ran a machine learning search for genes where the chemical's targets and the disease's genes overlap.

Seventeen shared targets emerged, and the learning models narrowed them to six hub genes that classified the disease with very high accuracy in the data. Single-cell analysis showed those genes switching on in distinct liver cell types. Simulations suggested PFOA binds stably to two of the gene products, and in dish-grown liver cells dosed to mimic the disease, PFOA exposure did shift the hub genes' activity. A mechanism through disturbed fat handling and inflammation is proposed, needing animal and human confirmation.
plos-pone-0358070:
Sean Hartmann led a team of eight authors applying explainable AI to MRI scanning, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. MRI scans are slow and costly, and backlogs delay diagnosis. Instead of a black-box model, the team used rule-learning AI whose advice technicians can read and judge.

Hartmann's approach mined the scanning process for steps that can be trimmed without losing image quality. Readable rules matter in medicine, where staff must defend each change to a clinical workflow. Faster scans mean more patients served on the same machines. The study shows a path where AI improves a hospital process while staying open to human checking, a pattern many clinical settings will demand.
plos-pone-0358570: Lam and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on genes and type 2 diabetes in Vietnam. They looked at two known gene variants, one in IL16 and one in IL1B, both tied to inflammation. The study group was the Kinh, the largest ethnic group in Vietnam. Gene risk can differ between populations, so local data help doctors judge what a variant means for Vietnamese patients.

Guest's notes and illustrations enriched her edition.

The Four Branches and the native tales preserve a Welsh storytelling world of magic, honor, and shape-shifting, committed to parchment in the Middle Ages from older oral stock. Guest's translation became the founding presentation of Welsh literature in English and a cornerstone of Celtic myth studies. Modern versions exist, but hers made the field.
tob-10070:
Evelyn Underhill addressed Practical Mysticism, by its subtitle, to normal people rather than scholars or monks. Her claim is plain: mystical awareness is not a rare gift for saints. It is a capacity ordinary readers can practice, starting with truly paying attention to the world around them.

Short chapters use art, nature, and everyday moments to show what contemplation looks like in a working life. Underhill strips away technical language and treats attention, love, and self-forgetting as learnable habits. Readers who suspect mysticism belongs only in monasteries are her target audience, and she writes as a calm, plainspoken guide for them.
tob-13570:
Abraham Ortelius, a Flemish mapmaker, published the Theatrum Orbis Terrarum at Antwerp in 1570. Its name means Theatre of the World. He gathered the best maps of his day, cut to one size and bound as a single book.

Seventy maps show the whole known world and its regions, built from the work of many mapmakers whom Ortelius credits. Merchants, rulers, and scholars could now see the earth in one ordered set of pictures. Historians call it the first modern atlas, and it taught Europe what the world looked like for generations.
tob-4170:
Thomas Bulfinch retold the legends of chivalry for American readers in The Age of Chivalry, the medieval volume of Bulfinch's Mythology. King Arthur and the Round Table, the quest for the Holy Grail, Lancelot and Guenevere, and Charlemagne with his paladins fill its pages. Bulfinch drew on Malory and the romances, smoothing them for family reading.

Victorian storytelling at its most earnest, the volume aimed to let readers enjoy poetry and romance whose allusions filled English literature. Generations of Americans met the knights first through Bulfinch, before facing the older texts themselves. As an introduction that assumes no Latin and no prior knowledge, it did its work superbly and remains in print.
tob-4270:
Volume thirty-nine of the Sacred Books of the East, part one, presents Legge's Texts of Taoism in a further copy of the 1891 translation. Lao Tzu's Tao Te Ching opens the volume: eighty-one short chapters on the Way that can be spoken and the power of doing nothing by force.

Chuang Tzu follows, with parables of useless trees, happy fish, and a man who dreamed he was a butterfly. Legge's introductions and notes frame both for Western readers with care and respect. Verified from the 1919 edition, the volume opened the Taoist canon to the English-speaking world and still serves as its classic gate.
un-ga-res-2070:
Gibraltar, the small British-held port at the mouth of the Mediterranean Sea, is the subject of Resolution 2070, passed by the UN General Assembly in 1964. The Assembly had read the reports of its decolonization team and heard the case in committee debate.

Spain and the United Kingdom are invited to open talks at once, as the team's agreed text of 16 October 1964 had urged. Both states must then report the outcome to the team and to the Assembly at its next session. The short text opened a dispute over Gibraltar that the UN is still seized of today.
un-ga-res-a-69-70: Three regional hubs for peace and disarmament work get a nod in Resolution A/69/70, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The hubs serve Africa, Asia and the Pacific, and Latin America and the Caribbean. The text also recalls the UN Disarmament Information Programme. Set up in 1982, it teaches the public about arms control and builds support for the UN's aims in that field.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: General Assembly Resolution 2070 (XX), from the twentieth session in 1965, concerned Gibraltar. The Assembly studied the decolonization committee's reports on the territory and heard debate. It then invited the governments of Spain and the United Kingdom to begin talks without delay. The talks were those foreseen in the committee's agreed statement of 16 October 1964. The two governments were to report the outcome to the committee and the Assembly at the next session.

Resolution 69/70 of the General Assembly, adopted at the sixty-ninth session in 2014, deals with the three United Nations regional centres for peace and disarmament. They serve Africa, Asia and the Pacific, and Latin America and the Caribbean. It stresses maintaining and revitalizing the centres. It appeals to states and other donors for the voluntary contributions they depend on. It asks the Secretary-General to keep supporting them within existing resources.
un-sc-res-1270:
The question of Sierra Leone came to a vote in Resolution 1270, adopted on 22 October 1999. The Lomé Peace Agreement of July 1999 had ended the fighting on paper. Rebels had lately seized hostages, including children and United Nations staff. Aid could not reach parts of the country at all.

The Council sets up the United Nations Mission in Sierra Leone, UNAMSIL, for six months. Up to 6,000 troops, including 260 observers, will help carry out the peace deal. The mission will aid disarmament of some 45,000 fighters and watch the cease-fire. Under Chapter VII it may protect civilians facing direct attack. The older observer mission ends at once, and reports are due every 45 days.
un-sc-res-1370: Bearing number 1370, this resolution of the Security Council is dated 2000 in the catalog. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-1470:
UNAMSIL was extended as Liberia's war pressed on Sierra Leone on 28 March 2003. The Secretary-General's report of 17 March described fresh strains on security. Fighting in Liberia spilled refugees across the Mano River region. Sierra Leone's own police and army still lacked the means to hold the country alone. The Special Court and the truth commission carried the work on impunity and reconciliation.

The Council extended UNAMSIL's mandate for six months from 30 March 2003. Troop and police contributors won its thanks. The mission's progress in reshaping its size and deployment was praised. UNAMSIL was urged, as Sierra Leone's own forces grew able, to plan its drawdown in step with the threat. The Secretary-General owed detailed plans for the rest of the drawdown once its third phase was running. The funding gap in the disarmament trust fund caused concern. Building Freetown's administrative reach stayed the Council's core demand.
un-sc-res-1570: Resolution 1570, a 2004 act of the Security Council, survives here as a Wikisource transcription of the UN's record. The Council speaks for world peace and security, and a resolution is its strongest written instrument. This entry keeps the instrument intact: preamble, numbered decisions, and the reporting duties that usually close such a text.
un-sc-res-1670:
One month of grace was all the Council granted UNMEE on 13 April 2006. Eritrea's tight limits on the mission had cut its working capacity sharply. Both parties had agreed to accept the Boundary Commission's rulings as final and binding, yet the border stayed unmarked. The witnesses to the Algiers Agreements had met in New York in February.

The Council extended UNMEE's mandate for a single month. It demanded that both parties comply fully with resolution 1640 (2005). That text required Eritrea to lift its restrictions on the mission and Ethiopia to accept the border ruling. Member states were called to keep supporting UNMEE and the peace process with funds. The Council said plainly that if it found the parties had not complied within the month, it would review the mission's future, its shape, and its mandate. The short leash showed how close the mission had come to collapse.
un-sc-res-1770:
Iraq's UN mission gained a wider job under Resolution 1770, adopted in 2007. The mission, UNAMI, had advised Iraq since 2003, but violence and political deadlock were deepening. The Council expanded what its staff could do across the country.

The text asks UNAMI to push talks among Iraq's rival groups, support elections and a review of the constitution, and help refugees return home. It also covers aid coordination and human rights reporting. For readers, the resolution maps the civilian side of the Iraq effort, run beside a war fought by others. Readers can see the mission's full task list set out in one place.
un-sc-res-1870:
Voting on 30 April 2009, the Council adopted Resolution 1870 on Sudan. The 2005 peace deal that ended the long north-south war was entering its final stretch. National elections were due in 2010, and a southern referendum in 2011. The disputed Abyei area still lacked a funded administration, which fed local tension.

The Council extends the United Nations Mission in the Sudan, called UNMIS, until 30 April 2010. The mission should back credible elections with the United Nations Development Programme. It should also get ready to help with the 2011 referendum if asked. More staff should go to Abyei to calm clashes and guard civilians. Both parties must honor the Abyei ruling and the peace deal in full.
un-sc-res-270:
Villages in southern Lebanon came under Israeli air attack in August 1969. On 26 August 1969 the Security Council condemned the raid. Lebanon and Israel had both addressed the Council. The members voiced grief at the loss of civilian life and property. They also recalled the Council's earlier warning after the Beirut airport raid.

The resolution deplores all breaches of the ceasefire. It deplores the spread of the fighting to new areas. It declares that military reprisals of this kind cannot be tolerated. If they went on, the Council said, it would weigh stronger steps under the Charter. The aim was to stop the raids from starting again.
un-sc-res-370:
Cyprus's peacekeeping force was renewed during the Vienna talks on 13 June 1975. The Secretary-General's report of 9 June held that the force was still needed to keep the cease-fire. Talks between the two communities had opened in Vienna under resolution 367 (1975). He urged that the talks be kept up and quickened. Both parties had agreed to six more months of the force.

The Council restated resolution 186 (1964), which created the force, and its backing of the General Assembly's settlement terms. The parties were urged to act with the utmost restraint. They had to press on with determined, cooperative efforts toward the Council's goals. The stationing of the force was extended for six months, to 15 December 1975. All parties were again asked to give the force their full cooperation. The Secretary-General would continue his good offices mission and keep the Council informed of the talks' progress.
un-sc-res-570: This library holds Resolution 570 as an official Council record, dated 1985 in its catalog. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-670:
Iraq's sanctions net was closed over the skies on 25 September 1990. Baghdad still held Kuwait and claimed to annex it. Foreign nationals were kept against their will, and Kuwaitis faced forced removal and abuse. States reported steady attempts to evade the trade embargo of resolution 661 (1990).

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council confirmed that the embargo covered all transport, aircraft included. Every state had to bar aircraft from taking off if they carried cargo for Iraq or Kuwait beyond medical supplies and food in humanitarian need. Planes bound for Iraq had to land for inspection as directed. Flights between a state's territory and Iraq or Kuwait had to be reported to the sanctions committee. Iraqi ships used in breach of the embargo were to be detained in port. Iraq's Decree No. 377 and all acts against the Council's resolutions were declared null and void.
un-sc-res-70: Help from one UN body to another is arranged in Security Council Resolution 70, passed on 7 March 1949. Article 83 of the Charter lets the Council draw on the Trusteeship Council for its work in strategic trust areas. The Council now asks that body, where trust deals allow and where safety lets, to do the tasks of Articles 87 and 88 for such areas on the Council's behalf. Those tasks cover the study of reports and the hearing of pleas from the lands.
un-sc-res-870: Entry number 870 in the Council's official sequence is a resolution the catalog dates to 1993. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-970:
Sanctions relief for the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was extended by the Security Council on 12 January 1995. Belgrade had sealed its border with Bosnia and Herzegovina against all goods except food, medicine, and clothing for basic humanitarian needs. Monitors of the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia watched the closure. The Council said keeping that border shut was a condition of the relief.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council suspended the restrictions named in resolution 943 (1994) for a further one hundred days. The rules guarding the Bosnian protected areas stayed in force. Every thirty days the Secretary-General had to report whether the conference co-chairmen certified that the border stayed effectively closed. If he reported a failure, the suspension would end within days. The Council kept the question under close review, ready to take further steps on the measures against Belgrade.
un-sc-res-un-security-council-meeting-82:
Eastern Ukraine is the subject of the Security Council's 8270th meeting, held in 2018 and preserved in this official record. The Council had not taken up the conflict for fifteen months. Briefers told members the war in the Donbass was still alive, with tens of thousands of ceasefire breaches recorded that year and about 1.6 million people driven from their homes.

Senior officials from the United Nations and the OSCE, the European security body that monitored the front line, gave the briefings. Member states then stated their positions on the fighting and on the stalled Minsk peace deals. The record shows a Council divided over blame and next steps.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Sierra Leone gets a full UN peacekeeping mission in Resolution 1270, adopted on 22 October 1999. The Lomé Peace Agreement of 7 July 1999 had ended the civil war on paper, and rebel leaders had returned to Freetown. Disarmament of ex-combatants was being prepared. Hostage-taking of UN and ECOMOG personnel by rebel groups had drawn condemnation.

The Council establishes the United Nations Mission in Sierra Leone, UNAMSIL, at once for six months, with up to 6,000 military personnel including 260 observers. UNAMSIL takes over from the observer mission UNOMSIL and must help carry out the peace agreement and the disarmament plan, deploy at disarmament centres, watch the ceasefire, and support elections. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorizes UNAMSIL to protect its own freedom of movement and, within its means, civilians under imminent threat of violence. It calls on all armed groups to disband and surrender their weapons without delay.

Sierra Leone's peace process was moving forward when this text passed on 18 September 2001, and UNAMSIL, the United Nations mission backing it, is renewed. The mission's mandate is extended for six months from 30 September 2001. Fighting in nearby Liberia and the wider Mano River region still kept life fragile for civilians and refugees.

The Council praised the mission's role in advancing peace and asked for regular reports on how its operations were working. It backed steps toward state authority across the country, open elections, and turning the Revolutionary United Front into a political party. Helping refugees and displaced people return home, where the mission was deployed, also remained part of its work.

Sierra Leone's uneasy peace is the concern of Resolution 1470, adopted on 28 March 2003. The UN Mission in Sierra Leone, UNAMSIL, was helping the government hold the country together. War in nearby Liberia threatened the Mano River region, refugees were many, and Sierra Leone's own police and army were not yet strong enough to keep order alone.

The Council extends UNAMSIL for six months from 30 March 2003 and backs its phased drawdown plan. It urges faster work to restore state authority, above all in the diamond fields, and better control of diamond mining. It voices worry about the funding gap for settling ex-fighters back into civilian life. It also backs the Special Court and the new Truth and Reconciliation Commission, and demands an end to illegal crossings from Liberia.

Western Sahara's referendum mission, MINURSO, is extended until 30 April 2005 in this text of 28 October 2004. The dispute remained at an impasse. The aim of a just, lasting, and mutually acceptable political solution that provides for the self-determination of the people of Western Sahara is repeated.

Alongside the extension, a mid-term report is asked for within three months on how the situation is evolving. That report is also to address the mission's size and way of working, including options for cutting staff. Member states are called on to fund confidence-building measures, such as family visits, that increase contact between people divided by the long conflict.

Resolution 1670, adopted on 13 April 2006, warns Ethiopia and Eritrea that their peace is fraying. Eritrea had banned UN helicopter flights in October 2005 and tightened restrictions on the UN mission, UNMEE, which the Council said gravely hampered the mission's work and staff safety. Ethiopia, for its part, had still not accepted the boundary commission's ruling in full.

The Council kept UNMEE in place and demanded that both parties let it move freely throughout its area of operations. It stressed that lasting peace required full marking of the border on the ground, which could not happen while the mission was hobbled. Both governments were reminded that they had agreed to accept the commission's decision as final and binding.

Some lists call this a Sierra Leone text. It is not. The land in question lay in East Africa. It had been run by Britain for the UN since the war. On 9 December 1961 it became free, led by Julius Nyerere. Resolution 170 passed five days later, with no votes against.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit Tanganyika. The Assembly did so the same day. Three years on, the state merged with Zanzibar. The union took the name Tanzania. It kept the same UN seat. Under Nyerere, the capital became a haven for groups fighting to free the rest of southern Africa from white rule.

Iraq's assistance mission, UNAMI, is extended and widened for twelve months on 10 August 2007. Iraq now had an elected, constitutional government, yet sectarian violence threatened its unity. All communities, it is underscored, need to join an inclusive political dialogue and national reconciliation.

The renewed mandate gives the mission a more active role. As conditions permit, its head is to advise and support Iraq on political talks, elections, constitutional review, and settling internal boundary disputes, and to promote regional dialogue. The mission would also back aid delivery, refugee returns, and human rights work. Member states are called on to keep funding and staffing the mission's expanded tasks.

Sudan's mission is extended as the peace deal nears its decisive tests in Resolution 1870, adopted on 30 April 2009. The Comprehensive Peace Agreement had reached a critical stage. The Abyei Interim Administration was unfunded, census results were delayed, national elections were planned for February 2010, and the 2011 referendum was approaching.

The Council extends the United Nations Mission in Sudan, UNMIS, until 30 April 2010. It welcomes the parties' agreement to send the Abyei boundary dispute to arbitration at the Permanent Court of Arbitration. It calls on them to implement the ruling and fund the interim administration. UNMIS must support the National Elections Commission toward February 2010 elections and prepare to assist the 2011 referendum if asked. It must protect civilians under imminent threat, including from the Lord's Resistance Army, and help demarcate the 1956 north-south border. The Secretary-General must develop benchmarks for measuring the mission's progress.

Villages in south Lebanon bombed from the air brought this Council rebuke of 1969. On 26 August, it adopted Resolution 270. Lebanon had laid the attack before the Council in a letter. The text voices grief at the loss of civilian life and goods. It recalls the 1949 armistice deal between the two states.

The Council condemns the planned air attack by Israel. It deplores all violent breaches of the ceasefire. It also deplores the spread of the fighting zone. Reprisal raids and grave truce breaches cannot be stood for, it declares. If such acts recur, the Council warns, it will weigh stronger steps under the Charter.

Resolution 370, adopted on 13 June 1975 by fourteen votes to none, keeps the Cyprus force for six more months of uneasy calm. The Secretary-General's June report said the force was still needed to hold the ceasefire and help the search for a settlement. He also reported on Vienna talks between the two communities' representatives, judging that negotiations should continue and speed up, and that success would demand flexibility and reciprocal gestures from everyone.

UNFICYP's stationing was extended for a further six months, as Cyprus's government agreed was necessary. The long line of Cyprus resolutions since 1964 was reaffirmed. The extension came less than a year after the coup and invasion that had split the island in two.

A judge of the International Court of Justice resigned in the summer of 1985, leaving a seat to fill. Judge Platon D. Morozov, named in the text, had resigned on 23 August 1985. The rest of his term still had to be served by someone. Resolution 570 was adopted unanimously on 12 September 1985.

Under Article 14 of the Court's Statute, the Security Council fixes the date of the election for such a vacancy. The Council set the election for 9 December 1985. It would be held at a meeting of the Security Council. A meeting of the General Assembly, during its fortieth session, would vote on the same day. The step is a short, routine one. It keeps the Court, the main court of the United Nations, at full strength.

Resolution 670, adopted on 25 September 1990 by fourteen votes to one, with Cuba against, closes the skies in the sanctions on Iraq. Iraq still occupied Kuwait, refused to free detained foreigners, and was mistreating Kuwaitis, the Council charged. States reported persistent attempts to evade the trade embargo imposed in August, and several had already cut down Iraq's diplomatic presence.

To seal the leaks, the Council confirmed that the embargo covered all means of transport, aircraft included. States were called on to stop cargo flights to and from Iraq and occupied Kuwait, except approved humanitarian shipments, and to detain Iraqi aircraft that violated the rules. It also warned that Iraqi decrees defying the Council's decisions were null and void.

Strategic trust territories were the Council's own responsibility in 1949, but another United Nations body could help with the work. Under Article 83 of the Charter, the Council keeps control of security questions in those areas. For other matters, it may use the help of the Trusteeship Council. Resolution 70 was adopted on 7 March 1949.

The Council asked the Trusteeship Council to carry out part of the work on its behalf. The Trusteeship Council would examine the reports and petitions that came in for the strategic areas. It would send the Security Council its findings and advice. Political, economic, social, and educational matters were all covered. Its questionnaires and reports were to be shared with the Council in advance. The arrangement let the Council keep its legal control while drawing on the other body's daily experience with trust territories.

Four extra days for the United Nations force in the former Yugoslavia came on 1 October 1993. The force, called UNPROFOR, worked in Croatia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Resolution 870 repeats the Council's determination to keep the force safe and free to move for all its missions. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extended UNPROFOR's mandate for a short added period ending on 5 October 1993. It also decided to remain actively seized of the matter. The tiny extension was a bridge while the Council argued over its future.

Resolution 970, adopted on 12 January 1995 by fourteen votes to none with Russia abstaining, rewards Belgrade for sealing a border. Belgrade's authorities had shut their frontier with Bosnia to all goods except food, medicine, and clothing for essential humanitarian needs. Monitors from the international conference on the former Yugoslavia had verified the closure, which an earlier resolution made the price of relief.

Because that condition was met, the Council extended the partial suspension of sanctions against Serbia and Montenegro for a further fixed period. It stressed that the closure had to stay effective, urged prosecution of violators, and praised the monitors' work. Sanctions relief, the structure implies, lasts only as long as cooperation does.
verne-twenty-thousand-leagues-1870:
Jules Verne published Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas in 1870, a novel of travel beneath the oceans. Professor Aronnax joins a hunt for a sea monster that has attacked ships. He and his companions end up aboard the Nautilus, a submarine run by Captain Nemo. Nemo refuses to let them leave.

The voyage crosses every ocean and reaches the South Pole under the ice. Readers meet giant squid, lost cities, and vast schools of fish. Nemo aids oppressed peoples yet sinks ships without mercy. The book mixes science, wonder, and moral doubt. It helped create modern science fiction as a popular form.
villars-comte-de-gabalis-1670:
The Abbé de Villars published Le Comte de Gabalis at Paris in 1670, the original French text of the famous dialogues. A German count instructs a young abbé in the secret sciences across five conversations. The book fixed the Rosicrucian image in French letters and bridges the manifestos and the French occult revival of the next century.

Sylphs, gnomes, undines, and salamanders people the elements in the count's teaching. The wit sparkles; Villars seems to laugh while he reveals. Church authority banned the book, which only spread it further. French readers took its elementals into their permanent imagination. The 1670 Gabalis is the source from which the English Count of 1680 and all later elemental lore descend.
wallace-contributions-natural-selection-:
Alfred Russel Wallace reached the theory of natural selection on his own, in the Malay Archipelago. He gathered his key essays in Contributions to the Theory of Natural Selection in 1870. Wallace was Darwin's co-discoverer and loyal ally. The collection is a founding document of evolutionary anthropology.

The essays cover mimicry, protective color, island life, and the limits of selection. In the closing essay he breaks with Darwin: natural selection, he argues, cannot explain the human mind, which needed some higher power. Darwin was dismayed; the essay fed debate for decades. The volume shows Wallace thinking for himself inside the theory he helped to found.
